CHAPTER V 
MISCELLANEOUS 


16. Contracts.—(1) The Board may, in connection with its trading 
activities, enter into contracts provided that provision therefor exists in 
the sanctioned budget. 


(2) The ای سا‎ delegate to the Chairman such powers for entering 
into contracts on its behalf as if may think fit. 


(3) The contracts shall not be binding on the Board unless they are 
executed by the Chairman and the seal of the Board affixed thereto. 


(4) The Chairman or the Secretary or any member of the Board shall 
not be liable for any assurance or contract made by the Board; and 
liability arising out of such assurance or contract shall be discharged from 
the moneys at the disposal of the Board. 


17. Power to make grants.—(1) The Board shall disburse grants in 
accordance with and at rates and on terms sanctioned by the State Govern- 
ment in respect of each industry, from time to time. ‘I'he State Guvern- 
ment may, on its motion or on the recommendation of the Board or of the 
Khadi and Village [ndustries Commission, modify or supersede the financial 
rates and terms previously sanctioned. 


(2) The Board may reduce the rates at which grants are payable in 
individual cases to such extent, as it thinks necessary, but shall not enhance 
such rates except with the prior approval of the State Government. 


(3) Grants shall be paid to institutions registered under the Societies 
Registration Act, 1860 (XXI of 1860), or under the Bengal Co-operative 
Societies Act, 1940 (Ben. Act XXI of 1940), or a Public Trust. 


18. Power to advance loans.—The Board shall advence loans in 
accordance with and at rates and on terms sanctioned by the State Govern- 
ment in respect of each industry frum time to time. 


19. Power to borrow.—The Bourd may, with the previous sanction of 
the State Government, borrow on the security of its funds or assets. 


20). Power to write off losses.—(1) The Hoard may write off losses up to 
Rs. 1,000 per annum in the following cases سے ؛‎ 


(x) loss of irrecoverable value of stores or of public money due to theft, 
fraud or the negligence of individuals or other cases; 


(b) loss of irrecoverable advance other than loans; and 


(c) deficiency und depreciation in the valuo of stores aubject to the 
conditions— 


(i) that the loss does not disclose a defect of system, the amendment 
of which requires the orders of the Stute Government; and 


(ii) that there has not been any serious negligence on the part of 
individual employee or employees of the Hoard which might 
possibly call for disciplinary action requiring the orders of the 
State سا‎ 


(2) The Board shall take suitable action against the persons responsible 
for the loss and send a report to Government on the action taken. 


Keception.—Nothing contained in this rule shall apply to losses 
orcasioned by irrecoverable loans. Sanction of the State Government shall 
be obtained before such Josses are written off, 


21. Custody of common seal.—The common seal of the Board shall 
remain in the custody of the Executive Officer of the Board,

Government of West Bengal, Labour Depart- . 


rent, by its order No. 2260-I.R. /1R/41L-26/58, 
dated 3rd June 1958, referred an industrial dispute 
between Messrs. A. R. and B. Kalwar Oo., 11 
Nidhiram Maji Lane, P.O. Khurut, Howrah, and 
their workmen represented by Bus Workers’ Union, 
to the Second Labour Court for adjudication —re- 
garding the issue mentioned in the order of refer- 
ence, 
issue 


(1) Whether the «discharge of the following 
workmen is justified? To what relief are 
they entitled ? 


(a) Sri Birendra Nath Ghosh. 
(b) Sri Abhinandan Jha. 


Findings 


The case of the Union, briefly stated, is as 


follows :— 


Measra. A. R. and B. Kalwar 00. are owners of 
7 buses plying in Route Numbers 52 and 58 in 
Howrah. The workmen Of the buses plying in 
thore rontes organised themselves undet a ۲٢۸| 
for tho redress of their grievances. The formation 
bf the Wnion was not taken in good grace by the 
abbve Company. Shri Birendra Nath Ghose is the 
Secretary of the Union and Shri Abhinandan Jha is 
one of the active worketa of the Union. They 
were سوہ یھ‎ of the ahovo Company. The Com- 
pany discharged Shri Birendra Nath Ghose from 
19th January 1958 and Shri Abhinandan Jha from 
éad January 1958 without showing any reason. So 


Juatified., 


The Company has raised a preliminary objection 


that the Union which has espoused the case of the‏ ے 


two discharged workmen is not a true representa- 
tive of the workmen of the Company, that the 
other workmen of the Company have nothing td do 
with the present dispute and that os such this is 
not an مآ‎ dispute. As to the merits of the 
case, the Company states as follows: 


Sometime in November 1957 two Punjabi em- 
ployees of the Company went on leave. After 
expiry of their leave they came to join thoir duties 
in January ۱908. Shri Birendra Nath Ghosh was 
one of the conductors working under the Company, 
He represented to the management that Punjahis 
should not he allowed to work under this Company, 
The management did not agree to such a proposal, 
In the morning of 18th January 1958 Shri Birendra 
Nath (those lay down in front of bus No. WBU 32 
belonging to the Company in which the above two 
Punjabi employees were engaged and therehy pre- 
vented the bus from starting from Ramrajatola bus 
stand at the scheduled time. On that day after 
finishing his duty Shri Birendra Nath Ghose came 
to the office of the Company at about 10 p.m. to 
deposit the day's collection. One of: the proprie- 
tors of the Company asked his explanation for his 
conduct in the morning. At this Shri Birendra 

ath (those became angry and said that he would 
not give any explanation. Then the ahove proprie- 
tor asked him to be polite. Then Shri Ghose became 
more angry, abused the proprietor and tried to 
assault him with his shoe. Some persons present 
at the office prevented the assault. Then the above 
proprietor verbally dismissed Shri Ghose on the 

round of this gross misconduct. Shri Amarjit 
Singh, a conductor under the Company. was on 
lenve from the latter part of November 1957 to the 
early part of January 1958. Shri Abhinandan Jha 
was taken as a substitute in the leave vacancy of 
Shri Amarjit Singh. Shri Amarjit Singh returned 
rom leave and joined his post, and so the services 
of Shri Abhinandan Jha were automatically termi- 
hated. So the Company contends that the termi- 
nation of service of the above two workmen was 
justified, The Company denies that it discharged 
them on account of their trade union activities, 


Decision 


The Company has not adduced any evidence in 
support of the preliminary objection raised hy it. 
The lawyer of the Company haa depended on tha 
evidence of some of the witnesses of the Union for 
his argument that this is not an industrial diapute. 
Two of the witnesses on behalf of the Union have 
admitted that the Union of which they are now 
members is Howrah Zilla Bua Karmi Parisad, 
whereas the Union named in the order of reference 
is Bus Workers’ Union. P.W. 1 Shri Birendra 
Nath Ghose has explained that he and other em- 
ployees of the Company were formerly memheus of 
Howrah Branch of Bus Workers’ Wnion and that 
later they formed Howrah Zilla Bus Karmi Puari- 
sal. So hia evidence does not show that the em- 

loyees of the Company were not members of the 
Hire Workers’ Union or are not members of Towrah 
Zilla Bus Karmi Parisad. It has been argued by 
the lawyer of the Company that the Bus Workors’ 
[2100 has no right to represent the workmen in 
question, as they are no longer members of that 


R654 
eS ee 


Union. But P.W. 1 says that Howrah Zilla Bus 
Karmi Parisad was formed in September or October 
1958. The order of reference is dated 3rd June 
1958. So at that time the employees of the Com- 
any were members of that Union. The Company 

as not been able to show that this part of the 
evidence of P.W. 1 is false. So I hold that the Bus 
Workers’ Uniqn which has espoused the cause of 
the two discharged workmen was a true represen- 
tative of the workmen at the relevant time, i.e., 
nt the time the dispute arose and at the time Gov- 
ernment made thie reference. It is alao on evidence 
that a substantial number of the employees of the 
Company were members of that Union at the rele- 
vant time. So I hold that there is no substance in 
the preliminary objection raised by the Company. 
Hence I reject it. 


The Union has examined four witnesses in sup- 
port of its 0186. Shri Birendra Nath (those, P.W. 1 
and Shri Nilkanta Das, P.W. 4, have stated the 
Union’s case in respect of Shri Birendra Nath 
Ghosh. They say that on 18th January 1958 one 
of the proprietors asked Shri Birendra Nath (those 
whether he had deposited the day’s collection and 
on the latter’s reply in the affirmative the former 
asked him not to go to duty from the following 
day. They deny that Shur ا‎ Nath (those 
abused the proprietor or tried to assault him. Shri 
Abhinandan Jha, P.W. 2, and Shri Amarjit Singh, 
P.W. 3, have stated the Union’s case in respect of 
Shri Abhinandan Jha. They say that they work- 
ed together for somgtime and that Shri Jha was 
not a substitute of Shri Amarjit Singh. 


The Company has examined three witnesses in 
support of its case. O.P.W. 1 Shri Bijalh 
Mukherjea who is a starter at Ramarajatola bus 
stand speaks of the incident in the morning of 18th 
January 1998. O.P.W. 2 Shri Bima) Kumar Dey 
nays that he had gone to the. office of the Company 
at about 10 p.m. on 18th January 1958 in order to 
use the telephone of that Company. 116 has spoken 
of the incident about the conduct of Shri Birendra 
Nath Ghose at that time. O.P.W. 3 Shri Kartick 
Chandra Kalwar says that he is the proprietor in 
question who was abused and threatened by Shri 
Birendra Nath Ghose. He has stated the Com- 
pany’s case. P.W. 4 Shri Nilkanta Das who has 
corrohorated Shri Rirendra Nath Ghose as to what 
took place at night on 18th January 1958, was a 
conductor working under the Company and has 
since heen dismissed. So he cannot be called a dis- 
interested witness. 0.۱۲۰۱۷۰. 2 Shri Bimal Kumar 
Dey who has spoken about the same incident, is ۸ 
disinterested witness. Though he is a chance wit- 
ness, 11 appears that he has spoken the truth. 
O.P.W. ۱ Shri Bijali Mukherjee has stated that 
Shri Birendra Nath Ghose obstructed the move- 
mont of the bus. Though he does not aay that Shri 
Birendra Nath Ghose lay down in front of the bus, 
his evidence is clear on the point that Shri Ghose 
atom) in front of the bus. Shri Ghose himself 
admits that he went to the Ramrajatola bus stand 
in the morning, though he had no duty in the 
morning of that day. So thia much is clear’ thit 
something happened at Ramrajatola bus stand in 
the morning of 18th January J958. The evidence 
of P.W. 1 Shri Birendra Nath Ghose and P.W. 4 
Shri Nilkanta Das that the proprietor discharged 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 4, 1960 


(Paat 1 


ts উপ 


Shri Birendra Nath Ghosh at night on 18th Janu, 
ary 1958 without uny provocation is unbelievable as 
being improbable. So I accept the version of the 
Company as to what took place then. Hence I hold 
that Shri Birendra Nath (101 has been guilty of 
gross misconduct and as such his discharge is 
Justified. So he is not entitled to any rolief. 


As to Shri Abhinandan Jha, the Company has 
not aduced any evidence except the oral testimony 
of O.P.W. 3 that Shri Jha worked as a substitute in 
place of Shri Amarjit Singh. The case of the Com- 
pany is that Shri Amarjit Singh went on leave in 
November 1957. OPW. 3 Shri Kartick Ch. 
Kalwar could not deny that Shri Abhinandan Jha 
worked under the Company prior to November 
1957. O.P.W. 3 says that Shri Amarjit Singh 
worked under the Company for training for about 
6 months before going on leave in November 1957. 
When Shri Amarjit Singh was on training before 
going on leave, there can be no question of appoint- 
ing a substitute in his pluce. On the other hand 
the evidence of Shri Ablinandan Jha and of Shri 
Amarjit Singh is that the latter worked as an 
assistant to the former in tho same bus for some- 
time. ‘This evidence fits in with the evidence of 
Q.P.W. 3 that Shri Amarjit Singh was under train- 
ing. So I hold that the contention of the Company 
that Shri Abhinandan Jha worked as a substitute 
in place of Shri Amarjit Singh is untenable. As 
the Company has not shown any other reason for 
the discharge of Shri Abhinandan Jha, I hold that 
his dischargo is unjustified. Hence I order that he 
be reinstated in the post of a conductor in which 
he was working. It appears from the evidence that 
he was employed elsewhere for a considerable 
period after being discharged by the above Com- 
pany. It also appears from evidence that he was a 
daily-rated worker under the Company. So I order 
that he be paid compensation equal to his wager 
for 150 daya. The above order shall take effect 
within a month of the publication of the award in 
the “‘Caloutta Gazette’’. 


Taken at my dictation and corrected by me.

6. The first objection taken hy Shri Mukherjee 
is that this reference ig not maintainable because 
the «dispute referred cannot be deemed to be an 
industrial dispute, the industry being a dead 
industry, and reliance is placed in this behalf on 
the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of 
Pipraich Sugar Mills Ltd. reported in 1957 (T) 
...۱ا‎ page 235. In the rth case the Supreme 
Court held that where the employer has closed his 
husiness and the closure is real and bong fide, any 
dispute arising with reference thereto would be out- 
side the purview of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
because the provisions of the said Act apply only 
to a dispute which arises out of an existing 
industry, the sine qua non of the dispute being 
that the right which is the subject-matter of the 
dispute must accrue while the industry was in 
existence. The same view was reiterated by the 
Supreme Court in the case of Barsi Light Railway 
Company Ttd., reported in 1967 (1) L.LJ., 
page 243, In these cases the dispute arose out of 
the claims of the workmen for retrenchment 
compensation under section 2017 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act aftor the business had been closed on 
transfer. The definition of retrenchment in section 
2(00) of the Industrial Disputes Act was also 
considered in these cases and it was held that 
retrenchment connotes in its ordinary acceptation 
that the business itself is being continued but that 
a portion of the labour foree is discharged as 
surplusage and that the definition, though very 
wide, did not cover termination of services of all 
the workmen on a bona fide closure of the whole 
business. 


7 The decision in Barsi’ Light Railway 
Company’s case was given on 27th November 1966 
and thereafter on 27th April 1957 the President 
promulgated صا‎ Ordinanee called the Industrial 
Disputes (Amendment) Ordinance, 1957, for 
amending the Industrial Disputes Act by which 
nection 251 F was amended and a new section 
26017۰171" was introduced into the Act and the amend- 
ment was given retrospective effect from Ist 
December 1956. The new section 25FFF provides: 


(1) Where an undertaking is closed down for 
anv reason whatsoever, every workman 
who has been in continuous service for not 
Jess than one year in that undertaking 
immediately before such closure shall, 
subject to the provisions of sub-seotion 
(2), be entitled to notice and compensation 
in accordance with the provisions of 
section 25F, as if the workman had been 
retrenched : 


Provided that where the undertaking 1s closed 
down on account of unavoidable circum- 
atances beyond the control of the employer, 
the total compensation to be paid to the 
workman shall not exceed his average pay 
for three months. 


Sub-section (2) of the section is not relevant for 
our purpose and so it is not quoted.

9, his amendment of the Industrial Disputes 
Act with the introduction of section 20FF EF which, 
in view of the retrospective effect given to it, is 
applicable to the present case,‘the closure having 
taken place on 3lst March 1957, has changed the 
law and affected the decisiona of the Supreme Court 
in the uhove cases. Since section 9211 FF provides 
that on the closure of an undertaking the work- 
men shall he entitled to notice and compensation 
in accordance with the provisions of section 25F, 
as if the workmen had been retrenched, it can no 
longer, be contended that the claim for such 
compensation on the closure of an undertaking is 
not an industrial dispute. It was, however, argued 
that since the definition of retrenchment in section 
2(00) of the Act had not been amended the decision 
of the Supreme Court that the ordinary accepted 
medning of ‘‘retrenchment” did not cover the 
discharge of all the employees of an undertaking 
on account of bona fide closure was still valid. 
This argument cannot be accepted because section 
95k EE lays down that on closure the workmen 
affected should be deemed to have been retrenched 
and this must be taken to have artificially 
axtended the definition of retrenchment to cover a 
case af closure also, This was also the view taken 
hy the Punjab [igh Court in the case of Maharaj 
Wenving Mills versus State of Punjab, reported in 
1958-T1-L.1..3., 625. It was held in this case that 
section 251 FF was obviously designed to bring a 
workman affected by closure of an undertaking 
within the definition of ‘retrenchment’ and that 
the artificial definition of the word ‘‘retrenchiment”’ 
had the effect of artificially prolonging the life of 
the undertaking or had the effect of making the 
muchinery provided under the Act available for 
working out the right to compensation of such 
workman. It was further held that though the 
amendment did not specifically না for 
reference of auch a dispute to a Tribunal as an 
industrial dispute, this was implicit in the amend- 
ment. The Kerala High Court also took a similar 
view of the umendment in the case of Ravikrishna 
Weaving Mills versus State of Kerala reported in 
189509-11-1:.11 760. 


10. Tt was next argued that this was a matter 
in which section 33C of the Industrial Disputes 
Act was the only section applicable under which

the Goverument had taken action under that section 


and sent the matter to the JTabour Court for 
determination of the amounts due to the workmun 
Wonder sub-section ۶ of the section, the Covern- 
ment had exhausted its power under the Induatrial 
Disputes Act and could not again refer the matter 
to the Tribunal for adjudication. Reference was 
made in this connection to the decision of the 


Madras High Court in the case of South Arcot 
Eleetricity Distribution Company td. | versus 
Klumalai reported in) 1959-[-L.L.J. 624. In this 


case the Government of ۶۱۸ا :لا‎ had taken over 
the undertaking of the Company and transferred

petitions filed before the Labour Court, Madras, 
under section 3)۱ of the Industrial Disputes Act. 
Overruling the contentions of the Government and 
the State Electricity Board the High Court held

authority of this decision it has been contended 
that the Labour Court. to which this matter had 
been referred by Government had no justification 
to refuse to determine the claiins of the workmen 
und that the matter has heen. concluded سا‎ the 
order passed by the Labour Court. It has also 
been contended that no fresh industrial dispute had 
been raised by the workmen after the decision of 
the Labour Court which coula have been referred 
by the (hovernment under section 1( of ۵(۵ 
Industrial Disputes Act. 


11. A certified copy of the order passed by the 
First Labour Court together with a copy of the 
written stutement filed 1 the Company before that 
Court has been produced before me (Exta. 1 and 
2). In the written statement the Company had 
challanged the jurisdiction of the Labour Court to 
decide the matter under section 33C(2) of the Act 
and stated that the said sub-section was not 
attructed by the facta of the case. It appears from 
the order passed by the Labour Court that the 
Company had further contended that the workmen ' 
should have raised an industrial dispute and the 
snine should have been referred by the Government 
under section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act 
to a Tribunal. All the contentions were upheld 
by the Labour Court and it was also held 01: 
determination of the amounts due to the workmen 
involved decision of several questions and among 
others of the question whether the closure was 
justified and due ہا‎ circumstances beyond — the 
control of the Company and that these questions 
really formed the subject-matter of an industrial 
dispute. Whatever view may be taken about the- 
order passed by the Labour Court I do 1701 find 
any justification for the contention that after the 
matter had been disposed of by the Labour Court 
the Government had no further power to refer the 
dispute to a Tribunal under section 10 of the Act. 
As to the argument that no dispute had heen 
raised by the workmen after the decision of the 
Qzabour Court it is sufficient ہا‎ refer to Ext. 4 
which is a copy of a letter yritten on behalf of 
the Union to the Labour Commissioner on 3) 
March {959 in which it was mentioned that an 
industrial dispute existed between the Company and 
ite workmen over the payment of retrenchment 
compensation and after referring to the order 
passed by the Labour Court it wns prayed that the

A ৯ সস 


dispute might be referred to a Tribunal under 
section 10 of the Act. The issue to he referred 
to the Tribunal was also specified in this letter, 
As ulready pointed out, a claim for retrenchment 
compensation on closure under section 251 FF was 
certainly an industrial dispute and the power of 
the (fovernment to refer such dispute under section 
10 was implicit in the section. The Company 
itself had urged before the Labour Court that the 
, matter constituted an industrial dispute which 
should have been referred under section 10. The 
mere fact that the Government thought it fit at the 
first instance to refer the matter to the Labour Court 
under section 338C(2) of the Act cannot stand in 
the way of a subsequent reference of the dispute 
to a Tribunal when the Labour Court took the view 
that section 338C(2) was not attracted to the facts 
of the case. There was no question of the 
exhaustion of the Government’s power {o make a 
reference under section 10 when no such referenee 
had hoen made جا‎ the Government before the 
preaent reference. It was argued that the decision 
of the Labour Court should have the force of res 
judicata. But the Labour Court did not make any 
award or give any decision on the merits but only 
held that it had no justification to do so and 
that it did on the objection of the Company which 
id now faking up a contrary position. I do not 
think that it can be permitted to do so. There- 
fore no question of applying the principle laid 
down by the Supreme Court in the case of Burn 
& Co., 1967-23 . 226, which waa relied upon 
by Shri P. R. Mukherjee can arise in this case. 


12. It is, therefore, clear that the Government 
had the power to refer the dispute to the Tribunal 
under section 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act. 
So far as the facts are concerned the closure of the 
mill on 918৮ Mareh 1957 is admitted and the bona 
fide nature of the closure was not disputed at the 
hearing. The workmen discharged as a result of 
the closure will, therefore, be entitled to retrench- 
ment compensation under section 25} FF which 
having been given retrospective effect from 28th 
November 1956 would be applicable to this case. 
With regard to the quantum of such compensation 
it was argued on hehalf of the Company that the 
workmen could only claim such compensation up 
to a limit of three months’ average pay under the 
Toviso to sub-section (1) of the said section, 
yecause, the mill had been closed down on account 
of unavoidable circumstances beyond the control 
of the Company. But the notice of closure 
(Ext. A) does not show that there were any 
unavoidable circumstances beyond the control of 
the Company, which led to the closure. The only 
reason mentioned in the notice is that the mill was 
being worked at a heavy, 1083 and that continuance 
of running of the mill would result in further 
serious lows. Under the Explanation to the afore- 
said proviso financial losses or other financial 
difficulties cannot be deemed to be unavoidable 
circunfstances beyond the control of the employer 
within the meaning of the proviso. 


13. It was, however, argued that the above 
Explanation would not apply here but that the case 
shonld be governed*® by 0179 tion as in the 
Ordinance which did not در رٹ‎ Explanation. 
The Company, it was contended, had acquired the 
right or privilege of having this claim decided on 
the basis of the terms of section 25FFF ag in the 
Ordinance and though the subsequent Amending 


[Parr I 


Act (18 of 1957) repealed the Ordinance, the repeal 
did not affect the right or privilege so acquired 
by the Company in view st the provisions of 
section 6(c) of the General Clauses Act (X of 
1897). But can it really be snid that the absence 
of the Explanation in the Ordinance had conferred 
a substantive right or privilege on the Cumpany 
which the Company was entitled to claim? The 
Explanation only prescribed a mode 0£ inter- 
pretation of the expression ‘unavoidable circum- 
stunces beyond the control of the employer’? used 
in the proviso. Tho Company did 00৮ certainly 
acquire the right of paying retrenchment compen- 
sation up to a limit of three months’ average pay 
to the discharged workmen simply hecause of the 
absence of this Interpretation clause رز‎ the 
Ordinance. The question whether the mill had to 
be closed for unavoidable circumstances beyond the 
control of the Company is a question of fact which 
the Company will have to establish in order to get 
the benefit of the proviso. Tho notice issued by 
the Company did not mention that the mill had to 
he closed for any such circumstances beyond its 
control. Tt cannot be contended that the Janguage 
of the proviso without the Explanation conferred 
on the Company the right to claim that financial 
losses alleged in the notice constituted unavoidable 
circumstances beyond the control of the Company. 
Losses in business cannot be deemed to be 
unavoidable or beyond control because such Josses 
can be avoided by proper and prudent manage- 
ment, ا‎ intellient anticipation of business 
prospects, by reducing expenditure and in various 
other ways. No evidence has been given by the 
Company that the losses incurred or anticipated as 
mentioned in the notice of closure were unavoidable 
or beyond its control. Thus, even apart from the 
explanation the Company has not been able to show 
that tho claims for retrenchment compensation 
should be confined in this case to only three 


months’ average pay of the workmen concerned. 


14. I hold accordingly that the 1,398 workmen 
affected by the closure whose names are mentionod 
in Annexure A appended to the written statement 
of the Victory Jute Products Employees’ Agsocia- 
tion are entitled to compensation from the Company 
under section 25FFF of the Industrial Disputes Aot. 
They will get notice-pay, i.e., one month’s pay in 
lieu of notice and compensation dopending on’ the 
length of their service as provided in séction 26F 
of the Act. The length of service of each workman 
ag mentioned in Fxt. 6, having heen accepted as 
correct by the Company and the pav of ench work- 
man, shown in the Company’s chart, Ext. C, 
having been accepted as correct by the Whions, 
the compensation payable to each should be 
calculated on the basis of the said documents, The 
Company should pay the amount due to each work- 
man within three months from the date of 
publication of this award.

1068 (vide Annexure A to the written statement

Tribunal and that they wanted revision of the same 
and that the Company merely pointed out that

the submission of charter of demand on 2nd Sep-

revision of the wages, bee is and scales fixed by 
the Appellate Tribunal’s Award of 1956 should be 
construed as a notice in writing contemplated under 
section 19(6) of the 571 Disputes Act, 1947, 
on the part of the Union to terminate the aforesaid 
awnrd. As such, in my opinion, there is no legal 
bar to the adjudication of the question of revision 
of existing wages, grades and scales of pay and 
dlenrness allowance by this tribunal. In the afore- 
saul circumstances the requirement of a notice 
under section 19(6) of the Industrial Disputes Act 
haw been substantially complied with by auhmia« 
sion of charter of demands. So, the legal objection 
raised by the Company fails as of no substance.

New Delhi, the 26th April 1960 


NOTIFICATION 


In exercise of the powers conferred by sub-section (3) 01 section 24A of 
the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 (4 of 1939), the Central Government hereby 
makes the following rules, the same having been previously published as 
required by -section 193 of the said Act. 


THE MOTOR VEHICLES (DIPLOMATIC AND CONSULAR OFFICERS 
VEHICLES) RECISTRATION RULES, 1960. 


1. Short title and commencement.—({1) These rules may be called the 
Motor Vehicles (Diplomatic and Consular Officers Vehicles) Registration 
Rules, 1960. 

(2) They shull come into force on the Ist June 1960. 


29 Doefinitions.—In these rules, unless the context otherwise requires : سے‎ 
(n) ‘Act’? means the Motor Vehicles Act, 1939 (4 of 1939) ; 


(b) ‘‘competent authority’’ means:— 

(a) in relation to a Diplomatic Officer or a Consular Officer who has 
hia residence in Delhi where the vehicle is normally kept, the 
Secretary to the Government of India, in the Mimatry of 
External Affairs (Protocol Division), or 

(b) in relation to a Diplomatic Officer or a Consular Officer who has 
hia residence at any other place, the Chief Secretary to the 
State (iovernment ; 

(c) “Consular Officer’? means a carecr Consular Officcr in the regular 
employment of a foreign or Commonwealth Government ; 

(d) ‘‘Form’’ means a form appended ,to these rules; 

(৬) ‘prescribed’ means prescribed by rules made by the State Govern- 
ment under the Act. 


3. Registration, how to he made. 1) Every application for registra- 
tion of a ae vehicle under section 24A of the Act by or on behalf of 
any Diplomftic or Consular Officer shall be made in quadruplicate in form I 
and be addressed to the competent authority. 


220 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 4, 0 


Ezplanation.—An application for the registration of a motor vehicle 
owned by a Diplomatic Mission or Consular Office shall be made by or on 
behalf of the Head of the Mission or the Consular Ofhce, us the case may 


be. 


2) The competent authority shall forward two copies of the application 
to the registering authority concerned together with a statement certifying 
the statua of the person applying for registration and indicating whether 
or not he is entitled to exemption from payment of registration fees and 
shall return one copy of the application with the above statement ما‎ ۷ 
person. The other copy of the application may be retained by the competent 
authority for record. 


(3) The registering authority concerned shall, on receipt of the applica- 
tion duly endorsed under the provisions of sub-rule (2) register the vehicle 
in the name of that officer: 


Provided that an application by or on behalf of u Consular Officer who 
is not entitled to exemption from payment of registration fees shall also 
be uccompanied by the prescribed fee. 


(4) The registering authority concerned shall issue to the owner of a 
motor vehicle registered by it under sub-rule (3), a certificate of registra- 
tion in Form IT and shall enter in a record to be kept by it particulars of 
such certificate. The certificate of registration shall be delivered to the 
person applying for registration or be sent to him by registered post 
acknowledgement due. 


(5) The registering authority shall assign to the vehicle for display 
thereon in the manner specified in rule 4 a distinguishing mark (in these 
rules referred to as the registration mark) consisting of the letters ‘CD’ in 
the case of a motor vehicle belonging to a Diplomatic Officer or the letters 
‘CC’ in the case of a motor vehicle belonging to a Consular Officer, followed 
by a mumber containing not more than four figures. 


4. Exhibition of registration marks.—(1) The registration mark to he 
assigned under sub-rule (5) of rule 3 shall be clearly exhibited, both at 
the front and rear of the vehicle on a plane surface of a plate of any metal 
the size of which shall be sixteen inches by five and half inches— 


(i) with deep blue background, the registration mark and the number 
being in white, in the case of a motor vehicle of a Diplomatic 
Officer ; 

(ii) with yellow background, the registration mark and the number 
being in black, in the case of a motor vehicle of a Consula 
Officer. 


(2) Tho registration mark shall be in English letters and numerals and— 


(i) save in the case of a motor cycle or an invalid carriage, the letters 
shall be not less than 24 inches high and 5/8ths inch thick’at any 
part, the numerals shall be not less than 34 inches high and 
3/4the inch thick at dny part, and there shall be a space between 
any letter ond any numeral and between any letter cr any 
numeral and the edge of the plane surface of not less than 
+ inch and a space between any two letters and between any two 
numerals of nat lew than 3/8ths inch; and 


(ii) in the case of a motor cycle or an invalid carriage, of dimensions 
not less than 1/8rd of those specified in clause (1), 


(3) The plane surfaces aforesaid shall not be inclined from the vertical 
by more than 30 degrees. The letters and numerals shall be exhibited ۸ 
follows, that is to say— 

(i) in the case of a transport vehicle both registration marks ehall 
exhibit the letters and numerals in two- separate horizontal lines, 
the letters above and the numerals below; and 

(ii) in all other cases, the rogistration marks may exhibit the letters 
and numerals either in two horizontal lines as aforesaid or in cne 
horigpntal line.

mark exhibited at the front of a motor cycle or an invalid carriage may be‏ 
displayed on a plate in line with the axis of the vehicle and shalt, in such a‏ 
Case, be displayed on both sides of the plate.‏

8. Production of vehicle at time of registration.—Tho reyistoring 
authority shall, before proceeding to register a motor vehicle under these 
rules, require the person ayplying for registration to produce the vehicle 
before it or such other authorjty as the State Government may by order 
appoint in this behalf in order that the registering authorily may satisty 
itself that the particulars contained in the application are true ond ) 
the vehicle complies with the requirements of Chapter V of the Act and of 
the rules made thereunder. 


6. AsSignm@nt of fresh registration mark on removal of vehicle to 
another State.—(1) When a motor vehicle registered in accordance with 
these rules in one State has been kept in another State for a period exceeding 
twelve months, the owner of the vehicle shall apply to the registeriny 
authority within whose jurisdiction the vehicle then is for the assignment 
of a new registration mark and shall present the original certificate of 
registration to that authority. 


(2) Kvery application under sub-rule (1) shall be made in quadruplicate 
in Form III and shall be addressed to the competent authority. 


(3) The provisions of sub-rules (2), (3), (4) and ©) of rule 3 shall upply 
to an application mado under sub-rule (1) of this rule us they apply to an 
application made pnder sub-rule (1) of rule 3. 


(4) When a fresh registration mark has been assigned the registering 
authority shall enter the mark و‎ the certificate of registration before 
returning it to the applicant. The registering authority shall also, in 
communication with the registering authority concerned which had pre- 
viously registered the vehicle, arrange for the transfer of the registration 
of the vehicle from the records of that registering authority to its own 
records. 


7. Reregistration of existing vehicles of Diplomatic Officers and 
Consular Officers.—Within three months from the commencement of these 
rules, every motor vehicle of a Diplomatic Qfhicer or a Consular Officer, 
which’ has been registered before such commencement under section 24 of 
the Act, shall be re-registered and shall be assigned registration marks in 
accordance with these rules. The registering authority concerned shall also 
issue to the owner of such vehicle certificate of registration under sub- 


tule (4) of rule 3. 


8. Change of residence.—(1) If the owner of a motor vehicle registered 
in accordance with these rules changes his residence us recorded in the 
certifieate of registration, he shall within thirty days of any such change 
intimate his new address in form IV to the registering authority Sy which 
the certificate of registration was issued, or if the new address is within 
the jurisdiction of another registering authority, to that other registering 
authority and shall at the same time forward the certificate of registration 
to that registering authority in order that the new address may be entere: 


therein. 

(2) A registering authority other thaa the original registering authority 
making any such entry shall communicate the new address to the original 
registering authority. 

(3) Nothing in sub-rule (1) shall apply to a case where the change of 


residence is not intended to exceed six months in duration or where the 
motor velticle is neither used nor removed from the address recorded in 


the certificate of registration.

9. Transfer or disposal of motor vehicies.—(1) Where a motor vehicle 
registered in accordance with these rules is transferred by way of sale or 
otherwise the transferor shall, within fourteen days report the fact of the 
transfer along with the full name and address of the person to whom the 
vehicle is transferred to the registering authority within whose jurisdiction 
the transfer is effected and shall جا‎ send copies of the 6ہ‎ 
report to— 


(a) the transferee ; 
(b) the competent authority; 


(c) the Collector of Customs of the port of importation of the vehicle, 
and where it is not possible to locate the port of importation, 
to the Collector of Central Excise or Customs nearest to the 
headquarters of the transferor; and 


(d) the original registering authority in whose records the registration 
of the তারি is recorded, if the transfer is effected in the juris- 
diction of another registering authority; and shall also surrender 
the number plate in respect of the vehicle to the registering 
authority in whose records the registration of the vehicle is 
recorded, when the transfer is to a person other than a Diplomatic 
Officer or a Consular Officer. 


Where the transferee is a Diplomatic Officer or a Consular Officer, an 
application by or on his behalf shall be made to the registering auchority 
for registration of the vehicle in accordance with these rules. 


10. Duplicate certificate of registration.—(1) The owner of a imotor 
vehicle registered under these rules may, if the certificate of registration 
of the vehicle is torn, defaced or mutilated and shall, 1f 1% 18 lost or des- 
troyed, apply in Form V to the registering authority by whom the 
certificate was issued tor the issue of a duplicate certificate. 


(2) On receipt of an application* under sub-rule (1) together with the 
prescribed fee in cases where the applicant is not entitled to exemption, 
the registering authority shall issue a duplicate certificate of registration 
in Form II clearly stamped DUPLICATE in red ink. 


(3) Where a duplicate certificate of registration has been obtaimed on 
the ground that the orginal certificate has been lost, the holder shall, if 
the original certificate is subsequently found, return the duplicate certi- 
ficate of registration immediately to the registering authority who issued it. 


11. 6095 of number plates.—If the number plate of a motor vehicle is 
lost, the owner shall intimate the fact in writing in Form VI to the regis- 
tering authority which has registered the vehicle and to the nearest pelice- 
station. 


(2) If the number plate is subsequently found or received by the owner 
he shall again report the fact to the registering authority and the police- 
atation aforesaid. 


(4) If the number plate is not found or received by the owner, he shall 
arrange to have a fresh number plate prepared and exhibited on his motor 
vehicle. 


12. Disposal of surrendered plates.—The number plates surrendered 
by Diplomatic or Consular Officers to the registering authority under 
rule (9) shall be destroyed by the registering authority within seven days 
from the date of surrender. 


13. Suspension and cancellation of Registration.—If under the provi- 
sions of section ور‎ or section 34 of the Act, the registration of a motor 
vehicle made in necordance with these rules is suspended or cancelled, then 
a copy of the order of suspension or cancellation shall be sent to the 
competent authority in addition to each of the authorities or persons to 
whom a copy has to be sent under those sections.

Your petitioner’s name appears in the list of Elected Members of West

2, Qn April 11, 1960, the Returning Officer called upon the Members 
of the West Bengal Legislutive Assembly to fill vacancies in the Legisla- 
dive Council of the said State to be caused by the retirement of nine 
members on June 4, 1960 with the previous approval of the = said 
lection Commission in the manner as provided in the said Representation 
of People Act, 1951, and Rules, framed thereunder and appointed May 10, 
1960 us the date for the said election aud the West Bengal Legislative 
Assembly as the place for the said election. The said election was con- 
trolled under the rules laid down in Chapters V and VI of the said Repre- 
sentation of the People (Conduct of Elections and Election Petitions) Rules, 
1956, The rules provide, inter alia, for voting by poll and by marking the 
ballot papers by single transferable votes as provided in the said rules and 
specially under rules 91 to 180 thereof. 


3. That on the said date, May 1007 1960, the said election took place 
in the said West Bengal Legislative Assembly und 244 Members of the said 
Assembly attended the said poll and the said ballot papers were marked 
according to the preferences of the suid electors in the manner provided 
under the said rules and by a single transferable vote. On the said date 
there were ten contesting candidates for the said nine seuts, being Respon- 
dent Nos. 1 to 10 and one candidate having retired by duly submitting his 
withdrawal notice and the said candidate is Respondent No, 11. 


4, The counting of the votes to the said election took place on the said 
date, May 10, 1960, after 2 p.m. immediately after the ae of the poll. 
The said Returning Officer declared nine persons to have been duly elected 
and a true copy of the suid declaration is annexed hereto and marked ‘‘A”’. 
Your petitioner craves leave also to refer to the ‘‘Result Sheet’’ at the time 
of the hearing of this petition.

7. That such improper rejection of the said valid ballot paper materially

New Delhi, the 29th June 1960 

(9.১... 751.—In exercise of the on conferred by section 3 of the 
Essentia] Commodities Act, 1955 (10 of 1956), the Central Government hereby

aud Control) Order, 1957, hereinafter referred to as the Order, numely :—

(Licensing and Control) Amendment Order, 1960.

“3A. Prohibition "۷ Installation 7 other Machinery.—No owner 
or person in charge of u roller mill shall, within the premises of 
such muill,—

otherwise than by such mill.

So, the point for consideration in this case 
le—whether the retrenchment of 8 workmen of the 
clerical staff and 9 workmen of the menial staff 
(Nos. 1, 3 to 8, 10 and 11) of the issue under

The broad — principles governing the rule of 
retrenchment are now well-settled by the Statute, 
namely, the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, as 
amended up to 1957 and by a series of judicial 
Pronouncementa by the Hon’ble Supreme Court and 


Labour Appellate Tribunal. These principles can 
bo 1010 down as follows :— 


(1) The management has the right to retrench 
workmen provided retrenchment is justified. It is 
the prima facie right of the management to deter- 
mine its labour force and the management would 
be the best Judge to determine the number of work. 
men who would become surplus on the ground of 
rationalisation, economy, or other reasons on which 
retrenchment can be sustained. An employer has 
the right to reorganise his business in any fashion 
he likes for the purpose of economy or conveniences 
and nobody is entitled to tell him how he should 
conduct his 8۰ 


(2) This right of the management to retrench 
its workmen is subject to certain statutory 
limitations, and to the observance of the principle 
of natural justice, The statutory limitations are 
contained in sections 2011 and 25G of the Industrial 
Disputes Act. The provisions of these two sections 
are mandatory and conditions precedent to 
retrenchment. This has been recognised in a series 
of judicial decisions, i.e., the decision of the 
Hon'ble Labour Appellate Tribunal in the case of 
Viswamitra Press reported in 1952 L.A.C. page 20 
at page 33, decisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court 
in the case of Swadesh Mitran Lid. reported in 1960 
1..1..J3., Volume I, page 504, ond in the case of 
State of Bombay and others va. Hospital Mazdoor 
Sabha and others reported in 1960 L..L.J., Vol. I, 
page 251 and the decision of the Hon’ble Calcutta 
High Court in the case of Royal Calcutta Golf 
Club reported in 1960 L.L.J., Vol. I, page 464. 


Section 25! of the Industrial Disputes Act lays 
down three conditions precedent to retrenchment, 
namely,— 


(a) hefore retrenchment workmen should be 
given one month’s notice in writing or 
paid one month’s pay in lieu of 8৫৯, 
notice; 


(b) the workmen should be paid at the time 
of retrenchment compensation which shal! 
be equivalent to 15 days’ average pay for 
every completed year of service or an 
part thereof in excess of six months; an 


(৫) notice in the prescribed manner shall be 
served upon the Appropriate Government. 
Section 260 lays down the principle of 
‘Inst come first go’’ which the employee 
must observe while retrenching the work- 
men. 


So far as the mandatory provisions of sections 
2917 and 25G of the Industrial Disputes Act are 
concerned, these provisions have been strictly 
complied with by the management in the instant 
case as admitted on behalf of the workmen 
concerned. The Company’s evidence is that all 
these mandatory requirements have been atrictly 
observed by the Company hefore the workmen 
mentioned in the 17808 under reference were actually 
retrenched on 10th June 1959. This is also admit- 
ted by P.W. 1 Sanjib Kumar Bhattacharji, one of 
the employees of the Company. This witness has 
admitted in evidence that retrenchment of the 
clerks in the present case was made on the rinciple 
of 51881 come first go’? and that ناک‎ of the 
refrenched clorks has got retrenchment compensa- 
tion according to law and no new handa have heen 
recruited by the Company to fill up the place of

Next 1 come to the question of justifiability or 
otherwise of the retrenchment of the workmen 
concerned. As T have already stated the manage- 
ment has the right to retrench the workmen 
provided the retrenchment is justified. The 
Justification of a retrehchment depends upon 
several factors which has got to be proved hy the 
management, The management has got to 
establish a case for retrenchment either on the 
ground of rationalisation, economy or sufficient 
causes. In the present case the case of the 
Company is that retrenchment had to be made for 
the purpose of reorganisation of its business at the 
Calcutta Branch as a measure of economy. on 
account of loss or fall in the profits in the tradin

the workmen concerned as alleged by the union 
in their separate written statements. 


Next. it is to he considered whether the Company 
was netuated by an extraneous consideration in 
effecting the retrenchment of the workmen 
concerned. Both the unions alleged that the 
Company was actuated by auch considerations. Of 
the expression ‘‘extraneous considerations’ the 
Labour Appellate Tribunal in the case of Viswa- 
mitra Presa referred to above has cited an 
illustration. The Hon’ble Tribunal has said that 
the increase of workload on the workmen retained 
would be an instance of extraneous considerntion. 
Tn the present case the allegation of the two unions 
is that as a resull of retrenchment, there has been 
un increase in the workload on the staff retained 
has been an increase in the overtime work 


1998 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, AUGUST 10, 1960 


of the employees retained. The Company meets 
this allegation by saying that the practice 
of overtime wages has been continuing from 
before the retrenchment and there’ has not 
been any appreciable increase in’ the over- 
time work of the employees retained after the 
retrenchment. I¢ is an admitted fact that the 
system of overtime payment has been continuing 
from several years before the date of the present 
retrenchment. Tvidence of P.W. 1 is to the effect 
(10181 since 1952 workmen of the Company have 
heen paid overtime charges and his clear evidence 
is that overtime charges are between Ra. 600 and 
Ra. 600 per month now as against Rs. 1,100 or 
Rs. 1,200 per month during previous years. But 
this witness as well as P.W. 6 Jamuna Singh and 
P.W. 7 Januki Prosad have said that after the 
removal of the office of the Calcutta Branch to 
Thamond Harbour Road in August 1959, the work- 
lond hag increased. But the Manager J).W. 1 has 
suid on oath that the work of the Calcutta Branch 
has not increased and that a certain amount of 
overtime is still heing paid to the employees and 
that has always been paid to the workmen for a 
long series of years. The overtime charts filed by 
the Company for the vears from 1956 to 1959 are 
Exta. B series. These charts go to show that there 
has been a fall in the total overtime wages for the 
Cold Storage Sub-staff in 1959 as against that in 
1958 but there has been a marked rise in the total 
payment of overtime wages in the general depart- 
ment regarding clerical and sub-stuff. The charts, 
Exts. B and B/1, go to show that there has been 
increase of about Rs. 6,000 per year in overtime 
wages in 1959 as against those in 1958. So the 
PW. Us evidence that the overtime charges at 
present are lesa than those in previous years is not 
a correct statement. 13০ that as it may, it is clear 
that there has been an increase irr overtime charges 
at the rate of Rs. 500 per month in 1969 as againat 
the same in 1958, and by resorting to the retrench- 
ment of the workmen concerned the Company has 
raved a aum of Ra. 4,000 per month as anid by 
1) W. 1 and is 9190 supported by Ext. F. So, the 
retrenchment has evidently heen made as a measure 
of economy. Although some of the P.Ws. have said 
that workload on the remaining emplovees has in- 
creased as a result of retrenchment, their statement 
is contradicted by D.W. 1, the General Manager, 
From the evidence on record I am not convinced 
that there bas been any appreciable increase in the 
workload upon the workmen retained after the 
retrenchment complained of. The overtime charges 
have been paid for a long tme and admittedly the 
pressure of work increases in December and also 
in July and Auguat for stock-taking (vide P.W. 2). 
The General Manoger. D.W. 1, has said in his 
evidenre that Cashier, Despatch Clerk and Receipt 
Clerk haa got to work overtime as also the Godown 
Clerk and that this is incidental to the nature of 
the work they are doing. T, therefore, find that 
in the context of evidence discussed above retrench- 
ment of the workmen concerned has not been done 
for any extraneous considerations. As it has heen 
observed by the Flon’ble Supreme Oourt in the 
ease of J. K. Iron & Steel Company reported in 
TX F.J.R. (1956). page 419, it is impossible to 
determine the juatifiability of retrenchment اہ‎ 
workmen without atrong question of good faith on 
the part of the Company which would largely 
depend upon finances of the Company, on the 
adverse effect that retrenchment would have on the 


(Parr I 


business and on whether retention would mean, the 
dead weight of an uneconomic surplus and so forth. 
In the present case as I have found the finances 
af the Company were definitely on an unfavourablé 
footing in June 1959 as compared with the year 
1958, i.e., just hefore retrenchment in question was 
resorted to. Secondly, by retrenching the work- 
men concerned the ae has been able to 
economnise in its business expenses and that no 
employee has been retrenched in exceas of the 
actual requirement as said by D.W. 1, and thirdly, 
had the retrenched employees been retained, it 
would have meant the dead weight for uneconomic 
surplus which the Company was evidently out to 
avoid, In the case of India Tyre and Rubber 
Com ne vs, their workmon reported in 13 F.J.R. 
(1957-58), page 108, it has been observed by the 
Hon’ble Madras High Court that “the dead weight 
of an uneconomic surplus as referred to in the case 
of J. K. Tron & Steel Company cited above can 
operate at any level of profits, There is nothing 
unlawful in an employer desiring to make even 
more profits by getting rid of a dead weight of 
an uneconomic surplusage’’, The Company need 
not prove that it was losing or making no profits. 
On behalf of the unions it has been urged that the 
Company could have resorted to measure of economy 
by compelling the four employees over 55 years 
l.e., the age of superannuation who aro atill working 
(vide Ext. 5) ae also by resorting to a cut in the 
salary of the employees. It is admitted that the 
Company has not resorted to any of these steps as 
a measure of economy. But it has been observed 
by the Hon’ble Calcutta 111৮1) Court in the case of 
Roval Calcutta Golf Club referred to above that an 
eniployer has the right to organise his business in 
any fashion he likes for the purpose of economy or 
convenience and nobody is entitled to tell him how 
he should conduct his business. So the Company 
in the present case in resorting to the retrenchment 
of the workmen concerned has acted within its 
rights and primarily as a measure of economy and 
rationalisation of its business of the Calcutta 
Branch. So, there is no want of bona fides or good 
fuith on the part of the Company in having 
resorted to the retrenchment of the workmen 
concerned as mentioned in the issue under 
reference, 


Having regard to all these facts and circum- 
stances, the past and the present conduct of the 
Company and the financial position of the Calcutta 
Branch of the Company on the eve of the retrench- 
ment, 1.e., on 10th June 19459 I come to the 
conclusion that the Company has retrenched the 
workmen concerned for economic reasons and in 
doing so, it has acted in good faith and without 
any improper motive of victimisation or unfair 
labour practice or for any extraneous considerations 
und in due obedience to the principle of natural 
justice, It has atrictly followed the atatutory rules 
regarding retrenchment as contnined in মো 
tions 25F and 254 of the Industrial Disputes Act 
As such the retrenchment of the workmen 
concerned 1৭ justified. 


The result, therefore, ia that the retrenchment 
of the eight workmen of the clerical staff ond the 
nine workmen of the menial staff who are still under 


Parr I] 


SS ————————— es 


retrenchment being justified none of them is 


entitled to any relief in this case, 
This is my award, 
Dictated and correeted by me.

\No. 3351P1.—28th July 1960,—In exercise of 
the power conferred by the proviso to article 309 
of the Constitution of India, the Governor 19 
pleased to make the following rules regulating the 
Tecriitment to the posta of Lady Telephone 
Operators in the West Bengal Police Department 
of the Government of West Bengal, namely :— 


RULES 


1. Short title. —These rules may be called tho 
West Bengal Subordinate Services (Recruitment 
uf Lady Telephone Operators) Rules, 1960. 


2. Application.—These rules shall apply to lhe 
recruitment to the posts of ,Lady Telephone 
Operators in the West Bengal Police Department 
of the Government of West Bengal, and shall 
come into force at once. 


3. Appointing authority.—An officer of the 
rank of Superintendent of Police shall be the 
uppointing authority. 


and a list of applications shall be kept in his 
office. A Board consisting of two Assistant 
Inspectors-General und the Special Superintendent 
of Police (1), I.B., shall select candidates after 
taking a written test and interviewing the candi- 
dates. The written test shall comprise of a1 
dictation in English and a few simple questions 
and full marks for such a test shall be 60. 


5. Qualifications.—A candidate must be a 
citizen of India as defined in Purt IT of the Consti- 
tution of India. She shall have passed at lenst 
the School Final Examination or its equivalent. 


6. Age of appointment.—A candidate shall be 
over 18 and under 20 years of age on the first day 
of the year in which the recruitment is made, bub 
the age limits are relaxable by the appointing 
authority under very special circumstances, 


7. Medical certificate.—A candidate shall be of 
sound health and shall have to produce a medical 
certificate from the Chief Medical Officer of Health 
of any district or from the authorised Medical 
Officers for the Police Department in Calcutta. 


8, Training.—A candidate shal] be appointed 
temporarily for 3 months in the first instance for 
undergoing a course of training during which 
period she shall be entitled to the initial pay in 
the time-scale with usual allowance admissible to 
her under the rules in force. On completion of 
her training, if she is found unsuitable she shall 
a discharged forthwith by the appointing autho- 
rity. 


9. Probation and confirmation.—On satisfao- 
tory completion of the training prescribed by cule 
8, ٢ candidate shall he appointed on probation for 
two years. The appointing authority may extend 
the period of ان‎ by a further period not 
exceeding one year. The period of probation shal] 
not be further extended without the special orders 
of Government obtained on a recommendation made 
by the appointing authority. During the conti- 
nuance of the probationary period or on its expiry, 
if a candidate is found unsuitable she shall be dis- 
charged forthwith by the appointing authority. 
Om successful completion of the probationary 
period a 01010010110 shall be confirmed. 


10. Leave——In the matter of leave the Lady 
Operator shall be guided by the leave rulea apph- 
cable to the subordinate services under the State 
(lovernment for the time being in force. 


11. Discipline, punishment and appeal.—In 
the matter of discipline, punishment and appeal, 
the Tiaady Operators shall be governed by the 
Bengal Subordinate Services (Discipline 070 
Appeal) Rules, for thé time being in force. 


By order of the Governor, 
M. M. BASU, ۵۷۰

Jommiasioner of Wakfs, West Bengal, has, after

Art, 1934 (Bengal Act XIII of 1934), into the 
affairs of the wakf-al-al-aulad, created by Sk. 
Sabiruddin, of village Kalsara, in the district of

January 1939, and enrolled in the office of the 
Commissioner of Wakfs, West Befigal, under ۰. 
No. 5879 (hereinafter referred to as the said wakf- 
ni-al-aulad), been of opinion that the affairs of the 
said wakf-al-al-aulad have been mismanaged to 
such an extent as to make it desirable for the pro- 
tection of the wakf property of the said wakf-al- 
al-aulad and in the interest of the beneficiaries 
thereof that the said wakf-al-al-aulad shoul be 
subjected to greater control and supervision and 
hus recommended to the State Government under

Act, 1934, applicable to wakfs other than wakfs- 
al-al-aulad;

1934), the Governor is pleased, after considering

(2) Leave on medical certificate may be granted to a municipal officer

(4) ]٢ the case of « municipal officer or servant in superior service not

15. (1) Extraordinary leave may be granted to any municipal officer or 
servant in special circumstances— 


(a) when no other leave is admissible, or 


(b) when other leave is admissible, but the officer or servant concerned 
applies in writing for the grant of extraordinary leave. 


(2) Except in the case of a municipal officer or servant in permanent em- 
ploy, the duration of extraordinary leave shall not exceed three months on any 
one occasion. 


(3) The authority empowered to grant leave may commute retrospectively 
periods of absence without leave into extraordinary leave, 


10. (1) A municipal officer or servant on earned leave is entitled— 


(a) if in permanent employ, to leave salary equal to his average pay or, 
to his average substantive pay for the 12 complete months, 
preceding the month in which leave is taken, whichever is 
greater; | 


(0) if not in permanent employ, to leave salary equal to his pay vn the 
day before the leave commences. 


(2) A municipal officer or servant on Jeave on 1777 affairs or leave on 
medical certificate is entitled to leave salary equal to half his average pay 
or, to half his average substantive pay for the 12 complete months, preceding 
the month in which leave is taken, whichever is greater, subject in either 
case to a maximum of Rs. 750. 


(3) A municipal officer or servant on extraordinary leave is not entitled 
to any leave salary. 


(4) For the purpose of this rule, ‘‘substantive’’ pay means the pay of the 
permanent post which the officer or servant holds substantively or on which 
he holds a lien or would hold a lien had the lien not been suspended. 


Note.—Average pay shall be calculated on tho average monthly pay 
earned during the 86 complete months immediately preceding the month in 
which the event occurs which necessitates the ০1601190101) of average pay. 


17. Leave on medical certificate for any period not exceeding a month, 
may be granted by the Chairman of the municipality concerned.

rote she was drawing at the time of taking leave, for u period which may

or to the end of six weeks from the date of delivery which is earlier. 


(2) 1,6৮৪ of any other kind, as ma be due, may be granted in continua- 
tion of maternity leave if the request for its grant be supported by a medical 
certificate. 


Note 1.—In the case of a female municipal officer or servant in tem- 
porary employ, maternity leave may be granted up to four weeks prior to 
and four weeks after the date of delivery, provided that she has been in

of delivery.

০৪111163019 for a period not exceeding u month. 


21. Quarantine leave may be granted to ao municipal officer or servant 
on the basis of a certificate from a medical officer-in-charge of any Govern- 
ment or municipal hospital or dispensary if his presence in 01166 or duty 
is considered to be injurious to the health of other municipal officers and 
servants due to the presence of infectious diseases in his family or house- 
hold. Such leave may be granted by the Executive Officer or if there ہر‎ no 
Executive Officer, hy the Chairman of the municipality concerned for a 
period not exceeding twenty-one days, or, in exceptional circumstances, 
thirty days. Any leave necessary for quarantine purpose in excess of (1118 
period shall be treated as ordinary leave. Quarantine leave may ulav be 
granted, when necessary, in continuation of other leave subject to the above 
maximum. A municipal officer or servant or servant on quarantine leuve 
shall not be treated as absent from duty and his pay shall not be intermitted. 


The following diseases only shall be treated as infectious diseases vithin 
the meaning of this rule: — 


(1) Small pox, 

(2) Scarlet fever, 

(3) Plague (pneumonic and/or bubonic), 
(4) Typhus, 

(6) Cerebro-spinf] meningitis, 

(6) Measles, and 

(7) Mumps. 


For persons employed in the preparation or distribution of food, the 
following additional diseases shall also be treated as infectious :— 


(1) Dysentery, 

(2) Enteric fever (typhoid fever), 
(3) Malta fever, and 

(4) Paratyphoid fever, 


22. (a) Special disability leave may be granted by the commissioners at 
a meeting to a municipal officer or servant who is disabled by injury acci- 
dentally incurred in, or in consequence of the due performance of his official 
duties, or intentionally inflicted in consequence of his official position, or 
by illness incurred in the performance of any particular duty which has the 
effect of increasing his liability to ilness or injury beyond the ordinary 
risk attaching to the post he holds subject to the following conditions : — 


(i) that the disahility, if due to disease, must be certified by the Chief 
Medical Officer of the municipality or if there is no such muni- 
cipal medical officer, by a registered medical practitioner ; 


(ii) that the period of leave granted shall be such as is certified by the 
municipal medical officer or a registered medical practitionr, 
as the case may be, subject to a maximum of twenty-four 
months. 


(b) Such leave shall not be admissible unless the disability manifested 
itself within three months of the occurrence to which it is attributed, and 
the person disabled acted with due promptitude in bringing it to notice 
of the commissioners of the municipality, provided that if the commissioners 
are satisfied as to the cause of the disability, such leave may be granted in 
cases where the disability manifested itself more than three months after 
the occurrence of its cause. 


(০) Such leave may be coffbined with leave of any other kind.

\ 


Part 1[ 


le ~— سا‎ 


sections 7 and 10 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 
1947 (XIV of 1947), an industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Balmer Lawrie & Co. 1480.) 21 Netaji 
Subhas Road, Calcutta-1, and their employees 
represented by Messrs. Balmer Lawrie & Co. 10. 
Employees’ Union, 19 Strand Road, Calcutta-1, 
regarding matters specified in the second schedule 
of the Act, to this Court for adjudication. 


Whether the transfer of 23 employees (as per 
list attached to the order of reference) from 
their original departments to Pool Section 
is justified P 

AWARD 


The case of the Union in its written statement 
in Short is that the very creation of the ‘Pool 
Department’ by the Company is a novelty which 
ia not to be found in any other commercial or 
industrial organisation. This ‘Pool Department’, 
for the existence and continuance of which no 
necessity exists, is used as a weapon by the 
Company by transferring the workmen therefrom 
their own departments. The workmen so _trans- 
ferred to the Pool Department aro to work from 
one department to another without fixity of any 
permanent and specified job, and as a result they 
are denied the scope of acquiring sufficient 
knowledge in their work meriting promotion. 
The Union thus contends that in the instant case 
the 23 workmen concerned have been wnjustifiably 
and unreasonably transferred to the ‘Pool Depart- 
ment’, and as such their transfer is mala fide and 
amounts to unfair labour practice. 


The Company, on the other hand, in its written 
atatement contends that the ‘Pool System’ has heen 
introduced by it with the object of improving the 
organisation and management of the Company’s 
affairs and business. According to this system 
when any member of the Company’s 8151 erical 
or subordinate—hecomes surplus to the require- 
ment of any particular department of the 
Company, he is withdrawn from that department 
and shown as being in the poo! until he 1s posted 
to any department with specific permanent job. 
Resides, the employees so transferred to the Pool 
Section do not sustain any loss in their service 
conditions or in emoluments. On the country, the 
Pool System enables the workmen to acquire 
knowledge nnd experience of the various type of 
work carried out by the different departments cf 
the Company, and such added knowledge and 
experience inake the workman concerned more 
useful to the Company and to himself. Thus the 
Company justifies its action in transferring the 
instant 28 workmen from their original depart- 
ments to the Pool Department. 


DECISION 


The case was fixed for hearing on 24-11-69 an 
which date the Union instead of 11 with 
tho case filed a petition praying for an adjourn- 
ment. Accordingly, the case was adjourned to 
14th June 1960. But on this date, the Union 
filed a petition stating that it has no dispute with 
the Company, and on it the learned Advocate for 
the Company has also made an endorsement to 
that effect. Tn this view of the matter, a ‘‘no- 
dispute’? award is passed in this cnse, and the

contractors of Messrs. )(. Patel & (Co. (P.)

issue

(1) Hautu Singh, (2) Shih Chandra Das, (3)

Notices were issued to both the parties, wlio 
filed written statements setting forth their respec- 
tive cases, The pleadings of the parties would be 
considered at the decisions of the issue herebelow. 


The Union states that the 18 persons mention- 
ed in the order of reference are all registered per- 
manent workmen of the employers named in the 
order of reference. There are two classes of work- 
men employed by the abovementioned employers 
—one class being termed as Khata workers and 
the other Nagda workers. Khata workers are 
those whose naines are recorded in a register main- 
tained by the employers. In the matter of employ- 
ment it is a condition of service that the Khata 
workmen get priority over Nagda workmen. The 
workmen named in the list attached to the order of 
reference are all Khata workmen of the above- 
named employers and were engaged in the work 


2754 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 11, 1960 


of blending tea, grossing, loading, unloading and 
other allied works. In the middle of February 
1959 there was a dispute between the workmen 
and their employers in respect of certain condi- 
tions of service. Thereufter the employers on 5th 
March 1959 dismissed these workmen without any 
charge-sheet or notice whatsoever. The matter 
was taken up for conciliation by the Labour 
Directorate and in course of the conciliation 
proceedings an agreement was arrived at between 
the parties in presence of the Conciliation Officer 
on 12th August 1959. A copy of the agreement 
appears as Annexure ‘‘A’’ to the Union’s written 
statement. Inspite of the above ayreement, the 
employers are not employing the workmen named 
in the list attached to the order of reference. The 
employers have employed and are employing new 
hands in the category. 


The Union, therefore, prays for an award declar- 
ing the dismissal of the 18 workmen as unjustified 
and directing the employers to reinstate the work- 
men with effect from 5th March 1959 and to pay 
them compensation for the period of their non- 
employment. 


Four of the employers, out of 5, namely, Bhuil 
Singh, Jaman Das, Sham Chand and Sukhu Das 
appeared and filed a written statement. The other 
employer, viz., Shyam T.al Shaw, did not file any 
written statement. All the 5 employers, however, 
appeared through an Advocate who filed a written 
statement for the 4 employers. The 4 employers 
in their written statement state that these employ- 
ers are not contractors in the real sense of the term 
and it would be proper to call thom workers. The 
workmen named in the list attached to the order 
of reference were not their employees. None of 
the workers mentioned in the hat were employed 
by any of the alleged contractors Nos. (i), (21), 
(iv) and (v). 


Sometime in August 1959 the Union represen- 
tative held out the hope that they would arrange 
to have the rates. enhanced in case they entered 
into an agreement with them. It was further 
given out that dire consequences would befall 
them, should they fail to sign the agreement. 


The workmen mentioned in the list were never 
their Khata workers, as wrongly alleged. The 
three alleged contractora at times drafted a few 
coolies to do their work and one or two persons 
out of the list might have worked under the con- 
tractors as tickka workers. 


The contractors, in the circumstances, pray that 
the Tribunal should make an award directing that 
the workmen in question are not the workmen of 
the alleged contractors and they are not entitled 
to any relief in 0015 case, 


Evidence was adduced by both parties, P.W. 1, 
Shri America Shaw, one of the workmen mention- 
ed in the list attached to the order of reference, 
deposed on behalf of the Union, and O.P.W. 1, 
Shri Shyam Chand Shaw, employer No. 4, deposed 
for the employers. P.W. 1 states that all the 
workfnen mentioned in the order of reference work 
under the opposite party, contractors, who work 
jointly aa contractors کون‎ Messrs, G. Patel & 


Co. (P.) Lid. P.W. 1 bas been working for the

last 8/9 years under these five contractors. Hae

the employers and this document was marked 
1720, 1. The workers were refused employment 
even after the agreement. P.W. 1 states that the 
workers pray that they should be taken back as 
Khata workers in preference to others. He also 
states that the employers have taken new men.

ull the five employers do work of loading and 
unloading under G. Patel & Co, THis father used 
to work before him and he has been doing this

Ext. A. Before the date of agreement (Ext. 1),

Patel & Co. is 2 pice and 4 pice per petty and the

রা realise their dues on piece-rate basis 
and pay the workers on daily basis. At first he

He also stated that these 18 men sometimes work-

Tn cross-examination the witness states that the

(10৮1). Again he stated that he told the Labour

Ext. 1 shows that o number of terms have been 
settled between the five veer and the Union, 
in regard to the work of the muttiahs. There is 
an Agreement as to the duty hours, the tiffin period, 
over-time work, employment and attendance and 
pay-book, It states that it is agreed that the 
Khata workers will get priority in point of 
employment as occasion arises and they will get 
priority over the Nagda workers. The learnod 
Advocate for the Union states that these 18 men 
were Khata workers under the five employers and 
they are to get priority in employment over other 
men. On a consideration of the evidence on record 
1 do not accept the contention of the employers 
and O.P.W. 1 that Agreement (xt. 1) was secur- 
ed under duress in the presence of the Labour 
Officer. On a perusal of the Agreement it does not 
appear that it contains any terms to which any 
exception could reasonably be taken by the employ- 
ers, O.P.W. | states clearly that he and his

৯১ 


partners, employers, received remuneration from 
Messrs. G. Patel & Co. on peice-rate basis and they 
on their part paid the muttiahs on the daily baais 
of Rs. 3 per diem. This clearly shows that the 
five employers employ muttiahs whom they pay 
on daily rates, while the employers themselves 
receive remuneration on piece-rates. The learned 
Advocate for the employers stated that the con- 
tractors are really manual labourers and when they 
cowd not do the work themselves they engaged 
some casual workers. The learned Advocate also 
stated thut these 18 men mentioned in the order of 
reference were never employed by the five con- 
tractors. He also pointed out that no permanent 
status could be attached to the Khata workers, us 
they were really casual workers. The evidence of 
0۶۳٢٢. 1 shows that although he denied that the 
18 workmen mentioned in the order of reference 
ever worked under him and other contractors, he 
states that it may be that the 18 men sometimes 
worked with them, From the evidence on record 
I come to the conclusion that these 18 workmen 
whose names are mentioned in the order of refer- 
ence worked as Khata workers under the five con- 
irgotors, and these five contractors made an Agree- 
ment (Ext. 1) with the Union in respect of the 
work of the muttiahs under them including the 18 
workmen in question, The Khata workers are 
always casual workers und they are = given work 
when work is available, but they get priority over 
the Nagda workers as it appears in the Agreement 
(Ext. 1) itself. The dismissal of a Khata work- 
man meuns that he is not given work. The 18 
workmen in question are Khata workmen and 
should be given work whenever work is available. 


In the circumstances, it is awarded that the 18 
workmen mentioned in the order of reference are 
1008৮ workers and they should be given employ- 
ment as occasion arises and they will get the 
priority in point of employment over the Nagda 
workers or any other workmen who might have 
been taken in their place after the present dispute 
arose. 

In the circumstances of the case 1 do not con- 
sider that any other relief is called for. This issue 
is accordingly answered.

was referred under section 10 of the Industrial 
Disputes Act to this Tribunal for adjudication of 
only one issue, viz., ‘‘gratuity’’. The employer, 
Messrs. Leonard Biermans, is a Company incor- 
porated in Belgium which has a factory in Calcutta 
for manufacture of playing cards and the Union's 
case is that the Company is a very prosperous con-. 
cern having almost a monopoly of the business of 
manufacture and sale of playing cards of high 
quality and is in a position to introduce a scheme 
of gratuity but has not done so inspite of the 
Union’s demand preferred in 1957, The Union 
claims that the Company should be directed to 
adopt a scheme providing for payment of gratuity 
ut the rate of half month’s wages for each com- 
pleted year of service in the event of death or 
retirement of a workman. 


The Company has pleaded its inability to intro- 
duce any scheme of gratuity 1n view of its dete- 
riorating financial position. It has denied that it 
18 & prosperous concern and stated that it waa 
actually incurring heavy losses year after year and 


in consequence is unable to hear any additional 
financial burden. : 


The 0896. Wits heard in this Tribunal from 23rd 
June 1960 to 24th June 1960. Two witnesses were 
exammed for the Company and one for the Union.
