The Company’s balance-sheets und other docu- 
ments as also certain documents filed by the Union 
were tuken in evidence and marked as exhibits. 


It should be noted here in the year 1904 certain 
disputes arose between the Company and its work- 
men which were referred to this Tribunal. They 
related among others to revision of pay scales and 
additional bonus for two years. The matters in 
dispute were, however, settled and an award was 

assed based on the terms of the said settlement. 
‘he Company revised the scales of pay and the 
demand for additional bonus was not pressed by the 
Union. In that case also the Company appears to 
have taken the plea of financial incapacity and it 
is said that the Union did not press the claim for 
additional bonus on that ground. 


The Company has produced before me _ its 
balance-sheets for the years 1953-1959 and also a 
summary of the figures in the balance-sheets 
(Exts. F and )٢ series), The balance-sheets show 
that the Company last made a profit of Rs. 14,660 
in the year 1903 and has since then been consist- 
ently sustaining losses which in the year ending 
3lst May 1956 amounted to Rs. 94,665. From 
19417 the Company’s financial year was changed 
and it was made to correspond to the calendar 
year, In that year the Company's losses amount- 
ed to Rs. 127,697 The Company's next financial 
year covered the period from Ist January 1958 to 
to 80th June 1959 and during the year the losses 
amounted to 10 4,08,269. ‘The Company's 
system of keeping accounts is to adjust the losses 
against the capital. By such adjustment the 
Company's capital has now been reduced to zero. 
Evidence has been given that the Company now 
operates only on loans and overdrafta which are 
also mentioned in the later balance-shects. The 
‘ompany accordingly pleads that it 1s not in a 
position to bear any further financial burden. 


The reasons for this position have also been 
explained by the Manager and the Accountant of 
the Company. The Company formerly used to 
export high quality playing card sheets printed in 
Belgium, but in 1953 the Government of India 
stopped such import. The Company also imported 
flint paper from Belgium, but since the quota 
syatem was introduced for such import the Com- 
pany’s quota was reduced from. year to year and 
the statement (Ext. FE) shows that while the quota 
was for Rs, 77,652 during 1954-56 it was reduced 
in later years and in 1958 it amounted to 
78. 14,559 and in 1960 to Rs. 19,418. The Com- 
pany has also to face severe competition from 
other card manufacturers in India and it has to 
sell high quality cards which it manufactures in 
India at a loss because it cannot increase the prices 
in view of the competition. According to the 
evidence, the Company makes a little profit out of 
its sale of ordinary cards which also it manufac- 
tures, 


The Union has contended that the balance- 
sheets of the পি did not present a correct 
icture of its financial position and a suggestion 
مہ‎ been made that tho figures in the  balange- 
sheets have heen manipulgted. Two letters from 
the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies have heen 


produced showing that the Company did not file 


its balance-sheets annually and that the balance- 
sheets from 1954 to 1959 were filed together in 
December 1959. ''he Union had also referred to 
the fact that the Company changed its auditors 
from time to time and has relied upon ৮ letter 
written by one of its nuditors on 15th November 
1955 which contained certain observations regard. 
ing irregularities in keeping the accounts. This 
letter is Ext. H and it was produced by the Com- 
pany. The letter does not show, however, that 
the irregularities mentioned were of a serious 
nature. I do not find any reason to suspect from 
this letter that the Company manipulated 0৭ 
accounts or the figures in the balance-sheets for 
any ulterior purpose. It has been pointed out that 
in the recent balance-sheets for 1957 to 1959 the 
figures of sales show on evidence over the fivures 
of previous years, The Company's Accountant 
has, however, explained, as stated above, that the 
increase in sales did not affect the losses. because 


a Company had to sell high quality curds at a 
Oss. 


It has been argued that the figures in tho 
balance-sheets should not be accepted as correct 
without proof from relevant books and registers, 
I should mention in this connection that the 
Union made an application on 2nd December 1959 
praying for a direction on the Company to produce 
certain registers and account books and allow 
ما‎ thereof. The Company objected — to 
such production and the matter was heard on 18th 
December 1959 when the Company was directed 
to produce the audited balance-sheets and to allow 
inspection of the account books mentioned in the 
application by the Union's lawyer in the (Com- 
pany’s office. The Union complainod on 6th 
January 1960 that the Company had not allowed 
such inspection. It appears, however, from the 
petitions and correspondence on record that the 
Company did not actually :efuse inspection either 
by the General Secretary or by the lawyer of the 
Unoin but objected to inspection by two repre- 
sentatives of the Union who accompanied the 
lawyer. In terms of the order passed on 18th 
December 1959 the Company was quite justified in 
refusing inspection by persons other than the 
Union’s lawyer, The persons objected to were 
retrenched employees of the Company. The ins- 
pection could have been made by the lawyer aud 
the Secretary of the Union but this was not done. 
This matter was heard on 27th February = 1960) 
when the Tribunal was informed that the appli. 
cation for production of the account books would 
not be pressed by the Union on condition that the 
Company produced its  balance-sheets for — the 
years 194-58. The Company then produced its 
audited balance-sheets for 1953-59 which were 
inspected by the Union’s lawyer. Finally the 
Union filed a potition on 30th May 1960 stating 
that it challenged the correctness of the figures in 
the balance-sheets and that the Company should 
support the figures by production of its account 
books and registers. It has heen argued that the 
balance-sheets should be wholly rejected because 
the Company has not adduced any evidence in 
support of the same from ita books and registers. 

Reference has been made دا‎ this connection to 
two recent decisions of the Supreme Courtr in the 
cases of Khandesh Spinning and Weaving Mills 
Company, Ltd., and Pelted Turkey Red Dye Works 


Paar 1[ 


Company, Ltd., reported in 1960, ۱ L.L.J. pages 
541 and 548 respectively. In these cases, however, 
the formula laid down by the Full Bench of the 
Labour Appellate Tribunal for the calculation of 
net surplus for award of bonus was being consi- 
dered and the question which arose for decision 
was whether the figures in a balance-sheet could 
be taken as proof of a claim of what portion of the 
reserve had actually heen used as working capital 
without any evidence being given in support of 
such a claim apart from the balance-sheet. It was 
held that a mere statement in a balance-sheet was 
not sufficient proof on the point and that the 
burden was on the party who asserted such stute- 
ment to be correct to prove the same by relevant 
and acceptable evidence. The observations in 
these two cases were thus made in connection with 
the particular question which arose for decision 
therein and it cannot be contended that the result 
of these decisions is that all the statements and 
figures in an audited balance-sheet should | 
suspected and held to be incorrect until they ure 
supported and corroborated by other evidence. 


In the present case we are concerned with no 
such question. The only question for our decision 
is whether the Company has the financial capacity 
to bear the burden of 8 (86010) scheme. The 
Company has taken the plea that it is sustaining 
losses and has relied upon the balance-sheets in 
support of the plea. The profit and loss accounts 
in the balance-sheets support that plea. What 
reason is there to suspect that all these figures are 
incorrect and have been manipulated for an ulterior 
purpose? It has not heen suggested what that 
ulterior purpose may be, Inspite of its deteriorat- 
ing financial position in 1954, the Company revis- 
ed the pay scales of its employees 11) agreement 
with the Union and the Union then withdrew the 
claim for additional honus presumably in view of 
the financial position of the Company. The Com- 
pany cannot then he accused of any anti-{ mon 
bias. It would he preposterous to suggest that 11) 
anticipation of a demand for gratuity which was 
preferred in 1957 the Company would have mani- 
pulated its balance-sheets for 1955 and ۱۹۹۰ 0110 
shown Josses therein. In the case of Associated 
fement Companies Ltd, (1999—I—I.1.J. page 
044) which was also a bonus case the Supreme 
Court held that the amount of gross 10115 aa 
ascertained in the profit and loss account should, 
as a general rule, be accepted without submitting 
the profit and loss account دا‎ a close scrutiny, 
unless it appeared that the entries on the debit 
side had been made deliberately and mala fide to 
reduce the amount of gross profits. The same view 
was reiterated in the recent case of Kapoor and 
Company, reported in 1900-17-71.) page 410. 

Tn the present case no particular item. on the 
debit side of the profit and loss accounts has heon 
chollenged as mala fide or incorrect and only a 
general and vague suggestion has heen made that 
the balance-sheets have been manipulated. The

Company did not merely file its balance-sheets but 
examined its Accountant and tendered him for 
cross-examination, He was cross-eaamined only 
with reference to the item of ‘general expensen’’ 
in the balance-sheets previous to the year ending 
on 186 May 1956. At that time, as the Account- 
ant explained, expenses under the heads of salaries 
of staff excluding wages, temporary allowances, 
medical benefits, legal expenses, bonus, insurance 
charges, postage and other such items were not 
seperately shown but were grouped together under 
the head “general expenses’’. ا مرا‎ a change 
was made and the different heads which were for- 
merly grouped together under the head of ‘“gene- 
ral expenses’’ were shown separately in the 
halance-sheets. He was not cross-examined with 
respect to any other item. It may he that the 
Company had a peculiar system of keeping 
accounts or had changed its financial yoar and 
auditor more than once or had not regularly 
filed its balance-sheets before the Rogistrar 
of Juint Stock Companies, but all these would 
be no ground for suspecting the statements 
in its balance-sheets or rejecting them, In a case 
like this where uo question of calculation of 
surplus is involved but the only question is the 
financial capacity of the Company, the general 
picture prosented by the balance-sheets should be 
taken fo he correct even though the figures therein 
might not have heen supported by hooks, registers 
and vouchers. The accounts were audited nai 
bear certificates of the auditors that they had 
inspected the supporting hooks and vouchers. 
They should therefore be taken to represent the 
correct financial position of the Company, us 
certified hy the auditors. 


In a caso of gratuity the financial capacity of 
the employer is a most relevant consideration, and 
as the Supreme Court observed رز‎ the ense of 
Indian Hume Pipe Co, Ltd., 1050-71-71). 
830, it is only when the Tribunal is satisfied 1 
the financial condition of the ewployer is satisfac- 
tory and the burden of a gratuity scheiye can he 
borne by the employer that a acheme of gratuity 
should he framed. As the Company has heen 
consistently sustaining losses for the last few 
vears it ia clear that it is not in a position to bear 
the burden of gratuity and the claim should, 
therefore, he rejected. JT award accordingly.

G.S.R. 656.—In exercise of the powers conferred 
by sub-section (2) of section 1 of the Estate Duty 
(Amendment) Act, 1958 (33 of 1968), the Central 
Government, hereby, appoints the lst day of July 
1960, as the date on which the said Act shall come 
into force. 


Explanatory Note 


(This note is not part of the notification but is 
intended to be merely clarificatory.) 

The Estate Duty (Amendment) Act, 1958, as 
passed thy Parliament received the assent of the 
President on the 19th September 1958. The pro- 
visions of that Act could, however, be given effect 
to only after the necessary resolutions under article 
202 of the Conatitution had heen passed hy the 
State Legislatures. Sub-section (2) of section 1 of 
the Act accordingly provided that the Act was to 
come into force on such date as the Central Gov- 
ernment may, by notification in the official gazette, 
appoint. The necessary resolutions under article 
252 having since been passed, the Central Govern- 
ment have decided to bring the Act into force with 
effect from the Ist July 1960.

at the Bengal Engineering College, Session 
1960-61. 


Tn terms of Government order No. 4192Edn., 
dated 23rd July 1938, as amended in Government 
order No. 136Kdn., dated 1010) January 1940, and 
Government order No. 5684Edn. of the 18th 
August 1952, Shri Hariprosad Horal, a student ot

nomination of the Donor, the Bimala Churn Law

ANNEXURE 


in the matter of a complaint under section 33A of 
the Industrial Disputes Aet, filed by two 
employees, namely, (i) Sitaram Mahato and 
(ii) Deodhari Kahar, against Messrs. Fate 
chand Jahurimull and others, 2/2B Armenian 
Street, Calcutta, in connection with Covern- 
ment order No. 144-1.R./1R /11L-657 /58, dated 
the 15th January 1959, (Case No. 145 of 1959, 
under section 33A.) 


BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL 
TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


Present: 


Shri K. K. MITRA, Judge, Fourth Industrial 


Tribunal. 


For the workmen: Shri Panchanan Bhattacherjee. 


For the Company: Shri Nalini Mohan Das Gupta, 
Advocate. 


This is an application under section 33A of the 
Industrial نا او‎ Act preferred by two employees 
namely, (i) Sitaram Mahato and (ii) Deodhar 
Kahar, against Messrs Fatechand Jahurimull and 
others, complaining that their services were wrong- 
fully terminated by the Company, without the leave 
of the Tribunal, in writing, before which a 
proceeding was pending at the relevant time. 


2018 


সি টপ সসেজ AIEEE‏ جوا 
সস সপ পপ সপ স্পা‏ 


It is contended that Sitaram Mahato was verbally 


diamissed on 8th October 1959 after he had put in 
three yeurs’ service under the employer, and that 
the other workman Deodhari Kashar was also 


similarly dismissed on 26th September 1959 after 
he had put in 14 months’ service. 


The opposite party, the employer filed a written 
objection challenging the maintainability of the 
application. It is 2 contended that Sitaram 

ahato was taken in employment as a temporary 
worker on 27th July 1959 and his temporary 
employment was terminated by way of retrench- 
ment on 7th October 1959. Regarding the other 
workman, viz., Deodbari Kahar, it 1s contended 
that he was also a temporary workman and that he 
voluntarily left the service on 22nd May 1959 when 

went away to his native place. It is thus 
স্পা that the applicants have'no case on merits 
as well. 


Obviously, an application under section 994 of 
the Industrial Disputes Act would be maintainable 
in law if the employer had contravened the provi- 
sions of section 33 of the Industrial Disputes Act. 
Under section 0ت‎ (b) restrictions had been 
imposed upon employer against discharge or 
punishment by dismissal or otherwise, any work- 
man concerned in the dispute while it is pending 
before the Tribunal, for ahy misconduct connected 
with the said dispute. If the employer wants to 
discharge by way of dismissal or otherwise any 
workman for anything considered as misconduct 
done by the employee which is connected with the 
dispute, he cannot take such action save and 
except with the prior permission in writing of the 
Tribunel. The case as made out by the employer 
is that the provision in section 33 was 
not violated at all when the workman Sitaram 
Mahato was in fact retrenched. It was also not 
necessary to take such permission of the Tribunal 
when the other workman Deodhari Kahar left the 
services of his own accord, It is urged by the 
learned lawyer for the 00 that the question 
of taking permission would arise only when the 
employer wants to discharge or punish, by way of 
dismissal or otherwise any workman. An employer 
bas otherwise the freedom to terminate the service 
of a workman for any reason whatsoever other than 
for misconduct connected with the dispute pending 
before the Tribunal. Evidently, section 33¢1)(b) 
of the Industrial Disputes Act puts a restriction 
and imposes an obligation upon the employer and 
lays down the procedure to be followed when he 
wants to punish or discharge by way of dismissal 
or otherwise any workman during the pendency 
of a dispute before the Tribunal. Section 33A of 
the Industrial Disputes Act confers a statutory 
right upon an employee, to move directly the 
تس و‎ without depending upon the discretion of 
the Government to refer the matter of controversy 
as an industrial dispute, for adjudication, when 
he feels that there has been a violation of auch 

rovisions. Naturally when an employee stands 

igmiaged, he ascribes the action taken against him 
by the employer as mala fide or arising out of a 
spirit of victimisation, or actuated by unfair 
labour practice. It is the common: case of both 
the parties that there had been termination of 
services of both these workmen during fhe pendency 
of the proceeding before the Tribunal. The 
termination of service arising from voluntary 


THE OALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, AUGUST 12, 1960 


{ Parr I 


Foo 


resignation, as alleged by the employer with respect 
to Deodhani Kahar or arising from bona fide 
retrenchment as alleged in the case of Sitaram, if 
established, would take away the dispute outside 
the scope of section 33 ‘of the Industrial Disputes 
Act. It is only in case of a termination of service 
as a result of a decision of the employer to 
discharge or punish by way of dismissal or other- 
wise a workman for any misconduct which can be 
linked up with the pending dispute, that adjudica- 
tion by the Tribunal in the same manner as in the 
case of an industrial dispute referred to it by the 
Government is called for. 


Let me now consider how the termination of 
services in these two cases took place. It appeara 
from Ext. 0 which is a copy of the award published 
in the ‘‘Calcutta Gazette’’, dated September 17, 
1969, that the industrial dispute relating to two 
issues, Viz., (1) Dearness Allowance and (21) 
Permanency of Service of certain workmen, as 
between the three employers’ viz., (i) Messrs. 
Champalal Agarwala, (ii) Messrs. Fati Chand 
Jahurimull and (iii) Messrs. Fati Chand Tara 
Chand, and their workmen was decided in terms of 
a settlement effected between the parties on the 
date of hearing of the dispute before the Tribunal, 
1.0., on ط270‎ August 1959. In terms of the settle- 
ment embodied in the award, workers were given 
increase in dearness allowance by Rs. 5 per month 
and temporary workers, if any, were to be made 
permanent on completion of one year’s approved 
service. In the background of the change in 
condition of service, effected by the award, let me 
consider which of the versions of the contesting 
parties is true. 


There is no controversy on the point that the 
vervice of Sitaram Mahato was terminated on 8th 
October 1959. The award published on 17th 
September 1959 became enforceable on the expiry 
of 30 days from the date of its publication. The 
date of termination is just a few days before the 
award became enforceable in law and, therefore, 
during the pendency of the proceeding. The 
contention of the employer is that Sitaram was 
appointed as a temporary worker on 27th July 1959. 
In support of the same a letter, dated 26th July 
1959, was produced at the time of hearing. [6 is 
however significant to note that the opposite party 
atated in the written objection filed on 1dth Januar 
1960, that a letter, dated 27th July 1959, purport 
to have been addressed by Sitaram was being 
enclosed and marked Annexure ‘‘A’’, though in 
fact no such letter was enclosed, as an annexure. 
At the time of hearing the letter, Ext. B, said to 
have been written by the brother of O.P.W. 1, 
Sumureala, a partner of the Company, is produced, 
as the letter referred in the written’ کو ہگ‎ 
The conduct of the employer is highly suspicioua 
and I am not prepared to place any reliance upon 
this document, Ext. B. Sitaram denied having 
given his thumb impression in any such paper. 
The impreasion by itself is blurred. The employer 
has got pay register nnd attendance register. 
These are not produced. Considering the evidence 
as a whole, ] accept the version of Sitaram that his 
service had heen terminated at a time when he had 
put in more than three years of services 
Apparently Ext. B is a manufactured dooument 
created with ulterior motive, 


Past 1] 


٭ سج ےم 
ہر 


Sitaram stated that he demanded increased wages 
as under the award and the employer refused to pay 
and drove him away on the ground that there was 
no work. It appears from Ext. 3, a_ letter 
addressed to a worker Suraj Pandey that he was 
given increase in D.A. at Rs. 56 and made 
permanent with effect from the very date, that 18 
8th September 1959, when Sitaram was discharged. 
But the fact remains that it is not the case of either 
the employer or the workmen that the dismissal 
was based on any allegation of misconduct. The 
remedy available under section 33A is restricted to 
case of discharge or punishment arising from an 
allegation of misconduct. When the discharge 
took place on an allegation by the employer that 
there was not sufficient work to keep the workmen 
employed, the point arises for consideration if the 
retrenchment is bona fide. But I am afraid, a case 
as to contravention of section 33(1)(b) cannot be 
made when the employer discharges an employee, 
not 10] any misconduct but for any other reason 
bona fide or otherwise. 


So far as the other workman, I find from his own 
statement that he went away home in the month of 
Jaistha. The employer alsn stated that he went 
away on 22nd May 1959. While the employee 
stated that he went away on leave, the employer’s 
version is that he went away after resignation after 
getting all his dues. From the evidence I am 
inclined to accept the version of the employer. So, 
Deodhari cannot get any relief whatsoever as 
clearly there was no question of his discharge or 
punishment By way of dismissal or otherwise. The 
application, therefore, fails though for different 
reason with respect to the two workmen. 


K. K. MITRA,

the plea that a refusal to employ was a lock-out

26. ۱ have given my best consideration to .he 
matter, and 4 am of the opinion that the objection 
of the learned Counsel, as atated above, is un- 
woithy of support for the following reasons. The 
issue really means that the listed workmen were 
not employed by the Company and the Tribunal 
has been asked to adjudicate on the jurisdiction of 
this non-employment of the workmen, The Com- 
pany has explained in its written statement the 
grounds for refusing to give employment to these 
workmen in question which were for various 
reasons including dismissal and discharge. It is 
competent for the Tribunal to confine its adjudica- 
tion to the points referred to it by the Government 
and also to matters incidenta] thereto. On the 

leadings of the parties, the Tribunal has to adju- 
ae on the issue as to the justification of the 
refusal of the Company to employ the workmen till 
the date of reference on the grounds as set forth 
by the Company, viz., dismissal, discharge, suspen- 
sion pending enquiry, etc. It is, therefore, clear 
that the Tribunal wil] he competent and even 
obliged to adjudicate completely as to the cause of 
the refusal of the Company to employ the listed 
workmen, to assess justification of such act on the 
part of the employer. In the circumstances. the 
suggestion of the learned Counsel for the Company 
that the case of 54 men, who are alleged to have 
been dismissed and the 41 men who were suspend. 
ed, were not within the issue No. 1 as referred to 
the Tribunal, is unworthy of acceptance. Tho 
Tribunal will, therefore, adjudicate completely on 
the non-employment of the 429 men listed in the 
order of reference and aacertain os to the justifica- 
tion or otherwise of such non-employment.

workmen, was passing in a procession along the 
Jessore Road, and never did he or the others 
terrorise the Durwans, nor expressed any intention 
of breaking the costly installations of the Company. 
He was also not in « position to accept the other 
charges as of throwing brickbats on durwans and 
the police pickets, forcible occupation of factory, 
etc, It is eerie stuted that under the leadership 
of Lalji Durwan along with police pickets, goondas 
rushed towards the peaceful processionists armed 
with iron rods, etc. and assaulted them seriously, 
causing fatal injuries to 10 persons. There is no 
evidence on record to show that any one of the 
workers was injured on 23rd February 1958, and 
the evidence of P.W. 3 Shah Muhammad, states 
that although durwans and other people were ston- 
ing the peaceful workmen near the factory, none 
of the workmen were injured. It is noticeable that 
while the explanations, Ext. I. series, state that a 
peaceful procession was passing by the factory, 
which was stoned and brickbatted by the durwans, 
the witnesses, being the General Secretary, P.W. 
1 and P.W, 3 Shah Muhammad state that there 
was u meeting near the factory and P.W. 3 states 
that no one of the meeting was injured, P.W. 1 
Shri Fatick Ghosh states that there was no tear- 
gassing by the police on 23rd February 1958. The 
police used tear yas on the road and on _ the 
durwans, who were chasing the people on the road. 
The tear gas was not used on the meeting. The 
workers were not tear-gassed. The evidence of the 
witnesses on the side of the Union shows that the 
durwans were stoning the workmen who were 
engaged in a meeting near the factory and the 
evidence of Shri Fatick Ghosh also shows that the 
durwans were chusing the workmen on the road 
Shah Muhammad says that no workmen was injur- 
ed. Exts. C series shows that as many as 9 of the 
durwans and other men on the Company’s side 
were injured on 23rd February 1958, and were 
given first-aid hy the R. G. Kar Medical College 
flospital. In view of the circumstances on record, 
and the disparity in the evidence on the Umion’s 
side, ] corae to the conclusion that the evidence 
adduced on the side of the Company in respect of 
the incident happening on 21:0 February 1958 
should he accepted. The learned spokesman for 
the Union pointed my attention to the fact that

40. The learned) spokesinan for the Union 


pressed that the order of suspension of the workers 
wus not proper, as there was no Standing Order of 
the Company under which it could suspend 06 
workers pending enquiry, and the Company had 
therefore no power to suspend any worker, Docu- 
ments, Exts. 17 and 1108) show that تا‎ March, 
1959, the Union’s objection on the proposed Stund- 
ing Orders for the Company was betug considered 
by the Labour Commissioner, and the evidence of 
QO.P.W. 5 Shri B. ما‎ Jaiswal is also to the effect 
that between February, 1958, and October, 19058, 
the Company had no Certified Standing Orders and 
they had submitted the Standing Orders for certi- 
fication before February, 1908. The learned 
spokesman for the Union cited the case reported 
in 1956 ۸.۱:1٠.. Madras, 150, to show that in the 
case of a private employment the powers of »us- 
pension may he specifically contracted for and 
even if the power exists, the employer cannot with- 
hold salary for the duration of the suspension 
unless the misconduct to enquire into which the 
suspension was ordered is proved to have been 
made out. This principle ix not in question here. 
The question raised here is if the Company can at 
all order suspension of a workman pending enquiry 
into charges against him. The decision of the 
Hon'ble Supreme Court m the case of Luxmidevi 
Sugar Mills, reported in 1997(1) L..L.J., 17, shows 
that suspension without pay even for an indefinite 
period pending enquiry or pending permission of 
the appropriate Tribunal to dismiss a workman 
could not be held to be a punishment which would 
require permission of the Tribunal before the same 
could be meted out to the workmen. In the case 
of Hotel Imperial, reported 01819029011) 15154), 
44, the Hon’ble Supreme Court approved of the 
decision of the Hon'ble Court in the case of 
Luxmidevi Sugar Mills. )ا‎ is stated that the ratio 
of the decisions of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in 
the case of Luxmidevi Sugar Mills or in the case 
of Susan Musa Sugar Mills. (9)9(1T) L.f.d., 388, 
was not bused on the presence or absence of 
Standing Orders, for there is very little difference 
between cases where Stunding Orders provided for 
au few days’ suspension without pay and the suspen- 
sion was continued for a much longer period and 
where there was no Standing Orders providing 
suspension without pay. The Hon'ble Court is of 
the opinion that though those eases did not express- 
ly proceed on the basis of an implied term in the 
contract of employment to suspend the employee, 
that must be the implicit basis on which — these 
decisions were given, The IJlon’ble Court ھا‎ 
therefore, of the opinion that the ordinary law of 
master and servant should be held to have been 
modified in view of the fundamental change intro- 
duced in Section 83> by that Jaw and a term should 
be imphed by Industrial Tribunals in the contract 
of employment that if the master has held a proper 
enquiry and come to the conclusion that the servant 
should be dismissed and 018 consequence suspend 
him pending permission requred under Section 


33, he has the powers to order such auspension. ١ 
therefore, appears that the employer has the right 
to suspend the workers pending enquiry into the 
charges against him and such a term should be 
considured to be implied in the contract of employ- 
ment. There is, therefore, no doubt that the

Issue No. 3 Medical attention for workers injured 
during working hours. 


57. In regard to Issue No. 3, the Union pleads 
that there is no first aid arrangement in the factory 
for attending workmen injured during working 
hours. The Union prays for arrangements for 
medical attention for workers during working 
hours. The Company states, in its written atate- 
ment, that provision for medical attention has been 
made in accordance with the requirements of law. 
In evidence P.W. 1, Shri Fatick Ghosh states that 
there is no arrangement for first aid or other 
medical facilities to the workmen injured in course 
of their work. O,P.W. 5 states in evidence that 
the Company has got first aid arrangements in the 
factory, that there is ۸ Compounder in the factory 
for medical attention of the workers and the Com- 
pany :ح‎ medical expenses to the workers who are 
injured during work and the Company also bears 
medical expenses when the workers are injured. 
A part-time Medical Officer, Dr. J. C. Biswas, was 
employed hv the Company, but he has aince 
resigned and he is now a doctor of the Municipality. 
The Companv has now got two other doctors, both 
graduates in Medicine, to whom they send cases for 
treatment. The witness also atates in his  crosa- 
examination that the Company has got no limitation 
for payment of medical expenses and in apecial 
cases, they allow medical expenses to the workers 
till thev are fullv fit. In these circumstances, it 
appears that the Company have made good arrange- 
ment for medical aid and these should continue. 


I award accordingly.

vacancy, shall be six months instead af 12 
months.

DEVELOPMENT DEPARTMENT 


Durgapur Industries Board 


RESOLUTION 


No. 201 /2D-1/6U.—25th June 1960.—In modification of the Finance 
Department resolution No, 22715F.B., dated 27th December 1955, consti- 
tuting a Board for the س۲۲ َو‎ und administration of industries in the 
Durgapur area such us Coke Oven, Tar Distillation, Power Generation, Gas 
Generation and distribution, production and sale of other chemicals and by- 
products, etc., the Governor is pleased to lay down the following rules in 
accordance with which the said Board shall act:— 


i—Constitution of the Board 


1. The Board shall be constituted by the State Government by notifica- 
tion in the official Gazette and shall consist of such members as the State 
Government may appoint.. The terms of office of members of the 1301৭] 
shall be as determined by the State Government from time to time: 


Provided that— 


(i) the State Government may by notification direct that a member 
shall cease to be a member from a specified date and the notifica- 
tion shall have effect accordingly ; 

(11) the State Government may at any time by notification appoint anv 
person to be a member of the Board in addition to the existing 
members; and 

(iii) a member may resign his office by giving a month's notice in 
writing addressed to the State Government. 


i i— Headquarters 
2. The Board shall have its headquarters at Calcutta. 


1tij—-Ceneral Powers and Duties of the Board 


3. The Board shall administer the funds placed at its disposal by tho 
State Government for the purposes for which the Board is constituted. 


4. (a) The Boanl shall exercise general supervision and control over 
the different industries that may be set up by it; 

(b) The Board shall frame its annual budget in such form as may be 
prescribed by the State Government and shall submit the same to Govern- 
meat for approval by such date as may be fixed in this behalf by the State 
(Jovernment. 

(c) The Board shall keep proper accounts of the moneys received and 
expended by it and publish an annual statement of accounts duly audited 
in the manner 00755010060 by the State Government and an annual report 
embracing its activities. 

(4) Within the budget provisions as approved by the State Government, 
the Board shall have power generally to do such things as may be considered 
necessary or expedient for the proper discharge of ita duties and functions 
এ such power shall not be limited in any way except as provided in these 
rules: 


Provided that this power shall not include power to purchase motor 
vehicles and air conditioning plants and incur other unusual expenditure for 
which prior sanction of Government ৪0481] be required. 


(e) The Board may, subject to provisions in the budget as approved 
by the State Government and subject only to the limitations prescribed by 
the Government in these rules, create posts for such periods and in suc 
pay scale and on such terms and conditions as may be considered necessary 
from time to time for the proper performance of its work, and make appoint- 
tnents thereto. 


5, Without prejudice to the general powers conferred in paragraph 
4(d) above, the rd shall have the following powers, that is to aay, 
powers— 


(i) to allot land for setting up new industries in Durgapur area cither 
in the private or متا‎ sector; 

(11) to demand security from its employees in such cases and of such 
amount as the Board thi fit;

(111) to exercise disciplinary control over its employees, provided that

6. The general powers conferred to the Board under paragraph 4(d)

(1) undertaking of works of a capital nature including purchase of

lukh shall be referred to the State Government for approval

(11) no post carrying pay exceeding Rs. 1,200 per month or a scale of

V—Powers and Duties of the Board during operational stage 


7. The Board shall exercise the following powers during the operational 
stage of any industrial undertaking that has gone into production or that 
might go into production subsequently سے‎ 


(i) It shall manage the undertakings set up by it or placed under its 
charge by the State Government, operate and maintain them, sell 
their products and may generally do such ‘things as may be 
deemed necessary or expedient for the preper discharge of its 
duties and functions in this regard. 

(21) It shall frame u separate annual budget showing the expenditure 
on operation and maintenance of the undertakings and the 
revenue receipts and shall submit the same to Government for 
approval by such date as may be fixed in this behalf by the State 
Giovernment. 

(11) Without prejudice to the powers conferred in sub-clause (i) above, 
the Board shall have the following powers relating to the 
management of the industrial undertakings, including their 
operation and maintenance, that is 160) say, powers—

indirect, subject to the provisions in the budget and to autho- 
rise purchase of general stores, spare parts, equipments, etc., 
and to incur expenditure on supplies und services, as may be 
necessary and expedient, up to a limit of Rs. ٤ lakh in each 


Case ; 

(b) to authorise, subject to provisions in the budget as approved by 
the State Government, employment of such staff, on such 
terms and conditions and for such periods, as it may from time 
to time consider necessary, provided that no post carrying pay 
exceeding Rs, 800 per month or a scale of pay the maximum, 
of which is above Rs. 860 per month shall be created by the 
Board without the approval of the State Government ; 

(c) to arrange disposal and sale of products of the industrial under- 
takings, at such prices and under such terms and conditions as 
it may deem reasonable and proper, provided that the rates 
fixed as well as subsequent changes in the rates, if any, shall 
be communicated to Government; 

(d) to fix tariff for supply of electricity, gas, water or other services 
at such rates and under such terms and conditions as it may 
deem reasonable and proper, provided that the rates fixed as 
well as subsequent changes in the rates, if any, shall be com- 
municated to the Government; 

(e) to enter into such negotiations and contracts and rescind and 
vary al) such contracts as deemed necessary or expedient for 
the proper discharge of its duties und functions ; 

(f) to sanction writing off of irrecoverable value of stores or money 
lost by theft, fraud, negligence or other causes and of losses of 
revenue, irrecoverable loans and advances and to sanction 
remission of and abandonment of claims in this regard up to a 
limit of Rs. 5,000 in each case;

No. 2310F.T.—6th August 1960.—In exercise of 
the power conferred by clause (a) of sub-section (1) 
of section 9 of the Indian Stamp Act, 1899 (II of 
1899), the Governor is pleased hereby to remit in 
the whole of West Bengal the duties with which 
an instrument of agreement in respect of tenements 
allotted by the (Government of West Bengal to 
displaced persons is chargeable under the said 
Act. 


Ezplanation.—In this notification a “displaced 
person” means a person who was ordinarily resi- 
dent in the territories pow comprised in East 
Pakistan, but who on account of civil disturbances 
or on account of the partition of India, has 
migrated— 


(a) in the case of persons migrating from the 
district of Noakhali or the district of 


Comilla, now forming part of East 
Pakistan, on or after the lat October 1946, 
and 


(b) in the case of persona migrating from any 
other area in East Pakistan, on or after 
the Ist June 1947, 


to the territories now included in the Union of 
India, with the intention of taking up permanent 
residence within auch territories, 


By order of the (Governor,

THE COMMISSIONERS FOR THE PORT OF 
CALCUTTA 


Notification No. By 2A 


THE following revised By-law No. 4A_ having been 
confirmed by the Government of India in the Ministry of 
Traneport and Communications, has been incorporated by 
the Commissioners in the By-laws for the Port of Calcutta 
(in substitution of the existing By-law No. 4A) in 
accordance with the provisions of section 126 of the 
Calcutta Port Act, 1890 (Bengal Act IIT of 1890):— 


By-law No. 4A—Grant of Stevedoring Licence 


“Stevedoring Licence’’.—‘4A (i) The Commissioners 
shall, from year to year, issue licences to companies, firms 
and individuals a proved by the Commissioners, permittin 
sich companies, firms and individuals to perform the wor 
of atevedoring vessels in the Port, and no stevedoro shall 
be allowed to work on board ظا ای‎ in the Port without 
holding such a licence. The mmissioners may without 
assigning any reasons revoke, cancel or suspend for any 
period of time any such licence at any time they think fit 
and proper or refuse to renew any such licence. 


(ii) The grant of stevedoring licences under clause (1) 
shall be subject to the applicants for such licences having 
fulfilled the following conditions, vis.:— 


(a) That the applicant has in his سرت‎ such number 
of qualified and fully trained staff, to execute pro- 
per supervision of work on board vessels, as is 
considered essential by the Commissioners and 
stipulated by them, and that the applicant under- 
takes in writing to engage workers, of the various 
categorien registered with the Calcutta Dock 
Labour Board, in suffinent numbers for the pro- 
ner discharge of his stevedoring duties and satisfy 

rovisions of booking such workers as is required 
۶ the rules and regulations governing stevedoring 
work in force in the Port; 


(b) That the applicant has in his possession for the due 
performance of his work, such proper and suffi- 
cient gear as may be preacribed by the Commis- 
sioners from time to time and undertakes to 
produce such gear for inspection by the person or 
persons authorised by the Commissioners on their 
behalf for this purpose before the application for 
licence is finally considered ; 


(6) That the apphcant furnishes documentary evidence 
that a Steamship Company or a Charterer of 
vessels authorised to appoint its own atevedors is 
prepared to enter into a contract with the appli- 
cant for stevedoring of its vessels; 


(3) That the applicant has financial ability to meet 
01017861028 to his workers and staff in the matter 
of wages and of compensation payable under tho 
Workmen’s Compensation Act and that he 
furnishes a suitable guarantee in this behalf from 
a Bank as approved by the Commissioners’ Chef 
Accountant and Financial Adviser, or deposit with 
the Commissioners security of such amount as 
may be prescribed by the Cumnnissioners from 
timo to time, in the form of cash or in public 
securities or in such other securities as may be 
approved by the Chiet Accountant and Financial 
Adviser in this behalf. 


(iii) A fee of Rs. 10 per licence shall be charged for the 
issue of a licence in the first instance; every licence shall 
be valid for one year only from the date of issue. Tho 
said fee shal] not be refundable under any circumstances. 


(iv) A licence may be ronewed for a year on payment of 
a fee of Ra. 5 per سس‎ which sball not be refundable. 
Applications in writing for renewal shall be submitted at 
least one month before the expiry of the licence. Appli- 
cations received after the period specified above shall he 
liable to an additional fee of Rs, 5 per licence at the dis 
cretion of the Chairman of the Commissioners. 


(v) The fees for the 18889 of a licence and for renewal 
thoreof may be revised by the Chairman from time to 
time, 


(vi) Individual stevedores or stevedoring companies and 
firms who, on the date when this By-Law comes into force 
are registered with the Calcutta Dock Labour Board as 
Registered Employers shall be eligible to he granted 
licences under this By-Law in the first instance upon their 
satisfying the provisions of the By-law. 


ry In the event of the name of any of the licencod 
stevedores being removed from the Employers’ Register of 
the Calcutta Dock Labour Board by the said Board, the 
licence granted to such stevedores under this By-law shall 
be liable to be cancelled, revoked or suspended by the 
Commissioners. ’ 


Explanatory Note.—The primary object of the revision 
of the By-law is to maintain the efficiency of stevedoring 
work in the Port at a high level. 


T. R. RAGHUPATHI, 
Secretary.

(Pang! 


Whether the stoppage of allowances to the 
cleaners of motor vehicles for being on duty 
between 11 a.m. and 1 p.m. within a radius 
of 5 miles and outside the radius of 5 miles 
from the Mill is justified? What relief, if 
any, are they entitled to in each case? 


AWARD 
Decision 
The present reference was received on 29th April 

1960 and notices were issued to the parties fixin 
26th May 1960 for appearances of the parties an 
for filing written statement by the Union. On that 
date the parties duly appeared and filed a joint 
petition of compromise stating that the transport 
cleaner will be given Ra, 1.25 oP. as tiffin allowance 
if-he is required to work at a place beyond a radius 
of 5 miles from the Mill, and that he will also be 
given overtiune allowance at double rates if he 18 
to work for more than 8 hours on any day or for 
more than 48 hours in any week. The terms of 
compromise appear to be fair, reasonable and law- 
ful and may be given effect to. The dispute is 
thus disposed of in terms of the petition of com- 
promise which do form a part of this award. 


Dictated and corrected by me.

BEFORE THE FIRST LABOUR COURT, WEST

In the matter of an industrial dispute between 
Messrs. The Bengal Paper Mills Co. Ltd. and 
their workmen (vide Government order No. 
1894-I.R. /IR/11L-264/60, dated 26th April 
1960) : 


The humble petition of the parties abovenamed , 


Respectfully sheweth: 

That the parties to this reference have come to a 
settlement 10 respect of the issues referred before 
this Court on the following terms :— 

1. Tiffin allowance of Rs. 1.25 nP. will be paid 
to the transport cleaner if he is required to be on 
duty at a place beyond a radius of 5 miles from the 
Mill during tiffin hours. 

2. Tiffin allowance will not be paid if the 
transport cleaner is to remain on duty at a place 
within the radius of 5 miles from the Mill during 
tiffin hours. 

3. When the transport cleaner will work for 
more than 8 hours on any day or for more than 48 
hours in any week, he shall in respect of overtime 
work be entitled to twice his ordinary rates of 
wages, 

In the circumstances stated above, the parties 
piay that your honour would be pleased to make an 
award in terms of this petition. 

And the petitioners as in duty bound shall ever 
pray.

Rules

tules, 1960.

3. The Director of Publicity, Qovernment of West Bengal, shall be the 
appointing authority. : 
4. The method of recruitment shall be by selection after open advertise- 
ment. 
5. Qualifications for the post shall be as follows :— 
(a) 1.۸. or I.Se. certificate of a recognised University; preference being 
given to Graduates; 
(b) experience of public speaking;

(d) knowledge and experience of presenting Bengal’s folk music, dances 
and other traditional forms of cultural entertainment; 
(e) good general knowledge of current affairs, with special reference to 
West Bengal; and 
(1) capacity to undertake continuous tours specially in the rural areas. 


6. The age of the candidate shall not be over 40 years on the firat day 
of the month in which the post is advertised. 


7. No person who is not of good character and in all respects” suitable

COMMERCE AND INDUSTRIES DEPARTMENT 


Weights and Measures 
NOTIFICATION 
No. 1065W.M.—18th August 1960.—In exercise of the power conferred 
hy the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution of India, the Governor is 
pleased to make the followimg rules regulating the recruitment to the post 
of Assistant Controller of Weights and Measures, West Bengal, namely سے‎ 


Rules 
The method of recruitment and the qualifications required for recruit- 
ment tu the post of Assistant Controller of Weights and Meusures, West 
Bengal, shall be as detailed below :— 
1. Method of recruitment— 
(1) Selection (direct recruitment); or 
(11) Promotion from Pape tae of Weights and Measures, West Bengal, 
on the recommendations of the Public Service Commission, West 
Bengal, provided not more than 25 per cent. of the total strength 
of vacancies in the posts of Assistant Controller of Weights and 
Measures, shall be filled by promotion, 


2. Qualifications for direct recruitment— 
A. Essential— 

(i) A degree of a recognised University ; 

(ii) Three years’ experience in a Government office or in a statutory 
body or in a commercial organisation of repute; 

(iii) Knowledge about manufacturing method of weights, measures. 
etc. 

BR. 06061831016+ 

(i) Knowledge of Bengali, spoken and written; 

(ii) Capability of interpreting tolerance charts for weighing and 
measuring instruments and — also metric nomenclatures and 
abhreviations for metric units; 

(111) Capalnlity of undertaking extensive tours; 

(iv) Acquaintance with the rural areas of West Bengal and the 
svatem of transactions in rural bazars and hats; 

(v) Acquaintance with the technicalities involved ×× stamping, 
verifying of weights, measures, weighing and measuring 
instruments. 

C. Age-- 

Minimum 25 years. 

Maximum 36 yenrs, relaxable in the case of an otherwise well- 
qualified aud experienced candidate.

Issue No, 1.—Wages and dearness allowance 


The Company has not produced its books ০01 
accounts to show its financial position. But 
O.P.W. ۱ Shri Bajranglal Purohit, a partner of

from his evidence that the financial position of the 
Company is not good. His evidence also shows 
that the wages paid by this Company is higher 
than that of at least two other companies 11) the 
same line in’ the locality. Both sides have 
produced charts showing the present wages of the 
workmen. The Company does not split 01) the 
wages into pay and dearness allowance; it pays a 
consolidated sum as wages. 11 is clear from the 
chart of wages that excepting in the case of two 
or three workmen who are very recent employees, 
the wages paid by the Company is fairly good. 
The Union has not been able to show that the 
ahove wages is less than the subsistence wages. 
It is also in evidence that the Company = granted 
increments of wages to its workmen during the 
last 2/3 years. The evidence adduced 07 both 
sides bring out the following facts ےب‎ 

(1) The Union has not been able to show that 
the wages paid by the Company is below 
the subsistence level; 

(11) The wages paid by the Company compares 
favourable with that paid by similar 
concerns in the locality; 

(ui) The financial position of the Company ia 
not good;

appears from evidence that before the case came up 
for hearing the Company increased festival holidays 
to 10 days in a year. So it meets the claim of the 
Union in respect of festival holidays. So 00 
award on this point is required. As to other 
holidaya, | reject the claim of the Union on ground 
of the financial position of the Company.

ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an industrial dispute existing 
between Messrs. Hoare Miller & 00, Ltd., 5

represented by the Hoare Miller Employees’ 
Welfare Association, 5 Fairlie Place,

BEFORE THE FOURTH INDUSTRIAL 
TRIBUNAL, WEST BENGAL 


Present: 


Shri K. K. MITRA, Judge, Fourth Industrial 
Tribunal. 


For the Union: Shri P. P. Pathak. 
Wor the Company: Shri ও. C. Sen, Advocate, 


An industrial dispute between Messrs. Hoare 
Miller & Co. Ltd., 5 Fairlie Place, Caleutta-1, and 
their workmen represented by the Houre Miller 
Employees’ Welfare Association, 5 Fairlie Place, 
Caloutta-1, over the following issue, has been 
referred to this Tribunal for adjudication, by the 
Government of West Bengal, Labour Department, 
order No. 468-1.R./1R/111-206/59, dated the 8th 
February 1960, and corrigendum No, 888-171 
TR / 111-206 /59. 


Whether the 42 retired workmen as per schedule 
enclosed are entitled to bonus for 1957 
which was declared in 1998? 


Both parties filed written statements, adduced 
evidence, oral and documentary, and advanced 
arguments in support of their respective cases, 


AWARD 


The contention of the workmen as made out in 
the written statement is that the Company is bound 
to pay Puja bonus as a condition of service in 1958 
to the 42 workmen mentioned in the schedule to 
the order of reference, though they had retired 
from service in 1957, 


‘The contention of the Company is that in accord- 
ance with its established practice, bonus was paid 
only to those workmen whose names were on the 
Company’s muster rol] at the time bonus was 
declared, It is further contended that these 42 
workmen retired from service between the months 
of August and December 1957 and they had receiv- 
ed the honus which was declared and paid during 
the Puja in 1957, us a condition of service and that 
they cannot claim bonus in 1958. 


The learned lawyer for the Company further 
urged that these people having retired from service 
we not “workmen” as defined in section 2(8) of 
the Industrial Disputes Act and, therefore, — the 
dispute is not maintainable. 


It is the common ense of both the _ parties that 
payment of banus on the eve of the Durga Puja 
acquired the foree of an implied condition — of 


service. Therefore, the employer bad the obliga- 
tion to make such payment of bonus on the eve of 
the Puja, irrespective of the question of profit and 
loss of any year. The simple question to be 
examined here is as to particular terms of the con- 
dition of service regarding bonus and which work- 
men were entitled to claim such bonus as a condi- 
tion of service in any particular year. The con- 
tention of the Union is that those workmen who 
had been in service in 1957 and retired ut any time 
during the said year, should still be legally entitl- 
ed to payment of bonus declared on the eve of the 
Pujas of 1958. 


Both parties relied on the decision of the Hon’ble 
Labour Appellate Tribunal as between the same 
parties, reported in the ‘‘Caloutta (jazette'’, dated 
the 12th April 1956, The issue us referred to the 
previous Tribunal runs as follows: 


‘‘Whether the workmen are 
receive any amount ۵ 
month’s basic pay as 
1953”’. 


Admittedly, the dispute arose as the workmen 
demanded that the quantum of bonus should be 
something more than one month's basic wages. 
The dispute came up for decision before the Sixth 
Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal, and the said 
Tribunal found that the workmen were nat entitled 
to receive any amount in addition to one month’s 
basic wage, aus bonus payable in 19938, As against 
that decision both the parties preferred appeal, and 
the Hon’ble Appellate Tribunal] decided the two 
appeals taking them together, and gave awaril 
allowing oie the appeal preferred by the work- 
men, It was ordered that the Company should 
pay 1/12th of the year’s dearness allowance to the

way of dismissal of the workman on an allegation 
of serious misconduct. The entire proceeding wits 
based on an allegation of complicity of Shri Ahir 
with an offence of theft, and in spite of the fact that 
there was no direct evidence to prove his guilt اہ‎ 
misconduct, he stood dismissed on the basis of the 
samo charge, The decision is clearly perverse and 
not only ugainst the weight of evidence but in spite 
of any evidence. The ban imposed upon the 
employer, under section 38(2)(b) of the Act, is 
that he cunnot take the proposed action of dis- 
missal of a workman connected with the dispute 
during the pendency of the proceedings of the 
Tribunal for any misconduct unconnected with the 
dispute without the approval of the Tribunal. 
11018 the employer just filed a petition under sec- 
tion 33(2) of the Act on 2nd December 1959 to 
which Shri Ahir submitted a reply in due course 
Subsequently, the employer withdrew the apph- 
cation, It is contended by the employer that the 
application for approval was withdrawn as the 
clployer found that the application was not main- 
tainable in law in view of the fact that no approval 
was necessary in this particular case. The only 
reason that is assigned by the employer in support 
of its contention is that the action taken by the 
employer was not subject to any approval of the 
Tribunal, and that the provisions of section 33(2) 
was not attracted as there was no certified Standing 
Oiders in respect of the industrial establishment 
concerned. A question, therefore, arises for con- 
sideration if, in the absence of Standing Orders in 
i particular industry, there can arise any complaint 
under section 83A on an allegation as to contra- 
vention of section 33(2) of the Act. The learned 
lawyer in support of his contention has relied on 
the decision of the Industrial Tribunal, Bombay, 
in the case of Anthony (K.'T.) and Messrs. Good 
Year Tyre and Rubber Co. of India (P.) Ltd., 
Bombay, reported in 1958, 1.1.3. Vol. ہا‎ p. 377, 
and the decision of the Industrial Tribunal, Patiala, 
in the case of Messrs. New Valley View Trans- 
port (1),) Ltd., Pathankot, and their workmen, 
reported in 1960, ۱,۱۰۰٠۰. Vol. 1, p. 104. Now, in 
hoth these cases it was held that the existence of 
the Standing Orders is a pre-requisite of the 
exercise of the power by the management, and the 
absence of the sume would take the case out of the 
mischief of section 33(2) of the Act. A coutrary 
view was however taken by the [Industrial Tribunal, 
Madras, in the ease of Muruglan and others and 
Messrs. Pioneer Milla TLtd., Coimbatore, reported 
In 1999, 15142 Vol. 1, p. 827, and by the Rajas 
than High Court in the case of Mansingh and 
Messrs. Mewar Teastile Mills Ltd., Bhilwara and 
another, reported in 1959, 15150]. Vol. f, p. 637. 
Clearly, therefore, the decisions’ are conflicting ا‎ 
the point. IT am concious of the fact that tt is 3 
cardinal principle of law that any penal provision 
in the statute must be strictly construed with due 
Importance given towards the use of the 17811100101 
word or words appearing in the statute. Section 
3904) of the Act enables an employer, in acrord- 


ance with the Standing Orders applicable to 4 


Paur T]

workman, to discharge or punish by way of ۔وزا؛‎ 
missal or otherwise any workman concerned in 
such dispute, But in the proviso to that sub- 
section it has been made obligatory on the part of 
the employer that he must not dismiss the work- 
man unless (1) the workman is paid one month's 
wages and (07) an application has heen made to the 
Tribunal for an approval of the proposed action. 
It would be enough for the employer to secure the 
approval of the Tribunal at they would be able to 
show that he had proceeded bona fide, and there was 
prina facie case for meting out the punishment. 
The proviso aftached to the seetion 338(2)(b) is 
obligatory, and the employer is bound to take 
approval of the proposed action from the Tribunal. 
Naturally if the employer proceeds in accordance 
with the Standing Orders, and there he prima 
facie case, the Tribunal would approve the action. 
In case however there is no কি Orders, that 
does not give a plenary power to the employer to

agree with the views expressed by the two Tribu-

referred to ahove. in the result, | 
hold that the action of the employer in dismissing

admitted by Haradhan (P.W. 2) that he attended 
the sittings of the enquiry and he was served with 
a carbon copy of the proceedings. 


The Union’s case is that Haradhan has been 
kept under indefinite suspension and ‘this 1s 
unjustified, while the Company’s case 15 that 
uradhan waa dismissed by the Company by a 
letter, dated 20th August 1958 (Ext. R), with 
effect from the date of suspension and that the 
letter of dismissal was sent to Haradhan wonder 
Certificate of Posting and also he was verbally 
intimated of his dismissal by the Manager 
(O.P.W. 1) as well as by Shri Bhanja Chowdhury, 
an otticer of the Howrah Manufacturers’ Associa- 
tion who also had taken part in the enquiry. 


It ix stated by Shri Haradhan (P.W. 2) that he 
was nevor dismissed and intimated of the alleged 
dismissal, It is difficult to understand why the 
Company would invent the false story of dismixsal 
after serving Shri Haradhan with the charge-sheet 
and holding an enquiry against him on = diffyroul 
dates. Thero is no reason to disbelieve the fact 
that Haradhan was actually dismissed by the 
Company and a letter of dismissal was sent to him 
under Certificate of Posting (Ext. R-1). Also the 
Manager (O.P.W. 1) says that Haradhan was 
personally intimated by him of the fact, and there 
is no reason to dishelieve the former’s evidence, 
Lastly, Waradhan (P.W. 2) has been constrained 
(0 admit in his cross-examination that Shri Rhanja 
Chowdhury, the aforesaid officer of the Howrah 
Manufacturers’ Association, had told him about 
the dismissal and asked him to accept the same on 
receipt of some amount as compensation, to whica 
he did not agree. 


In view of the evidence discussed above, ۸۵۱٥ 
he held that the dismissal of Haradhan is ao facet. 
The issue framed hy Government in the order of 
reference which is dated 16th January 1960 1s not 
for Huradhan’a dismissal. So, it 1s not neresvary 
for the Tribunal to adjudieate whether the dis- 
missal was justified or not. 

Tt ix evident that Haradhan had been susnended 
along with the service of charge-sheet upon him 
pending enquiry, and as the enqury resulted in his 


dismissal, the suspension must be held ৮০ be 
justified and cannot be regarded ھم‎ a punishment, 
separate from the final action of the Company. 
namely, dismissal, and so the suspension by itself 
cannot form the subject matter of an industrial 
dispute to be adjudicated separately from the 
auction of dismissal. As a result, it is held = that 
the suspension of Haradhan was justified and be 
is entitled to no relief on that account. 


This is the award of the Tribunal. 
ictated und corrected by me.

DECISION 


The parties have filed a joint petition of com- 
promise together with a memorandum of | settle- 
ment on 25th July 1960 praying that an award may 
be passed in terms thereof. Qn a perusal of the 
same, it appears that several extraneous matters 
have been settled besides those covered by the 
aforesaid issues 1 and 2 framed by Government. 
So much of the memorandum of settlement as is 


2902 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, AUGUST 25, 1960 


{Paar I 


১ ৯৯ 


related to the said two issues will form part of the 
award. The stipulations regarding extraneous 
matters will be operative according to law relatin 
to bipartite agreements between employers an 
employees, 

The petition of compromise and the memoran- 
dum of settlement be made annexures ‘‘A’’ and 
৭131 to the award. 

This 78 the award of this Tribunal. 

The parties deserve congratulation for being able 
to settle the dispute amicably which is the best 
method of maintaining industrial peace and har- 
mony and is best conducive to the welfare of both 
the industry and the workmen.

Annexure ۲۷ 
MEMORANDUM OF SETTLEMENT 


This settlement is made between Messrs. 
Pankaj Industries Private Limited of 340 Ram 
Saran Poddar Lane, Calcutta-33, and their work- 
men represented by Pankaj Industries Workers’ 
Union of 19/2 Russa Road South, 3rd _ Lane, 
Calcutta-33. After thorough discussions and 
negotiations in respect of all disputes pending up 
to date between the parties, this settlement has 
been arrived at settling all the disputes up to date. 


Terms of Settlement 


1. The main basis of this agreement will be to 
maintain peace and discipline in the factory and 
to increase production to the utmost capacity. 


2. All the workers, who were laid-off by the 
Company’s notices, dated 20th April 1960 and 
30th April 1960 and of whom who are still on the 
lay-off list, will be taken in employment, within 
seven days from date, 


3. The lay-off compensation will be paid in 
accordance with the provisions of the Industrial 
Disputes Ast within seven days of resumption of 
work by the respective workers. 


4. With the inclusion of the laid-off workers, 
the total strength of the factory will be 144 
(excepting the supervisory staff). 


6. With the said number of workers and on 
the availability of raw materials and normal con- 
ditions in respect of working of machinery and 
supply of power, the workers undertake and agree 
to give the minimum production of 70 doz. of brass 
torches (finished) and 120 doz. aluminium finished 
torches, in the present standard of quality per day 
of 8 hours’ work. It is also agreed that production 
of spare parts and components will be maintained 
within the capacity of the working strength. The 
wroduction of aforesaid minimum quantities of 

nished torches will be based on the schedule here- 
with attached. The revision of the production 
sohedule will be at the discretion of the manage- 
ment maintaining the minimum production as 
aforesaid. 


6. Any absenteeism beyond 3 per cent, of the 
total strength of workers will be taken into account 
while calculating the minimum production. 


7. In case any laid-off worker does not turn up 
within seven days of this agreement, he will be 
treated as a deserter and he will have no claim for 
299 and/or compensation, if any, due to 

im. 


8. In case, a worker, or workers do not give 
normal production the management will be at 
liberty to take disciplinary action against the 
worker or workers concerned, at the discretion of 
the management. The term ‘‘normal production’’ 
will mean production of components or other jobs 
in such quantities as would help complete the 
minimum production figures mentioned in clause 
6 above inclusive of different models and the review 
and congideration of the normal production will be 
made at an interval of every 10 days. 


Parr 1] 


9. The Union for and on behalf of the work- 
men takes the responsibility to maintain peace, 
discipline and order among the workmea, 


10. The management will introduce within one 
month of the signing of agreement, Production 
Bonus Scheme, in consultation with the Union. 


11. The question of wage structure as raised 
by the Union in their Charter of Demands, dated 
14th June 1960, will be taken up for consideration 
after six months from date provided the minimum 
production figures, as stated in clause 5 above, are 
muintained, In case no settlement is reached, the 
matter will be referred to voluntary adjudication. 


12. As an interim relief, the munagement 
undertakes to give a general increment of 12 nP. 
per head to those workers who are now receiving 
wages at Rs, 1.62 nP. or less per day. 


18. All amenities as provided in the Factories 
Act will be given to the workmen considering the 
working conditions permissible within the area 
und the present structure of the factory premises. 


14. Sick leave up to the extent of 15 days per 
year on half pay will be granted in bona fide cases 
and on production of medical certificate from a 
registered medical practitioner, till such time the 
State Insurance benefit is extended to this area. 


15, The present 14 days’ festival leave will be 
maintained, during the pendency of this agree- 
ment, in consultation with the Union. 


16. The Company will make their standin 
orders within a reasonable time. Till the sai 
standing orders are certified, the Model Standing 
Order Rules of the Government will be applicable 
to the employees. 


17. A committee consisting of four representa- 
tives from the employees and four of the workers 
including Union representatives will be formed 
within fifteen days from date to consider and 
roview the progress of work and to consider 
grievances, if any, and other incidental matters. 
The committee will submit its report and recom- 
mendations to the management, The committee 
will meet from time to time according to the 
requirements based on this agreement. 


18. The Union does not press the case of dis- 
missal of Shri Harihar referred to the Fifth Indus- 
trial Tribunal. The Union will also not press o1 
raise any dispute in respect of the workers who 
resigned or left or have been dismissed by the 
Management in the past. 


19 Provided the minimum production as men- 
tioned in clause 5 is maintained, the Company may 
consider to grant ex-gratia payment to workers on 
the occasion of the next Pujas. The nature and 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, ‘AUGUST 25, 1960 2903 


Lgl 


extent of such ex-gratia payment will be at the 
entire discretion of the Company. 


20. The Union, namely, Pankaj Industries 
Workers’ Union, is hereby recognised according 
to the‘ principles laid in the Fifteenth Labour Con- 
ference and either party will observe the same. 


21. This Agreement will remain binding be- 
tween the parties for one year from date. 


22. <A copy of this agreement will be filed each 
with the Labour Commissioner and the Fifth 
Industrial Tribunal. 

Signature on behalf of the Union: 

Pannalal Dutta, President, 
Pankaj Industries Workers’ Union.

Summary of the Minutes of the Proceedings of the 80۰ 
sioners’ Oth Meeting, held on the 23rd May 1960. 


AT the 9th Meeting of the Commissioners held on tho 
23rd May 1960, the following business was transacted :— 


1. Establishment of an auxiliary port at Haldia—Third 
Five-Year Plan.—Tho Commissioners approved the Chair- 
Inan’s proposal for the establishment of a subsidiary port 
at Haldia being included in the Third Five-Year Plan. 


2. Revision of the existing rates of various port oharges 
to suit the Introduction of the metric system of weights 
and measures.--The Commissioners sanctioned, subject to 
the sanction of Government, the Chairman’s proposal in 
the matter, 


3. Loan of the services of a Hydraulio Expert te the 
Commissioners by the United Nations Organisation.—The 
Chairman’s report in securing the services of Mr. McDowell, 
the U.N. Hydraulio Expert for advising the Commissioners 
on hydraulic probleme was recorded. ’ 


4. Aocident to the M.V. ‘‘State of Travanoorg Cochin’ 
on the 21st August 1959.—The Senior Assistant Conserva- 
tor’s recommendations were approved. 


5. Construction of a new Suction Dredger—Seoond Five- 
Year Plan.—The Commissioners approved in principle the 
placement of a repeat order for the Drodger ‘'Churni?’. 


6. Reconditioning and strengthening the quay walls ef 
Dook No. 1 Kidderpore Docks and installation of electric 
oranes—Tenders for the purohase of electric cranes—Second 
Five-Year Pian.—The Commissioners sanctioned, subject to

the sanction of Government, the placing of an order with 
Mossrs. Krupp-Indien-Handelsgosellschaft for the remain-

Rs.59,15,869 (foreign exchange component Rea. 35.84 lakhs 
in German J).M.) plus sales tax and variation, if any, in 
Customs duty, Port charges and rate of exchange. 


7, Repayment of the 3 per cent. 1050-60 (Second) loan 
of Rs. 100 lakhs and 3 per cent. 1950-60 (Third) loan of 
Rs. 100 lakhs.—-It was decided to recommend to Govern. 
ment that the sanction required under section 22 of the 
Calcutta Port Act #e accorded to the floatation ot two 
loans of Hs. 100 lakhs each carrying interest at 4 per cent. 


8. Block proposals.—The Commissioners also sanctioned 
rontine estabhshment proposals and routine proposals relat- 
ing to execution of works, grant of leases, purchase of

ANNEXURE 


In tho matter of an industrial dispute between 
Shri Purna Chandra Das, a_ oontractor of 
Messrs. Bharat Steel Co., Kali Mazumder 
Road, Salkia, Howrah, and one of his work- 
men named in the issuc bolow represented 
by Iron and Steel Workmen's Union, 63 Shiva 
Gopal Banerjee Lane, Chusury, Howrah. (Case 
No. VIII-C-147 of 1959.) 


BEFORE THE SECOND LABOUR COL RT, 
WEST BENGAL 


Present : 
Shri HEM RANJAN DEB, Presiding Oftirer, 


Second Labour Court. 
Appearances : 


For the Union: Shri 
Secretary. 


For the Company: Shri P. K. Nandy, Advocate. 


By order No. 20177118111 101.-74/69, dated 
Calcutta, the 12th May 1959, Government of Weet 
Bengal, Labour Department, referred an industrial 
dispute between Shri Purna Chandra Das, contrac- 
tor of Messrs. Bharat Steel Co. and one of his 
workmen represented by Iron and Steel Workmen's 
Union, to the Second Labour Court tor adjudication 
1egurding the issue mentioned in the order of 
reference. 


Robin Bhattacherjeo, 


Whether the termination dt employment — of 
Shri Brindaban Jana is justified? ‘To what 
relief, if any, is he entitled P 


The case of the Union. 
follows: 


Shri Brindaban Jana, the workman in question, 
hecame an employee of Shri Putrna Chandra Das, 
a contractor at essry, Bharat Steel Company on 
Ist April 1056. He served under the above 
contractor continugusly for one year and seven 
months; thereafter he approached the contractor for 


briefly stated, is as 


2059 


2060 THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, AUGUST 25, 1960 { Panr J 
eee ee eee ee a a 2207 ০ ى۶ ہت‎ 


un increment ot his wages on the ground that the 
latter compelled him to work for 9} hours dustead 
of 8 hours a day. Thereupon the contractor 
behaved roughly with him and discharged him 
verbally on 9th October’ 1957. Therenfter the 
matter was referred to the Assistant Labour Com- 
missioner, Howrah, before whom it was settled on 
7th August 1958 that the workman in question 
would be taken back in employment. Ln accordance 
with the settlement the workman went’ to the 
factory on the next day to resume work, but the 
contractor refused to take him back in violation 
of the settlement arrived at on 7th August 1958 
before the Assistant Labour Commissioner, 
Howrah. This was reported to the Assistant 
Labour Commissioner who enquired of the contrac- 
tor by his memorandum No. 3897/2/llow., dated 
19th July 1958, why the worker had not been 
taken back in employment. The contractor gave 
no reply to that memorandum nor did he take back 
the workman in question. 


The case of the contractor, in brief, 15 us 
follows: 


Tho contractor was doing the work of manu- 
facturing buckets on contract for Mesors. Bharat 
Steel Company. His contract with the above 
company was not of a permanent nature. When- 
ever the company gave him a contract for manu- 
facturing buckets, he used to employ workers to 
do the work and as soon as that work was over, the 
employment of the workers under him automati- 
cally ceased. When he got the next contract, he 
again called back his workmen and used to do that 
work. He had no fixed complement of workmen; 
he used to employ about 14 to 20 men to do the job 
according to the nature of the contract. So the 
contractor denies that there is any relation of 
master and servant between him and the workman 
and as such he contends that the present dispute 
is not un industrial dispute. He also denies that 
Shri Brindaban Jana worked under him for one yea! 
and seven months, that he behaved roughly with 
the worker and terminated his service on 9th 
October 1957 or that he agreed before the 
Assistant Labour Commissioner, [Howrah 60 
take back the workman for employment. 
1175 version as to what took place before 
the Assistant Labour Commissioner 18 that 
he agreed to engage the workman in question when 
he required his services next time. Accordingly 
he asked the workman to come for work in the 
month ot November 1958; but the workman Shri 
Brndaban Jana did never come back to him for 
employment. The contractor also asserts 61100 
Shri Brindaban Jana left bis employment of his own 
accord on 9th October 1957. 


DECISION 


So the first point for determination is whether 
there is a relationship of master and servant 
hetween the contractor and the workman in 
question The contractor has admitted that he 
engaged the workman in question from time to 
time; the only contention of the contractor is that 
the workman waa not in continuous employment. 
This anly leads to the conclusion that the work- 
man was in temporary employment; but this is not 
contrary to the relationship of master and servant 


between them. So I hold that there is no substance 
in the cdntention of the contractor that there is no 
relationship of master and servant between him and 
the workman in question. So I hold that this is an 
industrial dispute. 


The next question 18 whether Shri Bmndaban 
Jana left his employment of his own accord or his 
services were terminated by the contractor. Both 
sides have adduced evidence. The oral evidence 
is not 90101119158 on the point whether Shr 
Brinduban Jaua left the job of his own accord or 
his employment was terminated. But it 18 
dificult to understand why Shri Brindaban Jana 
should give up employment. Moreover, the circum- 
stances of the case and specially, the letter of the 
Assistant Labour Commissioner, to the contractor 
lead to the conclusion that Shri Brindaban Jana 
did not give up the job of his own accord. So I 
hold that the contractor terminuted his service. 


The vext question is whether such termination 
is justified. The Union has examined only one 
witness, viz., the workman in question in support 
of its contention that the وس کت‎ in question 
worked continuously for one year and seven months. 
But both the contractor and the Manager of Bharat 
Steel Company have deposed to the effect that the 
work of Shri Purna Chandra Das is of a temporary 
nature. So he cannot possibly have a permanent 
complement of workmen under him. I find no 
reason to disbelieve the evidence of 0189 
above two witnesses. Moreover there is one 
pertinent question on this point. Why should 
the contractor terminate the employment of 
Shri Brindaban 15085 Shri Brindaban Jana tries 
to give the reply by saving that he is leader of the 
Union but he cannot tell the registration number 
of the Union. Moreover he has not produced any 
evidence to show that he is cven an ordinaty 
member of the Union. So his suggestion that ۶۴ 
services were terminated on account of his leuder- 
ship of the Union is untenable. In view of the 
above consideration I hold that Shri Brindaban 
Jana was a casual emplovce under Shri Purrna 
Chandra Das, contractor. If the job for which the 
contractor had engaged Shri Brindaban Jana was 
over and if the contractor did not have anv work 
immediately on hand, it cannot be expected that 
the contractor would continue to pay the work- 
man his wages for no work. 


In view of the above findings, [ hold tliat ٥ 
termination of employment of Shri Brindaban Jana 
Is justified. As auch, he is entitled to no relief. 


Dictatod and corrected by me.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


Ditticulties were being experienced in the working of the West Bengal 
Eatates Acquisition Act, 1953, specially in the matter of preparing 
Compensation Roll. In order to remove those difticulties and expedite the 
preparation of Compensation Roll, 1t was tound necessary to remove those 
dithculties. ‘The West Bengal Estates Acquisition (Amendment) Ordinance, 
1960, which was promulgated on the 18th June, 1960, removed those difficul- 
ties by laying down a simplified procedure for the preparation ot 
Compensation Koll and also removing certain lacunae. 


‘The Bill seeks to enact the provisions of the Ordinance. 


BIMAL CHANDRA SINHA, 
Member-in-charge.

on.
