In course of the proceedings, the Company No. 
12 filed a written statement that it hus been sold 
to Shree Krishna Kumar Dal Mill, 1 Cross Road, 
Ramkrishnapur, Howrah, This sale has not been 
challenged by the Union. So, the purchaser Com- 
pany has been added as Company No. 12(a) to the 
aforesaid list. : 


The following issues have been framed by 


Government :— 


(1) Grades and scales of pay, (2) Leave, (3) 
House rent, (4) Bonus for 1957-38, (5) 
- Gratuity and (6) Working hours. 


DECISION 


In course of the proceedings, Companies Nos. 1, 
2, 11 and the Union have filed a joint petition of 
compromise on 25th May 1960 regarding all the 
issues. Also Companies Nos, 4, 7, 8, 9 and the 
Union have filed another joint petition of compro- 
mise on llth February 1960 regarding al] the 
issues. Further, the Union has filed a petition on 
14th June 1960 stating that it has no dispute in 
regard to Companies Nos, 5 and 10. At the time 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, AUGUST 30, 1960 


[Parv I 


of hearing on 27th July 1960 the Union has admit- 
ted the contention of the added Company No, 12(2) 
that there is no dispute between it and its work- 
men of the categories mentioned in the order of 
reference, 


As a result, a ‘no-dispute’ award is to be made 
in regard to Companies Nos. 5, 10, 12(a) as well 
as No. 12, and an award in terms of the compro- 
mise petitions aforesaid will have to be made in 
নিরব Companies Nos, 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 1]. 


Thus the dispute remains to be considered only 
in respect of Companies Nos, 3 and 6. 


The case of the Company No. 3 is that it has 
been closed for good on and from 9156 March 1960. 
So, there cannot be any subsisting dispute for 
adjudication between it and its workmen. The 
Union has accepted the closure so far as this case 
is concerned, but reserved its right to raise a dis- 

ute regarding the alleged closure; however, the 

nion has pressed issue No, 4 regurding bonus for 
1957-58. 


As regards Company No. 6, it has not entered 
appearance in this case though duly served with 
notice. So, the Union has pressed all the issues 
against this Company ex-parte. 


Issue No. 4—Bonus for 1957-58 


From the facts stated above, it will appear that 
this issue is to be decided only in respect of Com- 
panies Nos. 3 ‘and 6. 


No workman of these Companies hus been 
exainined in this case. The Union has examined 
one Shri Jagannath Missir*(P,.W. 1) who had 
never been in the employ of these two Companies. 
However, his evidence by itself demolishes the 
Union’s claim for bonus against these two Com- 
panies. For, he has categorically stated that he 
does not know what were the profits made by these 
two Companies in 1997-58. Here it is to be observ- 
ed that the initial onus for proving the available 
surplus lies on the purty which claims the bonus. 
The Union which has made this claim in this case 
has signally failed to dischurge this onus. So, the 
onus does not shift to the Companies to prove thut 
there was no available surplus for distribution as 
bonus to the workmen. It is to be noted that in 
the instant case the Union had called for the 
account hooks, etc., of the Companies for the rele- 
vant year in question which were produced by 
them, but the Union neglected to inspect the same. 
The proprietor of the Company No. 3 (0.P.W, 1) 
has stated in his evidence that his Company incur- 
red a loss of about Rs. 15,000 to Rs. 16,000 in the 
year 1957-58, but inspite of that the workmen were 
paid one month’s wages as bonus for the year, and 
there is no reason to disbelieve his evidence. 


As a result, it is held that the Union's claim for 
bonus for the year 1957-58 against Companies Nos. 
3 and 6 has nét been proved, and is altogether 
groundless, and is therefore rejected. 


_Now the only matter remaining for considera- 
tion consists of issues Nos. 1, 2, 3, 5 and 6 against 
the absent Company No.6, These issues ure taken 
up together for the sake of convenience, 


None of the Workmen of Company No. 6 hws 


been examiued in this case by the Union. The 
only evidence consists of the oral testimony of the 
aforesaid P.W. 1, We has not stated what are the 
prevulent conditions of service regarding the issues 
under discussion. In view of this paucity of 
evidence on the side of the Union which has to dis- 
charge the onus of proving its claim regarding the 
same, the demards made are liable to be rejected. 
However, the aforesaid two petitions of compro- 
mise may be considered as good evidence for the 
purpose of a proper decision of these 4 issues 
regarding the absent Company No. 6. For, the 
Companies which have made the compromise are 
situate in the same region as Company No. 6 and 
it may be presumed that they all function under 
similar conditions and circumstances. 


From the compromise petitions aforesaid it 
appears that no grades and scales of pay have been 
fixed, but the workmen have been given ad hoc 
increments of varying amounts. There are only 
3 workmen in Company No. 6 of the categories 
mentioned in the order of reference. One is a 
jamadar-cum-durwan-cum-weighing sircar, another 
is ৪, bill-collector and the third 1s a munib as 
proved by P.W. 1. From the said petitions of 
compromise it will appear that all these categories 
of workmen have been granted an ad hoc incre- 
ment of Rs. 10 irrespective of their present wages 
provided they huve completed 12 months’ continu- 
ous service, So, it is awarded that the aforesaid 
3 workmen of Company No, 6, namely, jamadar- 
cum-durwan-cum-weighing sircar, bill-collector 
and munib will get an ad hoc increment of Rs. 10. 
per month each irrespective of their present wages 
from the date of the publication of this award pro- 
vided each has put in 12 months’ continuous ser- 
vice by the date of publicatjon of this award. 


In both the petitions of compromise, the Com- 
anies have agreed to give one month’s privilege 
eave with pay per year to the permanent workmen 
(the qualification of permanency being 240 duys’ 
continuous service) of the categories mentioned in 
the order of reference, and that if any such work- 
men desires pay in lieu of leave without enjoying 
the same, the payment shall be made. This seems 
to be a fair term and there is no reason why this 
will not apply also to the workmen of Company 
No. 6. Hence, it is awarded that Company No. 6 
is to allow one month’s privilege leave with pay 
per year to the permanent workmen (the qualifica- 
tion of permanency being 24) days’ continuous 
service) of the categories mentioned in the order of 
reference, but if any workman desires payment in 
lieu of the leave or any portion thereof without 
enjoying the same, he should be paid in cash a sum 
equivalent to his wages for the unenjoyed privilege 
leave or any portion thereof. This provision regard- 
ing privilege leave will be operative from the 
beginning of the current financial year of the Com- 
pany. No privilege leave prior to that can ০৪ 
claimed by its workmen. 


Tt has been stipulated in the uforesaid petitions 
of compromise that the workers involved in this 
teference will be given 7 days’ festival holidays in 
a year. In view of this, it is awarded that the 
workers of Company No, 6 will be atlowed 7 days’ 
festival holidays with pay, and this provision will

পল সিটি শেল ০০০০ ১৯9 


come into effect from the commencement of the 
current financial year of this Company. 


In the petitions of compromise, no relief has been 
provided for the workmen regarding issues 3, 
and 6. So, it is awarded that the workmen of 
Company Mo. 6 will not get any house rent or 
gratuity, and the working hours will be the sume 
as now prevalent in that Company. 


Summary of the award 


(1) A ‘no-dispute’ award is made in respect of 
Companies Nos. 5, 10, 12 and 12(a). 


(2) A ‘no-dispute’ award is made in respect of 
Company No. 3 relating to the issues under dispute 
excepting issue No. 4) i.e., bonus for 1997-08 
which is pressed by the Union, but the claim under 
this issue is disallowed on contest. 


(3) An award be passed in regard to Companies 
Nos, 1, 2, 4, 7, 8, 9 and 11 on compromise, and the 
petitions of compromise, namely, that dated 25th 
May 1960 between Companies Nos, 1, 2 and 11 and 
their workmen, and the other, dated 1111 February 
1960 between Companies Nos. 4, 7, 8 and 9 and 
their workmen do form part of the award as 
annexures A and 


(4) Regarding Company No. 6 against which 
the reference has been heard ex-parte, it ia award- 
ed that the 3 workmen as proved by P.W. 1, name- 
ly, jamadar-cum-durwan-cum-weighing __ sircar, 
bill-collector and munib do get an ad hoc increment 
of Rs. 10 each per month irrespective of their 
present wages with effect from the date of publi- 
cation of this award provided each of them has 
completed 12 months’ continuous service by the 
said date. 


The claim of the workmen of Company No. 6 
regarding grades and scales of pay is disallowed, 
and the claim for bonus for 1957-58 is rejected. 
The workmen will not get uny house rent or gra- 
tuity, and the working hours will be the same as 
at present. 


Company No. 6 is directed to allow one mouth’s 
privilege leave with pay per year to its permanent 
workmen (the qualification of permanency being 
240 days’ continuous service) of the categories 
mentioned in the order of reference, but if any 
workman desires payment in lieu of the leave or 
any portion thereof without enjoying the same, 
they should be paid in cash a sum equivalent to 
their wages for the unenjoyed privilege leave or 
any portion thereof, This provision regarding 
privilege leave will be operative from the begin- 
ning of the current financial yeer of the Company. 
The Company No. 6 is further directed to grant 
7 dayw’ festival holidays with pay to the said 
worker and this provision will come into force 
from the commencement of its current financial 


year. 
This 1s the award of this Tribunal. 
Dictated and corrected by me.

reyulating the recruitment to the posts of the

RULES. 


The method of recruitment and the qualifica- 
lions required for recruitment to the posts specified 
below shall be as follows: 


Name of the post. 
Statistical Assistant (in charge of Administra- 
tive Statisties). 
Method of recruitment—Dirert 
Qualifications: 


(i) Candidates shall be graduates with Mathe- 
matics or Statistics or Economies as one of the 
subjeets. 


(ii) They should have not less than three years’ 
practical experience in (a) statistical field surveys 
for determining details about land utilisation 
including statistics of acreage, outturn ard = cost

condition of rural population, and (b) large scale

Statistics of which at least one yeur should have

(iii) They must not be over thirty-five years of

OFFICE OF THE DISTRICT MACISTRATE 
COOCH BEHAR. 


ORDER 


Dated Cooch Kehar, the 19th August 1960. 

Whereas I am of the opinion that it is necesary 
for maintaining supplies essential to the life of 
the community by preventing unlawful trade and 
smuggling of foodgrains, vegetables, 0118 and 
other foodstuff in any market or place of sale 
situated within five miles from the Indo-Pakistan 
border of this district; 


Now, therefore, in exercise of the powers conferr- 
ed by section 20 of the West Bengal Security Act, 
19909 (Act XIX of 1960), as delegated to me under 
section 38 of the said Act by the State Government. 
in their notification No. 2170-P/30-9/50, dated 
1185 April 1950, I hereby order that all transactions 
and movement of essential commodities excepting 
those exempted by me _ in writing, in hats, 
markets or any other place or sale lying within a 
belt of five miles in the district of Cooch Behar 
from the Indo-Pakistan border be prohibited 
after dusk. 


The above order shall remain in force for a 
period of three months from Ist September 1960. 
Any person contravening this order shall he 
punishable according to the provisions of law. 


Given under my hand and seal of the Court this 
1911, day df August 1960, 


J. K. LAHIRI, 
District Magistrate.

18. Thus the closure of the Calcutta branch

contemplated postulates the capacity «f the

where fur no reason the master is preventing ond 
hindering the servant from doing the work, the 
latter being able and willing to perform his, part 
of the contract &nd consequently the wages or 
sulary due to the workman cannot be -witbheld 
during the period of suspension. It is now well 
settled that the power to suspend, in the ২61) of 
a right to forbid the workman to work, is sot an 
imphed term in an ordinary contract between 
master and servant, and that such a puwer can 
only be either the creature of statute governing 
the contract or of an express term in the eoatract 
itself, Obviously, in this case there is no contract 
as between the master and servant empowering 
him to suspend or withhold the services of « work- 
man as a sort of punishment. No charg:-sheet 
nor any opportunity had been given as to the 
allegations of misconduct for which such  unish- 
ment had been inflicted. Clearly any dispute or 
difference between the employer and the employee 
connected with the terns of employment or a 
condition is an industrial dispute and, therefore, 
there is no reason why the punishment by vay of 
suspension and denial of payment of wages affect- 
ing the terms and the conditions of service should 
not be treated as an industrial dispute. I hold that 
the suspension is unjustified and the workman in 
question should be paid wages for three weeks 
which is the period of suspension for which wages 
had been withheld. ° 


issue No. 7 


This issue relates to the disinissal of a workman, 
Shri Ajit Banerjee. The contention of the 
employer is that the said workman who was a 
gate-keeper, sold two complementary tickets to 
Shri Jagadish Ch. Sur on 13th January 1989, and 
for that he was charge-sheeted on 16th January 
1959. After proper enquiry wherein Shri Banerjee 
was given opportunities for defence, he was found 

uilty and dismissed on 26th February = 1959. 

rom the evidence of P.W. 3, Shri Banerjee, the 
concerned workman, it appears that he got two

complementary tickets from a son of an Assistant 
Sub-luspector of Police of Khardah, and ৪০1৫ 
those two tickets to Shri Sur at 6 annas, which 
is the umount of Amusement Tax. So, Shri 
Banerjee admits that he had transferred tickets 
wt some consideration to Shri Sur. These two 
tickets were meant for some other persons and 
were available in the evening show. What Shn 
Banerjee actually did was to sell or transfer the 
tickets to Shri Sur who is an outsider, This ۹ز‎ 
clearly an act of misconduct on the part of ‘Shri 
Banerjee, no matter what monetary gain he made 
through such a transaction. The employer's right 
lo take disciplinary actiop against the employee 
is subject to the scrutiny and also to the  inter- 
ference by the Tribunal (i) when there is want 
of good faith, (11) when there is victimisation 0 
unfair labour practice, (iii) when management 
has been guilty of a basio error or violation of the 
principle of natural justice und (iv) when »n_ the 
11186071018 the finding is completely baseless our 
perverse, It is clear from the evidence that the 
workman had been properly charge-sheeted (vide 
Ext. A), and an enquiry had been held after Shri 
Banerjee submitted bis explanation and he was 
given full opportunity for his defence. It is quite 
possible that the employer took a serious view of 
the matter and as such took the extreme step of 
dismissing Shri Banerjee. There is absolutely 
nothing as shown that the employer was actuated 
by a spirit of victimisation, and that there was 
auy unfair labour practice. I therefore tind no 
reason to interfere with the action of the employer 
which is found justified. Shri Banerjee  accord- 
ingly cannot get any relief whatsoever.

of the Company disposed of and of hearing any explanation 
that may be given by the liquidator and also of deter- 
mining by a special resolution of the Company, the manner 
in which the books, accounts and documents of the Com- 
pany and of the liquidator shall be disposed of.

of the subdivisions and its effect on the standiag crops was not favourable in thirty-six subdivisions. Land prepanstion for the sowing 
of Aus and jute continued, But in sotne subdivisions the agricultural operations have been suspended for want of rains. The prospect 
of standing cropa was not satisfactory in seven subdivisions and in other places, it was on the whole fair, 


Fodder was insufficient in twenty subdivisions, Cattle epidemic was reported from five subdivisions, ‘There was ان۸۲‎ city of

ORDER 


No. 4407-L.R./IR/11L-239/60.—13th August 
1960.—Whereas under the Government of West 
Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 1530-1... / 
I /11L-239/60, dated the 6th April 1960, the 
industrial dispute between Messrs. Radha 
Chemicaly Co. Lad., Habra, P.O. Kalyangarh, 
24-Parpanas, aud their workmen represented by 
Radha Chemical Workers’ Union, 64 Chittaranjan 
Avenue, Calcutta-]2, regarding the issues men- 
tioned in the said order at matters specified in 
the second and the third schedules to the Industrial 
Disputes Act, 1947 (XIV of 1947), was referred 
for adjudication to the Fifth Industrial Tribunal ; 


And whereas the said Fifth Industrial Tribunal 
has submitted to the State Government its award 
on the said industrial dispute; 


Now, therefore, in pursuance of the provisions 
of section 17 of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947 
(XIV 4 1947), the Governor is pleased hereby to 
wwblish the said award as shown in the annexure 
ereto,

referred to as the Union), has been referred to this 
Tribunal for adjudication.

follows سس‎ ۱ 


(1) Wages.

(4) Bonus for 1996. 
(9) Retiring benefits.

On 3rd August 1960 the Union has filed a 
72 stating that there is chance of the matter 
eing settled amicably. So, it wants to withdraw 


from the dispute and pray that a ‘no dispute’ 
awurd may be passed. 

Therefore, an award be submitted to the Govern- 
ment on the footing that the industrial dispute 
under reference is no longer in existence 0৬ dis- 
clased by the Union's aforesaid petition, dated 3rd 
August 1960, which be made Annexure A to the 
award.

STATEMENT OF OBJECTS AND REASONS. 


Under section et of the Bengal গা... Recovery Act; 1913, 
interest upon public demand is chargéa the rate of 64 per cent. per 
annum for the period from the date of signing of the certificate up to the 
date of realisation. In many cases, certificate proceedings under the Act 
are etayed— 
‘(a) under orders passed by the Certificate-ofticers at the instance of the 
certificate-holders, or 

(6) under orders passed in appeals or in revision or by a Court at, the 
instance of the certificate-holders / 011 persons other than the 
certificate-debtors. 


lt is not fair to charge, in such cases, full interest for the period the 
certifieate proceedings are so stayed. It is, accordingly, ات‎ to grant 
remission of interest, or, to charge interost at a maximum rate of 3 per cent. 
per annum, in thé cases mentioned in (a) above, having regard to the 
circtmstances of the cases, and to grant remission of interest in the cases 
mentioned in-(b) above, for the period the certificate proceedings are stayed 
under the above circumstances. 


It is also proposed to empower the Collector to transfer cases from ۹ہ‎ 
Certificate-officer to another for expediting disposal of cases. 


The Bill has been framed with the above objects in view.

An industrial dispute between Messrs. 0٥ 
Restaurant (hereinafter referred to as the 
Company), © (New), 44/47 8S. S. Hogg Market, 
Calcutta, and their workmen represented by Karco 
Workers’ Union (hereinafter referred to as the 
Union), 4-0 Kalighat Road, Calcutta, over the 
following issues, has heen referred to this Tribunal 
for adjudication, by the Government of West 
Bengal, Labour Department, order No. 194-T.R./ 
TR /111,-237(A) /59, dated the 16th January 1960. 


(1) Revision of existing wages and fixation of 
minimum wages. 


(2) Gratuity. 
(3) Confirmation of service. 
(4) Food allowance. 


Both parties filed written statements, adduced 
evidence, oral and documentary, and advanced 
arguments in the case. 


AWARD 


The industry, in question, is a restaurant situated 
at Hogg Market employing about 45 workmen. 
This reataurant is evidently situated at a very 
important position in Calcutta facing the New 
Market which ia perhaps the biggest market in 
‘alcutta. Besides, a large number of fashionable 
cinema houses are situated in this partictilar area. 
The only witness examined by the employer stated 
in his cross-examination that the accommodation 
of the restaurant for the customers as well as the 
number of staff had been consistently increasing 
all through since the restaurant had been started. 


The contention of the Union is that the different 
categories of workmen should be paid in accordance 
with the pay-seales and other facilities as 
mentioned in annexure B(1) attached to its written 
statement. On the other hand, it is contended by 
the employer thut the existing wage rates call for 
no revision as these do not compare unfavourably 
with the wages paid by other restaurants in the 
locality, and that they are not in a position to 
shoulder any further financial burden on additional 
liability, 

T now proceed to consider the issues one by one. 


issue No. 1 


This issue relates to revision of the existing 
wages and fixation of minimum wages. It 
appears from the statement, Ext. 1, submitted by 
the Union, that there are at present 46 workmen 
in this establishment out of which 13 are described 
ns table-boys and 11 as mosalchis. Some of the 
table-boys get wages at Rs. 25 per month, and 
some at Rs. 28 while umong the mosalchis some 
are paid at Rs. 20 per month and the rest at Rs. 30. 
The workers are also supplied with two meals a 
day us well as tiffin which naturally should be 
included in wages. The value of the food is 
assessed by the employer at Rs. 20 per month, and 
that of the tiffin at Rs. 15 per month, and this 
amount is shown in Wage Register. So the 
minimum wages of the mosalchis come to Rs. 45 
per month tuking together the food and the tiffin 
allowances, A queation now arises for considera- 
fion if the wages paid to the employoes can be said 
to be appropriate. The Fair Wages Committee in 
dealing with the question of wages came to the 
couclusion that the wages of an industrial worker 
to be fixed must provide not merely for the hare 
subsistence of life but also for the preservation of 
efficiency of the worker; and that for this purpose 
the minimum wage must also provide for some 
measure of education, medical requirements and 
other amenities. Thia ia the minimum which he 
must have irrespective of the capacity of the 
industry or his employer to pay. Thus the floor 
level of wages is to be না If any 
employer is not 11) a و0‎ to pay even the hare 
minimum wages, it has no justification to exiat. 
The upper limit of wages must he set by what may 
be called the capacity of the industry to pay, not 
of a particular unit thereof, but of the industry- 
ewm-region basis. Taking the family unit of a 
workman as comprising of three consumption 
units, and the requirement on account of food at 


3032 THE CAILUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 8, 1960 


Rs. 5-8 per head and the total expenses per family 
distributing at 60 per cent. und 40 per cent. on 
account of food and either items as clothing, 
housing, etc., the minimum wage comes to 
_ Ra, 27-8. At 180 points of the cost of living index 
this sum of Ra. 27-8 comes up to Rs. 49-8. The 
cost of living index at the moment is above 400 
points. Apparently, the existing minimum wages 
at Rs. 55 for the mosalchis is quite insufficient 
to meet even the bare necessities of life of a work- 
man liable to support a family of three adult 
persons including himself. After piving my best 
considerations to the questions, deem it fair 
that no worker in this establishment should be 
aid at less than Rs. 65 per month, which is the 
hare minimum. I do not think that a workman 
working in the heart of the city should be pee 
less thon that in a flourishing restaurant. There 
is no dispute on the point that the table-boys 
numbering 13 ut the moment do not enjoy the 
benefit in the shape of free meal. Their salary is 
Rs. 26 per month for some, and Rs. 28 for the 
rest. Taking the value of tiffin at Rs. 15 per 
month which is accepted by both the parties, the 
minimum comes to Rs. 40 per month. Admittedly 
table-boys yet some extra earning in the shape 
of tips. P.W. 1, the only witness examined by 
the Union, said that generally the table-hoys get 
tips amounting to Rs. 1-4 daily. The witness 
examined by the employer estimated the amount 
at a higher figure. Naturally this earning is of 
variable nature as it is given in’ the form of 
baksis by customers when served by particular 
table-hoys. The minimum wages to be paid to a 
workman has got, to be decided’ giving due 
importance to the nature of the job performed, 
and the requirement of the workman to meet his 
necessities. It is true that the employer’s pocket 
is not in any way touched hy the earnings of the 
table-boys by way of baksis from the customers. 
But at the same time the particular nature of 
employment affords an opportunity to the work- 
men for having an extra source of income by 
serving the customers at the tables. Jt would 
therefore be hest to fix the minimum wages of 
the table-boys at Rs. 35 per month, and this sum 
along with the free tiffin allowance would make 
the total emolument Rs. 50 per month. The 
minimum wages of 11108010118 and the table-hnys 
are thus fixed at Rs. 30 and Rs. 35 per month 
respectively. Those mosalchis whose existing pay 
is above Ra. 20, and not exceeding Rs. 30, are 
allowed an increment hy Rs, 8 and their salaries 
be fixed accordingly. Similarly the table-hoys 
now getting Ra. 28 would get Ra. 36 per month. 
For the tea-maker and the assistant karigar who 
are now getting Ra. 30 per month, T fix their 
salury af Rs. 38 per month. The aalary of the 
assistant pantryman is now Rs. 25. I fix it at 
Rs. 35 per month. Those workmen, i.e., the 
cooks, the head ten-maker, the store-keeper, the 
bazar sarkar, and the pantrymen who are getting 
wages at various rates between Rs. 37 to Rs. 638 
as shown in Ext. 1, are allowed an increment by 
Ra. 6 and their wages would he accordingly 
fixed, T do not find any juatification for revising 
the wages for the rest of the workmen who are 
drawing more than Ra. 6% per month. The 
employer filed a chart showing the rates of wages 
of the different categories of workmen in some 
neighbouring restaurants {vide Ext. A). It is 
stated that the chart had been prepared upon 


[Parr | 


local enquiry. But neither the employers nor 
the workmen of those concerns are examined. 
It is not known what total amenities the work- 
men of those restaurants enjoy. Thore is nothing 
to establish the correctness of the statement 
contained in the chart Ext. A. I cannot therefore 
place any reliance upon Ext. A. It is true that 
the fair wages in a particular induatry should be 
fixed not merely on the basis of the paying 
capacity of the employer but also on region-cum- 
industry basis. There is no material before me 
to compare the wage-structure in this concern 
with comparable industries of similar size and 
টিয়া in the neighbourhood. From the 
»alance-sheet submitted by the employer از‎ 
appears that the annual sale 1+8 gradually 
increasing and the sale of foodstuff in the year 
ending ٦1۱۸۹۰ March (959, was Rs. 2,382,673. Of 
course in the audited balance-sheet the net. profits 
had heen shown at Re. 5,228 on the year ending 
dist March 1958, and Rs. 3,380 in the next year. 
Huge sums of Rs. 9,819 and Rs. 6,982 had been 
shown under the head of ‘‘General charges’’ in 
the two years: respectively. But the ا‎ in 
his report mentioned that this sum of capital 
expenditure could not be supported by proper 
evidence, Under the head of ‘‘wages = and 
salary”? the sum of Rs, 24,841 and Rts. 14,666 are 
shown in the year 1958. From the chart 
submitted by the Viren along with the written 
atatement showing the existing salary of the 
workmen numbering fifty, I find that the total 
comes up to Rs. 25,200 yearly. It is difficult to 
accept the correctnesa of the audited balance-sheet 
of two years which does not appear to have been 
regularly kept. The annual =p of the concern 
and its gradual prosperity are to be considered in 
ascertaining the paying capacity of the employer. 
In this consideration I hold that the employer has 
the capacity to increase the wages. But I do not 
consider it prudent to lay down any incremental 
sonles of pay for the workmen in the present 
circumstances as it is yet to be seen if the 
employer would be able to bear additional burden 
year to year. The wages as fixed would come 
into force from the Ist August 1960. The claim 
for giving retrospective effect, otherwise, stands 
disallowed. 


The Union demand introduction of «a gratuity 
scheme at 15 days’ pay for each completed year 
of services. The concern appears to be In good 
financial position. The sale of foodstuff ৮৮০৪ to 
the extent of 2.16 lacs in the year ending March 
1958, and the same was more than 2.32 lacs in 
the next financial vear. Considering the rate of 
wages, a substantial part of which is in the shape 
of food and tiffin allowance, supplied at the apot, 
there can be no doubt that the workers would 
have little surplus in hand at the time of termina- 
tion of their services. Thus T luy down that the 
workers would be paid gratuity on the hasis of 
146 days’ wages excluding food and tiffin ellowance 
for each completed year of services at the time 
of retirement from service or on voluntary 
resignation or on termination of service otherwise 
than by way of dismissal for misconduct. The 
maximum amount of gratuity is fixed at 15 
months’ wage. Gratuity would be available to 
the heir and legal representative of the workman 
on his death whilst in service. The scheme of

م۔.۔.۔۔ا۳٢‎ is subjected to that condition that no 
workers having putting in less than 5 years of 
completed service would be entitled to the sume. 


Issue No. 3 


The Union demand that all workers would be 
confirmed after six months of service. It is 
contended by the employer that the present 
system that a worker 1s made permanent after 
completion of 12 months’ service, should not be 
disturbed, Considering the nature of the job in 
a restaurant, [ think that the present system ar 
to retaining the workers temporary for one year 
is proper. Thus it is laid down that a workman 
chould be confirmed after one year of service. 


Issue No. 4 


It is demunded by the Union that the present 
system of supplying meals should be extended to 
all the workers. 


It uppears from the statements Ext. 1 and 
116. 100) that the table-boys numbering 13 and 
the jamadar Jillu are supplied with free tiffin only 
and not with meals. I have already stated that 
the table-boys get an income of Rs. 30 
approximately. per month per head from tips. 
There are reasons to think that the earnings from 
tips though fluctuating, actually work out at a 
better average per month in a year. The jamadar 
Jillu is stated -by the employer to be a part-time 
worker. The other jamadar Madan Lall is stated 
10 be permanent hand, I do not think that the 
part-time jumadar should be treated in the saine 
manner us the other workmen who are wholetime 
workers. So, there are reasons for denying the 
food ullowance to these workmen. and | do not 
like to interfere. 


It is demanded by the Union that the workers 
should be given an option to receive cash payment 
of Rs. 35 paid for food and tiffin. So far as 
tiffin is concerned, ] do not like to make any 
change. Naturally if the workmen are allowed to 
leave the restaurant for taking tiffin outside in 
the morning and evening, it would cause disloca- 
tion in the work. Regarding oonversion of the 
svstem of supply of free اسم‎ into cash payment, 
the employer .ا‎ no objection to make completely 
such change if at beat 75 per cent. of the work- 
men at present signify their intention for that. 
I think it would not be to the best of interest of 
the employer and the employee to make — food 
allowance optional in the sense that the workmen 
may or may not have cash payment in lieu of free 
meals. The system must continue either fully or 
it would be totally abolished. A partial alteration 
with liberty to workmen to have either, would 
involve greater ‘expense for ‘the — catablishment 
charges on that account. It is undenied that the 
value of food is not worth less of Rs. 20. A 
flexible rule as to conversion would obviously 
create some dislocation. It is thus decided that if 
at least 75 per cent. of the workmen signify the 
intention in writing to take cash = allowance at 
Rs. 20 in Heu of food within 30 days from = the 
date of publication of this award in ‘Calcutta 
CGazette,’’ the system of supply of free meals -will 
be totally abolished and replaced by the system 


Other- 


of payment in cash at Rs. 20 per month. 
wise the present system must continue.

The case of the Union, briefly stated, is os 
follows: 

About 10 years buck there was a Union of the 
workers of the company. That Union broke up due 
to the onslaught of the company. Ten vears later 
the present union, viz., »Metal Press Workers’ 
Union was organised. The Union was successful 


[Part I 


in extracting some facilities from the company as 
a result of collective bargaining. The Union also 
placed a charter of demands before the company 
and at the request of the company that charter of 
demands was referred to the Engineering Associa- 
tion of India of which the company is a member 
for amicable settlement. But ×٣ settlement was 
possible due to the delaying tactics adopted by the 
company. The success in extracting some benefits 
for the workers perturbed the company and it began 
to aeek for opportunities to পর the workers a 
good lesson. Such an opportunity came after the 
reopening of the factory after the Pujas in 1957. 
The Union demanded for temporary workers paid 
holidays for Durga Pujas which were given to 
permanent: workers. The company asked the 
Union to wait for two weeks and was told after 
two weeks that the demand could not be granted. 
This differential treatment between the permanent 
and temporary workers was strongly protested by 
the Union and the protest was answered by the 
company by the declaration of a lock-out on 11th 
November 1957 for an indefinite period. The lock- 
out was so unexpected that some of the workers 
who were scheduled to begin work at 7 a.m. went 
inside the factory as usual and were locked inside 
when the company suddenly declared the lock-out. 
Those workers were rescued with police help. The 
lock-out continued till 12th January 1958 and on 
the ‘basis of an interim agreement the factory was 
opened on 13th January 1958. Qn the first day of 
the reopening of the factory the company did not 
act up to the interim agreement and refused to 
take in four lorry coolies; thia was protested by all 
the workers. After the reopening the mannge- 
went removed tin sheeta and other raw materials. 
This shows that the management was preparing 
grounds to declare a second lock-out in order to 
starve the workers to submission. Further, within 
a month or so of the reopening of the factory ۹3 
workera under the so-called contract system were 
Jaid off. This action was strongly protested hy 
the workers, but the work inside the factory 
continued as usual until the company declared the 
second lock-out on 8rd March 1958. The declara- 
tion of the second lock-out was reported to the 
Labour Directorate and three conferences were held 
at the Tabour Directorate on the initiative of the 
Union. In those conferences the representative of 
the company raised numerous fresh issues, while 
the stand of the Union was always uniform. On 
4th August 1958, the management decided {o with- 
draw the lock-out, and on the eve of the with- 
drawal of the lock-out thev dismissed four 
workers, on charges levelled against them four 
months back. This action of the company was 
protested by the workers who tried to send a 
deputation to the company on that very day but 
were refused entrance into the factdry. On 8th 
September 1958 the Union came to know that the 
care of the above four dismissed workers had heen 
referred to the Second Labour Court for adjudica- 
tion and the workers decided to resume their work. 
Accordingly the work of the factory started on 10th 
September 1958. The Union prays that (1) curtuil- 
ment of facilities which results in differential 
treatment be stopped, (2) the termination 01 
services of four lorry coolies and of 23. ao-ealled 
contractor's workers ta wrong and unjust, and they 


he reinstated and given due compensation for the 
period of their unemployment, (8) the look-outs be

»periods of lock-outs and (4) compensation be paid

The case of the company, on the other hand, is 
as follows: 


Qu 6th March 1957 the Union submitted a charter 
of demands about revision of minimum wages, sick 
leave, bonus, abolition of contract system and other 
matters. Thereafter several tripartite conferences 
were beld in the office of Engineering Association 
of Tudia on the charter of demands submitted by 
the Union, and ultimately in October 1957 a draft 
agreement was drawn up covering all the issues in 
the dispute. This agreement was forwarded to the 
Union for approval by the above Association under 
a covering letter, dated 20th October 1957. The 
Union, however, did not agree to the terms of 
the draft agreement and requested the said 
Association by its letter, dated 7th November 1957 
to convene another joint conference with a view 
to finnhsing the agreement. While this negotia- 
tion was going on, on 9th November 1957 a crowd 
of more than 50 workers entered into the factory 
office and cash department and surrounded the staff. 
They demanded settlement of the charter of 
demands then and there. The officers of the 
compuny told them that this was not possible and 
usked them to leave the office. They however 
refused to do so. They stayed in the cash depart- 
ment for the whole of the day and night of 10th 
November 1957. It is only with the intervention 
of the Police Authority that they were made to 
vacate the office and the cash department on the 
following day, i.e., 1185 November 1957; but they 
continued to stay in the factory premises. They 
threatened, coerced and harassed the officers and 
other staff of the company. The management put 
up several notices asking them to refrain from such 
subversive activities, but to no effect. Ultimately 
the management had no alternative but to declare 
a lock-out on and from 11th November 1957. On 
10011) January 1958 an agreement was reached, as 
a result of which the factory was reopened on ط181‎ 
January 1958. The work in the factory had hurdly 
progressed satisfactorily for a fortnight after the 
reopening, when the workers again took law in 
their hands and indulged in all sorts of unlawful 
and subversive activities. On Sth February 1958 
the workers left the factory without the permission 
of the management and joined the  contractor’s 
workers who had been laid off by the contractor 
on that day. The workers did not allow some of 
the officers of the company to enter into the office 
or to go outside the factory gates. From that day 
the workers resorted to numerous devices with a 
view to harassing the management and virtually 
bringing down the production to "×۰ atandstill. 
They abused the representative of the muanage- 
ment in filthy language and detained the officers 
of the vompany in the factory premises everyday. 
They refused to collect their weekly wages due on 
Sth February 1958 which was a weekly pay-day. 
One of the terms of the agreement of 10th January 
1958, was that the company would pay an advance 
of two weeks’ wages to each worker and would 
begin to recoup from the third week after 
reopening, As the company wanted to recoup it 
on the third week, the workers refused to take 
their wages, us mentioned above. The workers 


continued to indulge in ucts of grossa indiscipline, 
coercion and intimidation. With the result, some 
of the staff had to abandon their work due to 
thrents of assault meted out to them by the 
workers. ‘The management put up several notices 
requesting the workers to maintain law and order, 
but to no effect. Ultimately the manugement had 
no option but to close down the factory with effect 
from 3rd March 1958. Thereafter some joint 
meetings were held between the representative of 
the management and the Union at the Labour 
Directorate, but no settlement could be arrived at 
due to the adamant attitude of the Union. In the 
ineantime Government of West Bengal, by an 
order, dated 11th July 1968, referred the dispute 
between the company and _ the workmen for 
adjudication to the Second Labour Court. The 
management was accordingly informed by the 
Assistant Secretary, Government of West Bengal, 
Labour Department, that work in the factory 
should be resumed immediately. Accordingly the 
management put up a notice on 28th July 1958 
intimating the workers that the factory would be 
reopened as from Monday, the 4th August 1958. 
But the workers did not report for duty on 4th 
August 1958, as required in the notice. There- 
after at the request of the company, (tovernment 
of West Bengal issued a notice under section 10(3) 
of the Industrial Disputes Act prohibiting 
coutinuance of strike by the workers. In spite of 
that notice the workers did not call off the strike. 
It was only after several notices put up by the 
management that work could be resumed in the 
fuctory as from 10th September 1958. The 
company therefore contends that: 


(1) there has been no curtailment of facilities 
resulting in differential treatment of work- 
men; 


(ii) the company did not terminate the service 
of the 23 workers and four lorry coolies 
who had all along been the employees of 
the contractors; 


(211) the company was forced to close down the 
factory on and from 1161) November 1957 
and again on and from 3rd March 1958 as 
a result of complete lawlessness prevailing 
in the factory; 


(iv) though the factory was reopened on 4th 
August 1958 the workers did not report for 
duty until 10th September 1958. So they 
are not entitled to any compensation for 
that period. 


FINDINCS 


issue No. 1: ‘The Union has not stated in ita 
written statement or in the evidence adduced by it 
what the existing facilities to a section of work- 
men in the factory were and how and when they 
were curtailed. On the contrary, the Union has 
stated in its written statement that after its 
formation it was successful in extracting some 
facilities us a result of collective bargaining. So 
far from curtailment of existing facilities, the 
Union itself has admitted that some facilities not 
exixting previously were granted due to the efforta 
of the Union. So I hold that there has not been 
any curtailment of existing facilities to a section 
of workmen in the factory. As such, no question 
of relief arises.

(Parr | 


Issue No. 2: The Union has contended that the 
lorry coolies, viz., Sarbashri Budhu Koiri, Gokul 
Koiri, Suklal Koiri and Mannu Kabhar_ were the 
employees of the company, viz., Messrs. Metal 
Press Works Jimited. But the company has 
contended that the above coolies were employees of 
unother compuny, viz., Kayar J,imited, who were 
given contract of transport by Messrs. Metal Press 
Works Limited. In support of this contention the 
company has examined O.P.W. 3 Shri S. P. Pandey, 
alleged to be an employee of Messrs. Kayar 
Limited and some other witnesses, and has also 
produced a copy of an agreement alleged to have 
been made between Messrs. Metal Press Works 
Limited und Messrs. Kayar Private Limited. That 
agreement is dated 25th October 1957. This shows 
that this agreement was,executed at ubout the time 
when the trouble between the Union and Messrs. 
Metal Press Works Limited started. It is true 
that the agreement states that a verbal agreement 
between the parties was made on lst June 1957; 
but there is no satisfactory evidence in support of 
the contention that any verbal agreement was made 
on 18 June 1957. It appears from the evidence of 
Shri S. P. Pandey on whose evidence the company 
relies mostly for its contention that the above four 
lorry coolies were the employees of Messrs. Kayar 
Private Limited that he is not a disinterested 
witness. It is also on evidence that most of the 
Directors of Messrs. Metal Press Works Limited 
are 180 the Directors of Messra. Kayar Private 
Limited. Moreover, in the draft agreement on the 
charter of demands which the Engineering Associa- 
tion of India on behalf of the company sent to the 
Union by their letter, dated 28th October 1957 
(Ext. F), clause VIII, reads as follows: 


“The demand for fixing hours of work for 
drivers and lorry coolies has been dropped 
as the existing system is quite satisfactory 
and as they ure not covered under the 
provisions of the Factory Act.’’ 


This clause drafted by the Engineering Association 
of [ndia at the instance of Messrs. Metal Press 
Works Limited is clearly an admission on the part 
of Messrs. Metal Presse Works Jimited that the 
lorry coolies were employees of that company. 


All these considerations lend support ہا‎ the 
contention of the Union that Messrs, Kayar Private 
Limited, if there is any company of that name, are 
only a ‘Benamder’ of Messrs. Metal Presa Works 
Limited. So I hold that Sarbashri Budha Koiri, 
Gokul Koiri, Suklal Koiri and Mannu Kahar were 
employed by Messrs. Metal Press Works Limited. 
The company has not shown any reason why their 
services were terminated. Asa matter of fact, the 
company has ‘disowned any connection with them 
at the time of termination of their services. So 
T hold that the termination of their services is 
unjustified, Hence | order that they be reinstated 
in service and be paid wages for the period of their 
forced unemployment by Messrs. Metal Press Works 
Limited, 


Issue No. 3: The company has contended that 
the 23 workmen mentioned in the list attached to 
the order of reference were not employees of the 
company but were the employees of contractors. 
In support of its contention it las adduced the 
evidence of some of the contractors as also of some 
officers of the company. Jt*has also produced 


agreement of contruct dating from ,28th March 
1955. There is no reason whatsoever for dis- 
believing the evidence on behalf of the company 
in this respect. The learned lawyer appearing on 
behalf of the Union has put the witnesses on behalf 
of the company to severe cross-examination on this 
point, and all of them have acquitted themselves 
well. On the other hand, the নি has not been 
able to produce any evidence in support of its 
contention that the 23 workmen were the employees 
of the company. Its argument seems to be that 
since soldering is an essential part of the work 
done by the company and since most of the 23 work- 
men were soldermen they must be presumed to be 
employees of the company. But there is nothing 
unreasonable for a company to have a portion of 
its work done by contractors, if that system suite 
its convenience. Moreover, the presumption urged 
by the Union has been satisfactorily negatived by 
the positive evidence adduced by the company on 
this point. So I hold that the 23 workmen 
mentioned in the list attached to the order of 
reforence were not employees of Messrs. Metal 
Presa Works Limited. As such they 819 not 
entitled to any relief at the hands of the above 
company. 


Issue No. 4: According to the Union, the 
workers protested to the company against 
differential treatment between the permanent and 
so-called temporary workers and as a result the 
company declared the first lock-out. So the Union 
contends that making of such legitimate protest 
should not have been met by the declaration of a 
lock-out and as such the first lock-out is unjustified. 
As to the second lock-out the case of the Union 
is that on the first day of the reopening after the 
first lock-out the company refused to take in four 
lorry coolies and this was protested by the workers. 
Further, the manugement began to remove tin 
sheets and other raw materials from the factory and 
thereby prepared the way for a second lock-out. 
The company also laid off 28 workers whom the 
company described as employees of a contractor. 
Che workers protested to all these activities of the 
management; nevertheless they continued to do 
their work as usual. Still the management 
declared the second lock-out only to vietimise the 
workers. 


The company, on the other hand, contends that 
on 9th November 1957, a number of workers went 
to the office and cash department and demanded 
settlement of their charter of demands then and 
there. As their demand was not complied with they 
continued to remnin there for the rest of the day 
und for the following day. So the company 
contends that it was forced to declare the )م6‎ 
lock-out. Some of the witnesses on behalf of the 
Union have admitted this much that some workers 
went on a deputation to the office on 9th November 
1957. This lends some support to the case cf the 
company on this point. As to the second lock-out 
the cnae of the company is that the contractor laid 
off hia employees. Their cnuse was taken up by 
the employees of the company and both — these 
groups of workmen started unruly conduct inside 
the factory. The Union had admitted this much 
that the workers made protest against the Inying 
off of the above 23 workers. The question is 
whether the protest was made in the way described 
by the Union or in the way described by the 
company. The company has examined a number

of pwitnesses to describe its version of the ০11010]11-

places specified in the visa’’; and 


(b) for sub-paragraph (8), the following sub-

paragraph (2)— 


(i) shall not, if the permit indicates the 
place or places for stay in India, 
visit any other place unless the

For 


Calcutta, the 24th September 1959, Government 
of West Bengal, Labour Department, referred an 
industrial dispute between اسر‎ Rungamuttee 
Tea Estate and their workmen represented by the 
West Bengal Cha Sramik Union to the Second 
Labour Court for adjudication regarding the matter 
specified in the issue to the order of reference. 


Whether the termination of employment of 
Shn T. V. Francis is justified. To what 
relief, if any, is he entitled? 


The case of the Union, briefly stated, is as 
follows: 


Messrs. Rungamuttee Tea Estate (hereinafter 
referred to 23 the company) maintain a workshop 
for attending to fitting, overhauling, repairing 
and welding of oil engine parts, roller machines 
and other machines used in the factories of Tea 
Estates. Shri T. V. Francis, a Welder-Fitter 
of the حسم‎ along with two other fitters used 
to do the above works of the workshop, and Shri 
Cham Sin, a China man, was appointed occasion- 
nily on a temporary basis by 0 company to 
ussist Shri T. V. Francis in doing the above work. 
Of the two fitters Shri Allen John was junior to 
Shri T. V. Francis in service and pay. Thus of 
the four men employed to do various works of the 
workshop, only one was senior to Shri .ا‎ ۴ 
Francis, while the other two, vis., Shri Allen 
John and Shri Cham Sin were junior to Shri 

V. Francis and they all belong to one category, 


that of fitter-mechanics. The work of‏ سپ 
when something is‏ ا welding is required‏ 
broken or damaged and this welding work was‏ 


only a part of the work of Shri T. V. Francis: for 
the rest of the time he had to do various mechanical 
works of manufacturing new parts, repairing, 
overhauling and attending to old machines. Shri 

V. Francis was appointed by the company on 
218 January 1955 on a clear understanding of 
doing the above works, and he actually did the

above works all ulong under the supervision and 
control of Mr. Lingy, the Engineer. Shri T, V. 
Francis wus elected Secretary of the Local Com- 
mittee of West Bengal Cha Sramik Union on 18th 
October 1958 and in that capacity he took an 
active part in organising the labourers of the ‘Pea 
Estate and in placing their grievances before the 
management, ‘The management did not take this 
trade union activity of Shri T. V. Francis in good 
grace and wanted to victimise him. In  conse- 
quence thereof the company by a letter, dated 29th 
April 1959, terminated the service of Shri T. V. 
Francis on the ground that there was insufficient 
welding work and that the Welding Department 
was being closed down. The union contends that 
the plea of abolition of the Welding Department 
is mala fide in that welding work is essential in 
all workshops. Further Shri T. V, Francis was 
not 0 whole-time welder; he was more of a fitter 
than of a welder, though as he knew the work of 
welding, his services were اید‎ utilised by the 
company for welding work. As he is a fitter as 
well, if there is any necessity of retrenchment, the 
two fitters, viz., Shri Allen John and Shri Cham 
Sin, junior to him ought to have been retrenched 
before Shri T. V. Francis. The union therefore 
contends that the termination of service of Shri 
T,. V. Francis is an act of victimisation and 3৪ 


unfair. 


The company, on the other hand, contends that 
Shri T. V. Francis was a welder simpliciter; he 
was appointed a welder and did the wor of welding 
only in 1955 and 1956. In 1957 he was given ৪ 
trial to show his ability as a fitter and was 
entrusted with the work of overhauling of a Legg 
Cutter Machine and dismantling and re-erecting ot 
Tea Roller Machine. He proved a failure in both 
these works due to lack of his knowledge and 
experience. Except for the above trial he did not 
do any work of a fitter. In the written statement 
the company as stated that Shri Cham Sin was 
employed in December 1954, i.e., before Shri 
T. س٦٦‎ Francis as a fitter and mechanic; but at the 
time of hearing the lawyer on behalf of the com- 
pany has admitted that Shri Cham Sin was 
appointed by the company long after Shri T. V. 
ere The company admits that Shri Allen 
John was appointed after Shri T. V. Francis, but 
its case is that Shri Allen John or Cham Sin 1s 
not in the same category as Shri T. V. Francis; 
because the former two are fitters and mechanics, 
while Shri T. V. Francis is a welder. The com- 

any denies that it terminated the service of Shri 
I ۲ Francis in order to victimise him for his 
trade union activity. The company contends in 
thie connection that apparently Shri T. V. Francis 
got himself elected as the Secretary of the Local 
Committee of the union in anticipation of his 
retrenchment, as it had already been decided to 
close the Welding Department and to sell the 
welding plant. The company therefore contends 
that it decided to close the Welding Department 
of the workshop for bona fide trade reason and as 
auch the termination of the services of Shri ۷۰ 
Francis is justified. 


FINDINCS 


The company has adduced evidence to show how 
the running of the Weldfng Department of the 
workshop became uneconomic and why it had to 
close that department. The union, on the contrary,

in many months Shri T. V. Francis has been

and not amp y a welder, The company nas tried

Messrs. James Finlay & Company Limited, 
Managing Agents of the above Tea Estate. There- 
in the Manager asked for the approval for the 
appointment of a welder, a fitter and a motor 
mechanic. The company says that Shri T. ۰ 
Francis to do the work of a mechanical fitter, and 
not be either a fitter or » motor mechanic. But 
the question arises who did the work of a fitter 
and that of a motor mechanic, It is in the 
evidence of both sides that one Shri R. K. Dutta 
was the motor mechanic. Who was the fitter? 
It is in the evidence of both sides that Shri Allen 
John is the electrical fitter; but it is admitted on 
all hands that a workshop requires the service of 
a mechanical fitter as well, Who was the 
mechanical fitter then? It is admitted in the 
evidence adduced ٦ the company that Shri Cham 
Sin was appointed by the company in December 
1957. The company has tried to suggest that 
even hefore his appointment by the company Shri 
Cham Sin used to do the work of a mechanical 
fitter under a contractor, named Wangtok. 
But it is clear from the evidence adduced on both 
sides that under the contractor Cham Sin did the 
work of extension of the factory and other con- 
struction work; the evidence on this point shows 
that at that time he did mainly the work of a 
carpenter. So before the appointment of Shri 
Cham Sin there was none else except Shri T.. V. 
Francis ia that welder and that as such 108 can- 
it is not the case of the company that such work 


Part [] 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, SEPTEMBER 8, 1960 2289 


সপ 


wus not necessary before the appointment of Shri 
Cham Sin. Even Shri Cham Sin does not say that 
he did not see Shri 1, V. Francis overhauling 
machines in 1955, 1956 or 1957. So there is no 
escape from the conclusion that by whatever 
designation Shri 1, V. Francis may have been 
described, he was doing the work of a fitter. So 
he must be classed in the same category with Shri 
Cham Sin who is admittedly junior to him. 


One trend of the argument made by the counsel 
on behalf of the company is that if it were not 
necessary for bona fide trade reason to terminate 
the service of Shri T. V. Francis, there is no 
reason why the company should have 00109 so. 
The union has stated the reply to the effect that 
Shri T. V. Francis was achiral on account of 
his trade union activity. The company 1085 
sugyested that Shri T. V. Francia became elected 
as the Secretary of the Local Committee after 
having prior knowledge 61186 his services would 
be terminated on bona fide trade reasons. In 
support of this contention of the company, the 
company has pointed out that it decided to sell 
the welding plant at about that time. But there 
is no evidence to show that Shri ٣. V. Francis 
had any prior knowledge of the intention of the 
company, to terminate his service. Even if it he 
held that it was necessary on the part of the com- 
pany to retrench one person for bona fide trade 


reason, it could nevertheless be argued that the 
company seized that opportunity in order to 
victimise Shri T. V. Francis for his trade union 
activity. So the contention of the union that the 
termination of Shri T. V. Francis is an act of 
victimisation cannot be brushed aside lightly. 


Irrespective of the question whether victi- 
misation wus at the back of the company’s mind. 
evidence clearly shows that Shri T. V. Francis 
was a fitter and that he was not juniormost in that 
category. Hence I hold that the termination of 
employment of Shri T. V. Francis is unjustified. 
So [ order that he shall be reinstated and be paid 
wages for the period of his forced unemployment. 
The above order shall take effect within a month 
of the publication of this award in the “Calcutta 
Gazette’.

No. 3951M.P.—Slst August 1960.—In exercise 
of the power conferred by section 34 of the Indian 
Electricity Act, 1910 (IX of 1910), and all other 
powers in this behalf, and in supersession of this 
department notification No. 2323M.P., dated the 
13th May 1960, published at pages 1923-24 of Part 
I of the ‘‘Calcutia Gazette’ of the 2nd June 1960, 
the Governor is plensed hereby to direct that with 
effect from the date of publication of this notifica- 
tion in the ‘‘Caleutta (tnzette’’ (hereinafter 
referred to as the said date)— 


(1) No high voltage or extra-high voltage trans- 
mission line shall, ordinarily, be erected over any 
art of any street or other public place, or in any 
actory or consumer’s premises not belonging to 
or under the control of the Central Government 
and not forming part of any mine, oilfield, railway, 
aerodrome, telegraph, broadcasting station or 
works of defence; and 


® 


(2) in special cases where the erection of high 
voltage or extra-high voltage transmission lines 
over or in such places cannot be avoided or where 
such transmission lines have been erected before 
the suid dute over or in any such place, the owner 
of every such transmission line shall provide for 
guard-cradle as an _ additional precautionary 
measure, and, if on account of the long span of 
the transmission line provision for  guard-cradle 
is not practicable, shall adopt the following addi- 
tional precautionury measures for rendering 06 
line electrically کا‎ in oase it breaks, 
hamely ;— 


In the case of transmission lines erected before 
the said date: Suitable earthing devices shall be 
11066] to the satisfaction of the Electrical 
1108 7۰ 


In the case of transmission lines to he erected 
after the said date: 


(a) At places where the transmission line 
passes over any part of any street or 
other public place of factory or consumer’s 
premises as stated above,— 


(i) the spans shall be reduced by 25 ver 
cent. of the average span of the line, 


(ii) double insulators in tandem with bridle 
clamps shall be provided at both ends of 
each span, and 


(iii) there shall be no joint in the conductor 
in the spans. 


(b) Protective devices shall be provided— 


(i) both at the sending and receiving ends 
in the case of interconnected systems, 
and 


(ii) only at the sending end in the case of 
radial lines. 


(c) For tower lines, angle towers with double 
strain strings shall be used on important 
road crossings. For less important roads, 
tangent towers may be el if the span 
is within 600 feet.

monts during tho ensuing Durga Puja. 


‘No. TM ‘765.—7th September 1960.—A_ reference is invited to the 
Government of West Bengal, Finance Department, Audit Branch, [xpress 
Memo. No. 2708F.. dated the 81۸۸ August 1960 (copy reproduced below), 
regarding the grant of Puja advance subject to the conditions specified im 
the (tovernment order. 


All Drawing and Disbursing Officers of the Government of West Bengal 
are hereby requested that the advance of pay sanctioned in the Govern- 
ment order quoted above, should be drawn and recovery thareof made 

‘strictly in accordance with the instructions given therein. 4 certificate 
to the following effect should also be furnished in each bill containing 
claims on account of the advance—‘‘Certified that the terms and condi- 
tions us 1010 down in the Government of West Bengal, Finance Depart- 
ment, Audit Branch, Express Memo, No. 2703}, dated 319 August 1960, 
have been fulfilled and that the advances have been sanctioned by the com- 
petent authority in respect of the person/persons for whom the Festival 
Advance has been claimed m the ۰ 


2. To facilitate accounting, the head of account to which the amount 
of advance will be debited should be shown clearly in the front page of 
the bill as “S—Deposits and Advances—Part 111 Advances not ‘hearing 
interest—Departmental Advances—Civil Advances—Festival  Advances’’. 
Yor facility of sorting of the vouchers in the Treasuries, the departmental 
major heads under which the pay and allowances of the Government servants 
concerned are debited should also be indicated thereon, 


3. As the Festival Advance is adjustable under the head ‘‘S—Deposits, 
etc.”, 18 separate schedule for this head should be prepared in Treasuries 
and submitted along with the supporting vouchers. The total of these 


schedules should agree with the umount appearing in the list of payments 
under this head, 

The recoveries of Festival Advance, which is to be made by deduction 
from the pay bills should be accounted for in the treasuries by transfer 
credit to the aforesaid head. 


4. In cases where the names of the Government servants for whom the 
advance is drawn are not shown in the body of the bill itself, a sepurate 
schedule detailing the names of persons and the amount of advance taken 
thy each of them should be furnished by the Drawing Officers along with 


each hill, 


hf. 11) support of the recovery of the advance when effected in the 
pay bills, the Drawing Officers should attach to the bills, sehedules in the 
enclosed Form No. Lf. The treasuries are required to indicate the 
No. and date of the Treasury vouched concerned on the schedules, detach 
them from the bills, arrange them according to the major head of accounts

(Copy of Express Memorandum No. 2703F., dated 3111 August 1960, from 
the Finance Department, Audit Branch, Government of West Bengal, 
to the Accountant-Genecral, West Bengal.) 


With a view to helping certain classes of Government servants so ax to 
enable them to ineet their commitments during the ensuing Durga Pujas, 
Government ure pleased to decide that if a permanent Government servant 
drawing uw basic pay [as defined in Rule 009) of the West Bengal Service 
Rules, Purt I] not exceeding Rs. 350 per month applies for an advance, 
he may be granted an interest-free advance not exceeding one month’s basic 
pay subject to a maximum of Rs. 200 in cases of Gazetted Officers and of 
employees “working in the Secretariat, the Public Service Commission, 
West Bengal, and the Board of Revenue and subject to a» maximum of 
Rs. 150 in case of others. The authorities competent to sanction — this 
advance are those mentioned in rule 320 of the est Bengal Financial 
Rules, Volume I. The advance will be recovered in six equal monthly 
instalments from the pay of the Government servant taking the advance, 
the first instalment being due on the first day of December 1960. The 
amount of each instalment should be rounded off to the nearest rupee, any 
balance being recovered in the last instalment, 


2. The concession sanctioned in paragraph | above may 81580 be 
extended— 


(a) to w temporary Government servant drawing a basic pay not 
exceeding Ra. 300 per month provided that the authority sanc- 
tioning the advance certifies that the advance is likely to be 
recovered in full and the temporary employee is expected — to 
continue in service for the next six months during which the 
recovery will be made; 


(b) to whole-time piece-rate workers 17 and temporary), the 
advance in their case not exceeding either one-twelfth of the 
total pay (excluding allowances) carned during the preceding 
12 months ending 3lst August 1960, or Rs. 150 whichever is 
less, provided that the heads of offices certify that the amount 
will be duly recovered in six equal monthly instalments from 
such employees. 


3. All applications for advance, on the strength of this memorandum, 
should be made as soon as possible and in any case, before the 8th Septem- 
ber 1960. The advance may be drawn on a_ working day only 
after the 2196 September 1960 but not later than 181 October 1960. 
Necessary bills etc., should be prepared accordingly. 


4. ‘The advance will be debited to “S—Deposits and Advances—Part 
[11—Advances not bearin interest—Departmental Advances—Civil 
Advance—Objection book Advance’’.

Issue 


. the discharge of Shri Ganesh 
رھت‎ Mitra is justified? To what 
relief, if any, is he entitled? 


The case of the Union, briefly stated, is as 


follows: Pag ۱ ۰: 

Shri nesh Chandra Mitra was serving the 
رٹ‎ a Store Clerk from February 4۴۰ 
His sulary was Ra. 35 per month. Tn November 


1955 he fell ill and the doctor diagonised his 
disease to be T.B. Tt took him about 30 months 
to recover completely. During this period of his 
illness he met the management at regular inter- 
vals and aubmitted his certificate of illness, and 
the management eassured him each time thut he 
would get his service as s00n as he would recover. 
۱٠١ became fit in Mareh 1958 and went to join 
duty with a fit certificate. But the management 
did not allow him to join duty on the plea that 
he was dixcharged, though no letter wes ‘issued 
to him. So ie Union contends that the die- 
charge of 90801 Chandra Mitra 18 
unjustified, 


(tanesh 


The case of the Company, on the other hand, is 
that Shri Ganesh Chandra Mitra worked up to 
۱۸١١ November 1965 and after that date he did 
not come back for work. 


Findings 


So the point ‘for determination is whether 
Shri (anesh Chandra Mitra offered to resume 
work in March 1958 and whether he was refused 
work then. Though the Company filed ٥ 
written statemeut, it did not appear al the time 
of hearing, though there were some adjourn- 
ments. The Union has examined two witnesses 
in support of this ease. Jt is clear from their 
evidence that Shri Ganesh Chandra Mitra 
appeared before the management in March 1958 
with a fit certificate and that he was refused 
work, So this clearly samvuunts to a discharge. 
As the Company has not adduced any reason for 
such discharge, I hold that the discharge of Shri 
Ganesh Chandra Mitra is unjustified. He has 
admitted in reply to my question that his present 
nge is 65. So‘there can be no point in ordering 
his reinstatement, as he is physically incapable of 
doing any work. In view of the fact, however, 
that he has been unjustly discharged, I order that 
the Company should pay him a compensation of 
Rs. 250. The above order shall take effert within 
a month of the publication of the award in the 
‘Calcutta Gazetto’’.

The case of the Company, on the other hand is 
us follows :— 


Sarbasri Jaleswar Dhara, Amrita Parui and!

of the mill. On 28th January 1968 at about

ax such, a charge-sheet on that charge was tssued

جبہ‎ ۱١۱۷٤) them.  Mnquiries in respect of the ehurge-

Findings 


The main grounds on which the Union _ bas 
queationed the propriety -of the orders of dismissal 
are: (1) Victimisation and (2) Sham enquiry. 


The Union has not adduced any evidence to 
show how and when the four workmen in question 
incurred the displeasure of the management on 
account of their trade union activities. So I at 
once come to the finding that there is on substance 
in the allegation of victimisation, 


As to the enquiry, the Company has _ produced 
the statement of the workmen concerned and all 
the witnesses unt the enquiries. The statements 
have been marked Ext, B series. These state- 
ments show that the charge-sheeted workmen

এ সস 


cross-examined some of the witnesses. The Union 
has not shown any reason why the witnesses 
should depose falsely at the enquiries or before 
me. Though no proceedings of enquiries have 
been prepared, the evidence of O.P.W. 2 Shri 
Gopendra Kumar Dutta, plates aud Welfare 
Officer of the Company, os also the statements 
of witnesses (Ext. B series) clearly show that the 
enquiries Were properly held. 


Sarbashri Jaleswar Dhara, Amrita Parui and 
Subid Ahi have been charged for (i) striking 
work, and (11) disorderly behaviour and acts 
subversive of discipline under rule 17(b) and (j) 
of the Standing Orders of the Company. The 
evidence adduced at the enquiries about striking 
work is not convineing; but there can be no 

uestion as to the decision of the Company about 

the second charge, viz., disorderly behaviour and 
acts stibversive of discipline. 39 it can be con- 
ceded that the Company has not been 1019 to 
prove the charge of striking work; but the other 
charge has been proved beyond any shadew of 
doubt. That charge by itself merits dismissal. 
There is a mistake in the charge-sheets about the 
relevunt sub-clause of the Standing Orders. 
Rule 17(j) of the Standing Orders does not. relate 
to disorderly behaviour or acts subversive of disci 
pline; it mentions something else. The proper sub. 
clause should be rule 17) which mentions dis- 
orderly behaviour and acts subversive 0 disei- 
pline. That mistake in the churge-sheets has uot 
in any way ,prejudiced the defence of — the 
charge-sheeted workmen at the enquiries, because 
the alleged misconduct has been clearly mentioned 
in the charge-sheets. As to Shri Kartiek Das, the 
evidence at the enquiry clearly proves that he 
refused to clean the bobbins. I the evidence 
before me he has contended that as it was his 
duty to clean bobbins, there was می‎ reason why 
he should refuse fo do oso. This conteniion 
cunnot be accepted نس3‎ against the  posilive 
evidence at the enquiry that he refused to clean 
the bobbins. This is) cleatly a misconduct 
coming under rule 17(a) of the Standing Orders 
of the Company. 

In view of the above considerations, T hold that 
{he dismissal of Sarbasri Jaleswar Dhara, Amrita 
Parui, Subid Ali and Kartick Das is justified, Aa 
such, they ure not entitled to any relief.

By Government order No. 1838-I.R./IR/101.- 
61/59, dated 22nd April 1960, an industrial dis- 
Shramik Union, Shramik Shivir, Talpukur, 24- 
pute between Messrs. Capstan Wire Products Pri- 
vate Ltd., M. M. Feeder Road, Ariadah, 24- 
Parganas (hereinafter referred to as the Company), 
and their workmen represented by Engineering

has been referred to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


The issues framed by Government are as 


follows :— 

(1) Wages. "

(3) T.eave and holidays.
