charge and dismissal. 

(5) Whether the action of the management in 
dismissing Shri Ramadhar Shaw and Shri 
Rabin Palit is justified? To what relief, 
if any, are they entitled? 

(6) Whether the action of the management in 
suspending Sarvashri Nirode Ranjan Dey, 
Khirode Lal Roy and Amal Chakrabarty 
for more than three weeks is justified ? 


To what relief, if any, are they entitled? — 


DECISION 


The Company has taken a preliminary objection 
that issues Nos. 1, 2 and 3 are barred by the 
principles analogous to those of res judicata. 
This contention of the Company has been heard 
and decided as a preliminary point, and the 
Tribunal’s finding has been as follows :— 


Order No. 7, dated 2nd Auguat 1960: ٢ 
Government order No. 1838-1.R./™/10L-61 /59, 
dated 22nd April 1960, an industrial dispute 
hetween Messrs. Capstan Wire Products Private 
Titd., M. M. Feeder Road, Arindah, 24-Parganas 
(hereinafter referred to as the Company) and their 
workmen represented hy Engineering Shramik 
Tnion, Shramik Shivir, Talpukur, 24-Parganas 
(hereinafter referred to as the Union), has been 
referred to this Tribunal for adjudication. 


[Parr I 


শপ এত 


Government has framed 6 issues, out of which 
the first 3 are as follow :— 


(1) Wages. 
(2) Dearness allowance. 
(3) Leave and holidays. 


The Company has raised a preliminary objection 
that these 3 issues cannot be adjudicated upon in 
view of the principles analogous to those of res 
judicata; for, the identical issues had been the 
subject matter of a previous Government order of 
reference being No. 3971-I.R./IR/100-110/58, 
dated 18th September 1958, which was made to 
the local Second Lahour Court wherein an award 
was passed in terms of a petition of compromise 
filed by the parties who are the same as in this case. 
On the prayer of the Company, this objection 
regarding muintainability of the first 3 issues in 
this case has been heard as a preliminary point. 


It is a fact that Government made n reference 
as aforesaid to the Second Labour Court wherein 
the issues were identical with the first 3 issues in 
the instant case.. The parties filed a ‘petition ০1 
compromise in that case. It contained several 
terms of settlement regarding all the issues in 
dispute. The Second Labour Court passed an 
award in terms of the said petition of compromise 
which was 177 by (Govermnent order No. 
1627-I.R., dated 22nd April 1959, in the ‘“‘Calcutta 
Gazette, Extraordinary’’, dated 80th April 1959. 


The Union gave a notice to the Company dated 
20th January 1960 which is as follows :— 


€ ‘To 
The Manager, 


Capstan Wire Products (P.) Ltd., 
.لد‎ M. Feeder Road, Ariadah, 24-Parganas. 


Dear Sir, 
Sub.: Agreement—termination of, 


(yovernment of West Bengal, 2nd Labour 
Court’s Award, dated April 1, 1959. 


Ref.: 


Please take notice, which we hereby serve upon 
your goodself that we intend to terminate , the 
operational period of the agreement as per award 
referred to above with effect from Ist April 1960 
5 اد‎ by section 19 of the Industrial Disputes 
4861, Je 8 


Yours faithfully, 
For Engineering Shramik Union, 
Nirmal Banerjee, 
President. 20-1-1960.’’ 


Tt is apparent that after the service of thia 
notice the Union raised a dispute, and Government 
has made the instant reference, the date of the 
order of reference being 22nd April 1960. 


The contention of the Company is that the notice 
is insufficient, invalid and premature, and the 
Government order of reference also is void جو‎ it 
has been made during the pendency of the award 
aforesaid. 


Part I] 


THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, SEPTEMBER 15, 1960 $117 


pe 


he Company contends that the normal period 
of subsistence of the award should be computed 
according to the provisions of section 19(6) read 
with section 19(3), of the Industrial Dispute Act, 
while the Union contends that the period of 
operation should be computed according to the 
provisions of sub-section (2) of section 19 as the 
matter was settled by an agreement. 


If the contention of the Company is accepted it 
must be held that the uotice is premature and 
insufficient, for according to seetion 19(6) of the 
Industrial Disputes Act, the award was to remain 
in force up to 22nd April 1960 and would continue 
to remain in force until the period of 2 months had 
elapsed from the date on which notice was given 
by any party intimating its intention to terminate 
the same. 


Now the notice (which is annexure B to the 
Union’s written statement) specifically stated that 
the agreement as per award was to be terminated 
from Ist April 1960. This date of termination 
fixed by the Union in this notice was in violation of 
section 19(6) of the Industrial Disputes Act, and 
necessarily it must be held to be insufficient, 
invalid and inoperative, and also it must be held 
that the award continued to remain in force in spite 
of the notice even after the expiry of its period of 
operation as envisaged: by section 19(6) of the 
Act, and hence the Government order of reference 
is bad in law as it has been issued during the 
subsistence of the previous award. 


Even if the Union’s contention is accepted that 
the period of operation of the award should be 
governed by the date in the notice itself, there is 
no escape from the aforesaid position; for para- 
graph 3 of the previous agreement provided as 
follows :— 


“It is agreed that the above terms of settlement 
shall come into force with effect from Ist April 
1989 and shall be تاس‎ on the parties for a 
period of one year after which it may be terminated 
by either side giving one month’s notice.”’ 


The words ‘‘after which’’ in the said clause are 
very significant. There can be no doubt that by 
the said paragraph 3 of the agreement it was 
intended that the agreement was to remain in 
force for one year with effect from Ist April 1959 
and after that period it might be terminated by 
either side giving one month’s notice. In 

assing, it may be mentioned that the provision 
or one month’s notice was illegal and must he 
superseded by section 19(2) ০ the Industrial 
Disputes Act wherein two months’ notice 1s 
rovided for in case of termination of a settlement 
i an agreement. However, in view of the afore- 
said clause in paragraph 3 of the agreement, the 
Union was debarred from serving the Company 
with 4 notice of termination during the period of 
subsistence of the agreement as provided therein. 
As the Union served a notice during that period, 
the notice must be held to be premature, insufficient 
and inoperatice [vide the principles laid down in 
the ease of National Carbon Co. (India) J.td. va. 
Gan (M. N.) and Ors. reported in 1958 L.L.J., Vol. 


1, page ۰ 


.compromnise, 


Even if it be held that the notice was proper 
and valid, the settlement would have continued to 
be operative till the expiry of 2 months from the 
date of expiry of the period of operation as 
provided for in the agreement itself, In other 
words, the agreement in any 0046 would remain 
In operation up to 3001) June 1960 and the Govern- 
ment would have no jurisdictiou to issue an order 
of reference regarding the issues in dispute in the 
previous case before that date, 1.9.) 00 June 
1960. The Government having issued the present 
order of reference on 22nd April 1960, it must be 
held that it is ultra vires and without jurjsdiction. 


It is apparent that in uny view of the case, the 
first 3 issues are barred by the principles analogous 
to those of res judicata. However, it is held that 
for the purpose of computation of the period of 
operation of the agreement in the previous case, 
the agreement itself is to be regurded to have been 
merged in the award of the Second Labour Court, 
and the computation of the period of operation 
must be made according to the provisions of section 
19(6) read with section 19(3) of the Industrial 
Disputes 4১০৮, It has been already held that the 
notice of termination given by the Union appears 
to be premature, insufficient and yavalid on such 
computation and for this reason the Government 
order of reference is without jurisdiction (vide 
principles laid downs in the case of Indian 
Aluminium Co. vs. Their workmen reported in 
1958 L.0.J., Vol. II, page 403, at page 404, para- 
graph 7). 


As a result, the Company’s contention that issues 
Nos. را‎ 2 and 3 in the instant case are barred by 
the principles analogous to those of res judicata 
is accepted, and the said issues will be left out of 


adjudication in this case. 


16th August 1960 is fixed 


De for hearing of the 
remaining issues. 


G@. KUMAR, Tribunal.

of compromise are fair and reasonable. So, (۷ 
an award be পা in terms of the petition of

by the parties and it do form a part of the award 
as annexure A 


The parties should be congratulated for the

to the maintenance of industrial peace and harmony 
between them in future.

MINISTRY OF HOME AFFAIRS 
New Delhi, the 8th August 1960 


G.S.R. 944.—In exercise of the powers conferred 
by sub-section (1) of section 3 of the All India 
Services Act, 1951 (61 of 1961), the Central 
Government, after consultation with the Govern- 
ments of the States concerned, hereby makes the 
following rules, namely :— 


1. Short title.—These rules may be called the 
All India Services (Conditions of Service— 
Residuary Matters) Rules, 1960. 


2. Power of Central Covernment to provide for 
residuary matters.—The Central Government may, 
after consultation with the Governments of the 
States concerned, make regulations to regulate 
any matters relating to conditions of service of 
persons appointed to an All India Service, for 
which there is no provision in the rules made or 
deemed to have been made under the All India 
Services Act, 1951 (61 of 1951); and until such 
regulations are made, such matters shall be 
regulated :— 


(a) in the case of persons serving in connec- 

' tion with the affairs of the Union, by the 
rules,‘ regulations and orders applicable 
to: officers of the Central Civil Services, 
Class I; 


(b) in the case of persons serving in connec- 
tion with the affairs of a State, by the 
rules, regulations and orders applicable 
to officers of the State Civil Services, 
Class I, subject to such exceptions and 
modifications “as the Central Government 
may, after consultation with the State 
Government concerned, by order in 
writing, make. 


3. Power to relax rules and regulations in 
ertain cases.—Where the Central Government is 
ttisfied that the operation of— 


(1) any rule made or deemed to have _ been 
made under the All India Services Act, 
1961 (61 of 1951), or 


(7 any regulation made under any such rule, 
‘“ulating the conditions of service of persons 
নল to an All India Service causes undue 
hardship in any particular case, it may, by order, 
dispense with or relax the requirements of that 
rule or regulation, as the case may be, to such 
extent and subject to such exceptions and condi- 
tions, as it may consider necessary for dealing with 
the case in a just and equitable manner. 


৬ 

4. Interpretation.—If any question arises 
relating to the interpretation of these rules ই: 
relating to application or interpretation of rule 
regulations or orders referred to in clauses (a) an 
(b) of rule 2, it shall be referred to the Central 
(iovernment, whose decision thereon shall be final. 


[No. 14/2/55-AIS(TIT). J 
B. N. TANDON, Dy. Secy.

In exercise of the powers conferred by clause

Amendment Order, 1960. 


(2) It shall come into force at once.

CHAPTER II 
THE CORPORATION 


Constitution of the Corporation 


3. (1) With effect from such date as the Central Establish- 
Government may, by notification in the Official Gazette, ment of 
appoint, there shall be a Corporation charged with the رس‎ 
municipal government of Delhi, to be known as the Munici- 


pal Corporation of Delhi. 


(2) The Corporation shall be a body corporate with the 
name aforesaid having perpetual succession and a common 
seal with power, subject to the provisions of this Act, to 
acquire, hold and dispose of property and may by the said 
name sue and be sued. 


(3) The Corporation shall be composed of councillors and 
aldermen. 


(4) Councillors shall he chosen by direct election on the 
basis of adult suffrage from various wards into which 
Delhi shall be divided in aceordance with the provisions of 
this Act; and aldermen shall be chosen by the councillors 
from among persons who are qualified to be councillors but 
are not councillors themselves. 


(5) The total number of councillors shall at the establish- 
ment of the Corporation be eighty: 


Provided that twelve out of the eighty seats of councillors 
shall be reserved for the members of the Scheduled Castes. 


(6) Upon the completion of each census after fhe 
establishment of the Corporation, the number of councillors 
shall be on the basis of the population of Delhi as ascertained 
at that census and shall be determined by the Central

Corrupt practices and electoral offences 


22. The following shall be deemed to be corrupt 
practices for the purposes of this Act:— 


(1) Bribery as defined in clause (1) of section 123 of the 
Representation of the People Act, 1951. 


(2) Undue influence as defined in clause (2) of the said 
section. : 


(3) The systematic appeal by a candidate or his agent 
or by any other person, to vote or refrain from 
voting on grounds of caste, race, community or 
religion or the use of or appeal to, religious 
symbols or, the use of or appeal to, national 
asymbols, such as, the national flag or the national 
emblem, for the furtherance of the prospects of 
that candidate’s election. 


(4) The publication by a candidate or his agent or by 
any other person of any statement of fact which 
is false, and which he either believes to be false or 
does not believe to be true, in relation to the perso- 
nal charatcer or conduct of any candidate, or in 
relation to the candidature, or withdrawal from 
contest of any candidate being a statement reason- 
ably calculated to prejudice the prospects of that 
candidate’s election.

taxed, the system of assessment to be adopted and the

(2) Any resolution passed under sub-section (1) shall be 
submitted to the Central Government for its sanction, and 
if sanctioned by that Government, shall come into force 
on and from such date as may he specified in the order of 
sanction. 


(3) After a resolution has come into force under  sub- 
section (2), the Corporation may, subject to the maximum 
rate, pass a second resolution determining the actual rates 
ot which the tax shall be leviable; and the tax shall come 
into force on the first day of the quarter of the year next 
following the date on which such second resolution 1s 
passed. 


(4) After a tax has been levied in accordance with the 
foregoing provisions of this section, the provisions of sub- 
section (2) of section 109, shall apply in relation to such tax 
as they apply in relation to any tax imposed under sub- 
section (1) of section 113.

of Khariff seeds in nineteen subdivisions.

Subdivisional Reports on the condition of Weather, Crops, etc., for the week ending the 18th May, 1960. 


Summary.— During the week under report there was scanty rainfall in twenty-nine subdivisions. Dry and hot weather prevailod in 
most of the subdivisions and its 9060৮ on the stauding crops was not favourable in twenty six subdivisions. Sowing of wus and juto cropa 
and land preparation for the same continuod. In some places agricultural operations have still boon suspended for want of rains. The 
prospect of standing crops was not satisfactory in twelve subdivisions and in somo places, it was on the wholo fair. 


Fodder was insufficient in twenty-five subdivisions. Cattle epidemic was reported from three subdivisions. Thero was soarcity of 
khariff seeda in sixteen subdivisions. 


The daily wages of a labourer varied from eighty-seven n.P. to Rupees two and fifty n.P.

11. ‘The statement of prior charges, us »ub- 
mitted by the Company in Ext. E(15), suffers 
from a variety of infirmities. [ ahall take up the 
question of normal depreciation as made out by the 
Company in Ext. 15019) and as calewlated in 195, 
K(1). ‘The chart xt. EK(1) for the calealution of

for the year ended 30th June 1958 ia not correct. 
Yhe caloulation is to be made according ہا‎ the 
decision of the Hon'ble Supreme Court) ح؛‎ the 
A.C.C. case on the notional normal depreeation 
as enunciated in the case of Surat Electricity Co., 
reported in 1956 L.A.C., 443, being the same case 
us reported in L9d7(IL) الما‎ 648. The Surat 
Klectricity Co. case was decided by the Hon'ble 
Labour Appellate Tribunal. The JHLlou'ble Judges 
of that Tribunal state that for the purpuse «f bonus 
formula, the initial and additional depreciation 
must be ignored in fixing the written down vulue 
and in determining the period over which the 
normal depreciation will be allowed. ‘The result 
will be a notional amount of normal depreciation. 
It is stated that the bonus formula itself 18 a 
notional formula. Under the Inecome-tax Act, 
normal depreciation is a sum equivaceat to such 
percentage of the written down value as ‘nay be 
prescribed [section 10(1)(vi) of the Income-tax 
Act]. This method is popularly called the 
“straight line method’’. The percentuge, how- 
ever, 1۱ to be calculated on the written down value 
of the buildings or machineries. It will appear 
from Ext. E(1) that the Company calculated 10 
per cent. of the second class factory buildings on 
the original value of the buildings on 30th June

with reference to the basic wage or basic pay of 
the workmen concerned and in making this eal- 
culation dearness allowance shall not be taken into 
consideration, In view of the reliefs already grant- 
ed to the workmen of different departments inclu- 
sion of dearness allowance in the calculation of 
production will create hardship to and impose 
“fadditional’’ heavy financial burden on the Com- 
pany. 1 do not like to disturb the present systeim 
in vogue in the company, namely, NISCO, i.e., 
০০ of production bonus on the basic wage 
0 ٠ 


Point No. 5: Introduction of same _ production 
schemes to all the four companies concerned. 


With regard to the three other Companies, 
Britannia Building and Iron Co., Ltd., National 
Screw & Wire Products Ltd. and = Tatanagar 
Foundry Co., Ltd., I bave already recorded my 
findings. J] am not going to disturb the existing 
production bonus scheme in Britannia Building 
and [ron Co., Ltd., as contained in the consent 
award, dated 12th August 1958 (Mxt. F/1), and 
the scheme of production bonus in vogue = in 


National Screw and Wire Products Ltd. as per 
agreement, dated 24th July 1958 (Ext. G = after 
objection). With regard to Tatanagar Foundry 
Co., Ltd., there being no scheme of production 


incentive bonus in existence at present the question 
of introduction of production bonus scheme in the 
line of what is in existence in NISCO does not 
arise at all. So, points Nos, 2 to 5 are answered 
against the claims of the union and Karmachari 
Sangha and in favour of the contentions raised by 
these three companies concerned. 

This is my award. 

Dictated and corrected by me. 

S. R. GHOSH, Judge.

An Act to amend the Calcutta Municipal Act, 1951. 


WHEREAS it is expedient to amend the Calcutta Municipal 
Act, 1951, for the purposes and in the manner hereinafter 
appearing; 


It is hereby enacted in the-Eleventh Year of the Republic 
of India, by the Legislature of West Bengal, as follows: — 


1. This Act may be called the Calcutta Municipal 
(Second Amendment) Act, 1960.

(hereinafter referred to as the said Act), for the words ‘‘and 
shall be convened’’, the words ‘‘and such meeting and the 
first meeting in each year to elect a Mayor and a Deputy 
Mayor under section 10 shall be convened’’ shall be 
substituted.

Statement of the act performed for which the 
decoration has been awarded 


During the floods in Septemben 1959, Shri Abani 
Kumar Basu, M.L.A., remained constantly present 
iu the flood-aftected arena in Uluberia P.S. of 
Howrah district for a period of over 12 days urging 
the 1001 people and helping by his own physical 
efidfts to protect the embankments in those areas 
from being overflowed and breached. In the 
Octuber floods when the flood waters of the Damo- 
dar exceeded all previous recorded level by over 
two feet, Shri Basu once again by his own example 
created fresh energy and enthusiasm not only 
amongst the villagers but also in the ranks of 
Government officers. While a disaster of the 
severest magnitude was being apprehended in con- 
sequence of the Abhirampur Bundh on CUuzarpur 
Canal and the maim Damodar embankment at 
Madhabpur being evertopped by flood water from 
the night of Ist October, he exerted himself and 
exhorted his fellow workers for a continuous periorl 
of ‘72 hours to raise the levels of those embank- 
ments which, if breached, would have engulfed 
not 1048 than 30,000 people. By his example and 
exertion the Damodar embankment waa raised by 
over 21 inches, earth bemg obtained rendily and 
freely through his intervention and nasistance from 
the homesteads affected by the floads. Shri Abani 
Kumar Basu thus displayed outstanding gallantry 
in saving the lives of his fellowmen at great perso- 
nal risk. 2

Statement of the acts performed for which the 
decorations have been awarded 


On September 9, 1959, at about midnight, a 
gang of about 26 dacoits, armed with unlicensed. 
wuns and other deadly weapons, raided the house 
of Shri Janaki Nath Chakraborty of Sonapur, P.S. 
Gazole of Malda district. While some of the 
dacoits mounted guard on the various approaches 
to the house to keep away the villagers, the rest of 
them broke into the house and began to ransack 
it assaulting the inmates brutelly. When as « 
result of this assault the lives of Shri Chakraborty 
and his son were in danger, Shrimati Chakraborty 
(wife of Shri Chakraborty) tacttully slipped out of 
the house aud ran towards the village raising an 
alarm for help. On hearing this alarm some 
members of the Village Resistance Group includ- 
ing Shri (alia Bhuimali and Shri Temku Bhuimali 
at once proceeded towards Shri Chakruborty’s 
house to resist the dacoits. Near the eastern 
approach to the house, Shri Galia Bhuimali who 
took the leading part came forward boldly and 
challenged the four armed dacvits on guard 800 
was replied with a gun shot. Diaregarding the 
injuries inflicted on him he ran up to render 
immediate help to the inmates of the house but 
succumbed to his injuries. Notwithstanding the 
death of the leader, Shri Temka Bhuimali who was 
following Shri Galia Bhuimali did not hesitate to 
rush towards the house to save the life und pro- 
perties of the intuntes. He was also shot at by the 
dacoits and injured. Owing to the bold resistance 
of these two active members of the Village Resis- 
tance Group, the dacoits found no further time to 
plunder and had to retreat. While Shri Galia 
Bhuimali lost his life on the spot, Shri Temka 
Bhuimali became invalid due to the gun shot 
injuries sustained hy him. Thus, both Shri (talia 
Bhaimal and Shri Temka Bhuimali performed out- 
stunding acts of dourage and self-sacrifice at great 
personal risks in saving the lives and properties 01 
1) Chakraborty and the members of his family.

10. In case of there being no quorum within

specified date, and at every such adjourned meet- 
ing the members present, whatever their number, 
shall have power to transact only such business 
which would properly have been transacted in 
the adjourned meeting. 

11. Questions arising at any meeting shall 
be determined by a majority of votes taken in 
such manner as the Chairman of the meeting 
shal] determine, and jn case of equality of votes, 
the Chairman shall have a second or casting vote.

1١ With regard to the objection of the Company 
{hat the retrenehed workmen having been paid 
more by way of retrenchment compensation are not 
entitled to claim gratuity in addition it is sufficient 
to refer fo the recent decision of the Supreme Court 
in the case of Indian Thime Pipe Co. and its work- 
men reported ۲ز‎ 10910117151. 830. Te was 
pointed owt in this case that while gratuity was a 
kind of retirement benefit, retrenchment compensa- 
tion was not a retiral benefit at all, such compensa- 
tion being intended to give a retrenched workman 
some relief and help hin to tide over the period of 
unemployment forced upon him in consequence of 
the retrenchment. On this ground it was held 
that a retrenched workman would he entitled to 
claim both gratuity and retrenchment compensation 
und that there would) be no queation of double 
benefit, beeause the claims would be based on 
different considerations. This decision was, how- 
ever, sought to be distinguished on behalf of the 
Company and reliance was placed on another 
decision of the Supreme Court on the same point in 
the case of Brahmachari Research Tustitute vs. its 
workmen, reported in 1959-11-L.L.J. 840, as more 
applicable to the facts of the present case. In that 
case certain retrenched workmen who had been paid 
retrenchment compensation were held not entitled 
fo gratuity in addition to such compensation on the 
basis of the scheme of gratuity which had been 
framed by the Company and later modified hy an 
award. hia gratuity scheme contrined a provi- 
ston that it would apply in all cases of retrench- 
ment or termination of service by the Company for 
any reason other than nuisconduct and alao in cases 
of resignation and that the period of service to

construing the said scheme it was held that the 
gratuity payable under the scheme was really a 
retrenchment compensation, though described ns 
gratuity, hecause it was payable on retrenchment 
and the qualifying period was only one year and

By Government order No, 6956-1.R./1R/ LOL- 
112/58, dated 23rd December 1959, an industrial 
dispute between Mosers. rudd [Industries Ltd.4 
22 Kerry Fund Road, Sodepore, 24-Parganas 
(hereinafter referred to as the Company), ١ه‎ 
their workmen represented by the Krudd 10000, 
tries Workers’ Union, House of Tala, Station 
Road, Sodepure, 24-Parganas (hereinaffer referred 
to as the Union), has been referred io this Tribu- 
nal for adjudication, 


The issues framed by Government have been as 
follow :— 
(1) Sick leave for all workmen not belonging 
10 the clerical and supervisory ۰ء‎ 
(2) Festival holidays for the temporary work- 
men not belonging to the clerical and 
supervisory staff. 


(4) Whether the dismissal of Sarbashree [lira- 
lal, Nannu Singh and Basdeo Ray 18 
justified? To what relief, if any, are 
they entitled ? 


Subsequently, issue No. 2 has been substituted 
by a corrigendum intimated by Government order 
No, 1890-1.R./1R/1L0L-12/60, dated 26th April 
1960, in view of which issue No. 2 stands as 
follows :— 

Festival holidays with pay for the daily-rated 
and weekly-paid permanent and 7 
workmen not helonging to the clerical and 
supervisory staff. : 


DECISION 


The facts relevant to the issues will be atated 
in course of the decision therecf. Now the issues 
are being taken up one by one, 


issue No. 1 


It is commen ground that no category of work- 
men in the factory is allowed si ‘k leave with pay. 
From the balune-sheets of عط‎ Company from 
1952 to 1958 it evpears that the Company ts 
running at a low. If a provision for sick leave 
with pay for the workmen not belonging to the 
clerical and supervisory staff be mad>, that would 
mean an additional financial burden on the Com- 
pony. It is contended on_ behalf of the Com- 
pany that this burden should not be imposed upon 
it in view of the deteriorating financial condition 
and also in view of the fact that the provisions of 
the Employees’ State Insurance Act are going fo 
he applied soon to the factory. But it 1s not 
known when the said provisions will come into 
forve in the factory. Also it is u fact that sick 
leave with pay 1s allowed to the workmen of all 
categories in other factories in the locality. So, 
in apite of the adverse financial condition of the 
Company it cannot refuse this particular amenity, 
namely, sick leave with pay to its workmen. As 
a result. it is awarded that the Company 1s fo 
allow 15 days’ sick leave with half pay annually 
to all workmen not belonging to the clerical and 
supervisory staft. The workmen will not be 
entitled to thir sick leave unless their application 
for leave is backed by a certificate from ١ regis 
tered medical graduate. Thi- leuve will be ctunu- 
lative up to one month. This provision for sick 


matically superseded as and when the provisions 
of the لع ایال‎ State Tusurance Act will be 
bronght into force m the factory. 


1٢۱ is common ground that the Company allows 
184 days’ festival holidays with full pay to all 
categories of workmen eacepting those who are 
daily-rated and  weekly-patd (whether they be 
perinanent or temporary). Also, the factory is 
kept completely closed on 154 days on account of 
festival holidays, while on the remaining 3 
festival holidays the factory remains open, but 
sectional holidays are allowed ںا‎ the workmen 
concerned in the festivals. In the instant case, 
(he Company has been cundid enough to admit 
that the daily-rated and = weekly-paid workmen 
should not be deprived altogether of festival 
holidays with pay. The Compeny’s witness (0.1), 
W. 1) has proved that in similar industries in the 
same region 10 days’ festival holidays with pay 
: granted to all types of workmen. So, the 
the Company is willing to allow 10 duya’ festival 
holidays with pay to the daily-rated and weekly- 
paid workmen of its factory. But the Union 
demands that they should be granted 184 days’ 
festival holidays with pey as are granted to other 
workmen. Tt is contended by the Company that 
this would mean a heavy financial burden which 
would be highly detrimental in view of its adverse 
financial condition. Now the = daily-rated = ond 
weekly-paid workmen of the Company cannot 
claim to have 184 days’ festival holidays with full 
pay on analogy with other workmen, for there is 
no rule or law that all types of workmen of a 
particular concern should be placed under identt- 
cal terms and conditions of service. I[t is a matter 
of common experience that difterent types of 
workmen are placed under different terms and 
conditions of service in) many concerns. The 
instant case is an example to the point. It is to 
be noted that admittedly there is disparity in a 
very vital condition of service of the workmen 
concerned in this issue under discussion, viz, 
mode of payment of wages, They get wages 
which are daily-rated and paid weekly, while the 
other workmen are mouthly-rated and are paid 
monthly. So, the former cannot claim by analogy 
to have 184 festival holidays with pay which are 
granted to the latter. Also in view of the present 
economic and industrial backwardness of the 
Nation, an attempt is being made to reduce the 
number of holidays in Government institutions 
There is no reason why the same policy should not 
he followed in industrial concerns also. Hence, 
اپ‎ 1৮ held that the daily-rated and weekly paid 
workmen (both permanent and temporary) will 
he allowed 10 festival holidays with pay. Also, 
more holidays with pay are not warranted by the 
present financial condition of the Company. 


Now a very important point comes in for conri- 
deration ١۱۲ has been found that the Company 
grunta 184 festival holidays to other workmen 
out of which the factory remains completely 
closed on 15} dave which can be called general 
festival holidays for the purpose of eouvemence, 
and remains open on 3 other festival holidays 


[art T] 
52252255522 


when sectional holidays are granted to the work- 
men concerned in the festivals. The daily-rated 
und the weekly-paid workmen will have the option 
to avail of any of the sectional holidays as well 
as the general festival holidays, but the total 
number of holidays to be enjoyed by them should 
not exceed 10 days in a year. But the Company 
should provide them with work for 8} days out of 
the 18} festival holidays granted to other work- 
men. Otherwise these daily-rated and weekly- 
paid workmen will be practically laid-off’ for no 
justifiable renson without any compensation during 
the said 84 days which will be absolutely unjust 
and unfair. If the Company cannot provide these 
workmen with any work for any of the said 8] 
days, it will have to pay their full wages for any 
of those 84 days on which they are not ৪০0 
provided. 


Thus the award on this issue in a nuteshel] is 
that the daily-rated and weekly-pail workmen 
(both permanent and temporary) will get 10 
festival holidays in a year with full pay. They 
will have the option to avail of any of the general 
holidays or sectional holidays, but the total 
number of both kinds of holidays to be enjoyed 
by them with full pay shall not exceed 10. QOut 
of the 18} festival holidays granted to other work- 
men, the Company will have to find employinent 
for the aforesaid daily-rated and weekly-paid work- 
men for 84 days, failing which the Company will 
have to pay full wages to such of the said daily- 
rated and weekly-paid workmen as may not be 
provided with work on the said 84 festival holidays 
or any of the same. 

It seems that to give effect to this arrangement 
the Company will have to keep the factory com- 
pletely closed on 7 general festival holidays and 
to keep it open on the remaining genera] festival 
holidays as well as on tho three sectional holidays. 


issue No. 3 


Qut of the three dismissed workers involved in 
this issue, two, namely, Shri Nannu Singh and 
Shri Basdeo Ray have not appeared at the time 
of hearing, and their case has not been also pressed 
by the Union. Further, it is proved hy the 
Supervisor of the Company’s = staff (O.P.W. 1) 
that those two workmen took payments of all 
their dues by way of final settlement, and they 
yave up their claim for reinstatement (vide Exts. 
B and C). So, it is held that these two workmen, 
namely, Shri Nannu Singh and Shri Basdeo Ray 
were rightly dismissed and they are not entitled 
to any relief. 

As regards the remaining workman, namely, 
Shri Hiralal, a petition of compromise has been 
filed after his examination-in-chief. The terms 
of the compromise are fair and reasonable, and an 
award be passed in respect of Shri Hiralal in terms 
of the petition of compromise which do form purt 
of the award as annexure ‘A’. 


This is the award of the Tribunal.

ANNEXURE 


In the matter of an industrial dispute between 
Messrs. Bowreah Cotton Mills Company 
Limited, Bowreah, Howrah, and their work- 
men, represented by Bowreah Cotton Mills 
Employees’ Union, Bowreah, Howrah. (Case 
No. ۷۱۱۱۰8۰124 of 1959.) 


BEFORE THE SECOND LABOUR COURT 
WEST BENGAIT, 


Present: 3 


Shri HEM RANJAN DEB, Presiding Ufficer, 
Second Labour Court. 


Appearances : 


For the Union: Shri Ram Sen. 


Shri R. Goswami, Assistant 


For the Company: 
Chamber of Com- 


Leal Advisor of Bengal 
merce and Industry. 


(iovernment of West Bengal, Labour Depart- 
ment, by its order No. 1617-1.R./1R /80-12/58, 
dated Caleutta, the 22nd April 1959, referred an 
industrial dispute between Messrs. Bowreah 
Cotton Mills Company Ltd. and their workmen 
represented by Bowreah Cotton Mills Employees’ 
Union to the Second Labour Court for adjudica- 
tion regarding the issue mentioned in the order of 
reference. 

Issue 


Whether the dismissa] of Shri Sushil Das 
and Shri Mukunda (those is justified? To 
what relief, if any, are they entitled? 


The facts of the case, in brief, are as follows: 


Messrs. Bowreoh Cotton Mills Company Ltd. 
(hereinafter referred to as the Company), as the 
name indicates, manufacture and sell cotton goods. 
After the cloths are manufactured, they ure sent 
to the Bundle Department; there the bundlevs 
wrap the cloths in paper into bundles, under the 
supervision of a mistry. Several bundles make a 


[Parr 1 


bale. After the cloths are put into bundles, the 
mistry makes a kutehha slip in respect of each 
bale. The bundle and the kutchha slip then go 
to the bale clerk, who prepares a pucca slip. 
Both the slips and the bale then go io a eae 
checker. After checking by the bale checker the 
bundles of cloth go to fhe baling press where they 
are pressed and made into a bale. Then bale 
leaves the ware-house. 


In April 1958 there were complaints that some 
customers of the Company received cloths short 
of or in excess of cloths that should have been 
found in some bales. Sarbashri Sushil Das und 
Shri Mukunda Ghosh were the bale checkers at 
the relevant time. On 19th May 1958 the Com- 
pany issued a charge-sheet to Shri Mukunda Lal 
Ghose in respect of discrepancies in bale Nos. 3207, 
4535, 2564 and 5133, for neglect of work on the 
allegution that the above bales were checked by 
him. On 17th April 1958 the Company issued a 
charge-sheet to Shri Sushil Das for neglect of work 
in respect of discrepancy in bale No. 4332 and for 
his omission to put his signature on the checking 
slip. The two charge-sheeted workmen zave their 
replies to the charge-sheet. Enquiries were hel: 
in respect of the charge-sheets. Eventually the 
Company dismissed them. 


The contention of the Company is that it was the 
duty of every bale checker to count the number of 
cloths in each of the bundles forminz a bale. 
The Company alleges that the two charge-sheeted 
workmen who were employed as bale checkers did 
not count the contents of the bundles of the bales 
রর respect of which charge-sheets were issued to 
them. 


The two charge-sheeted workmen have admitted 
that they did not check the contents of all the 
bundles of the bales in question. Their cunten- 
tion is that it was not their duty to do so. Their 
contention is that their duty consisted of com- 
paring the pucca_ slip with the kutchha ship, 
checking the weight noted in the slips according 
to the calculation chart and to examine tke cen- 
tents of one sample bundle only in a bale. 


Shri Sushil Das has admitted that he did not 
sign the checking slip in question. So the points 
for determination are: 


(1) Whether it was the duty of the two work- 
men as bale checkers to count every cloth 
in every bundle in a bale; 


(2) Whether failure on the part of Shri Sushil 
Das to sign the checking slip ia a 1118- 
conduct meriting dismissal. 


DECISION 


The Union has alleged that the two workmen 
were victimised on account of their Trade Wnion 
activities; hut the Union hos not adduced any 
evidence in support of this allegation. So 1 
straightway reject the same. It has been proved 
beyond any shadow of doubt that enquires in 
respect of the two charge-sheeted workmen were 
held. The Company has produced hefore :ne the 
atatements of the two charye-sheeted workmen and 
of witnesses at the enquiries; but it appears that 
the Enquiring Officer has not drawn up any 


report of enquiry to show how he came to the 
finding that the two workmen were guilty of the 
charges mentioned in the charge-sheets. 1, how- 
ever, find that Shri H. P. Sarma, who was the 
Supervisor-in-charge of the ware-house then snd 
who ought to know the system of work there best 
has stated at the enquiry that the bale checkers 
check the contents of one sample bundle. So he 
gives a complete lie to the contention of the “om- 
pany that it was the duty of the bale checkers to 
check the contents of | every bundle in a tule. 
(). P. W. 1 Shri Gopen Jutta, Labour Officer of 
the mill and O. P. W. 2 Shri B.S. Kotnis, Head 
Weaving Master of the mill, have stated before 
me that it is the duty of the bale checkers to check 
the contents of every bundle in a bale. But both 
of them have admitted that there is no written order 
to that effect. ‘The Company has suggested to 
P. W. 3 that the Company determines the duty of 
all men. Nobody can refute this contention: But 
when the Company determines the duty of a parti- 
cular category of workmen, it must pass an order 
to that effect and make that order known to 
that category of workmen. In the present 0889 
it has not been proved either at the Jomestic 
enquiry or before me that.the Company ordered 
that the duty of a bale checker was to check the 
contents of every bundle in a bale. As the Cum- 
pany found the two  charge-sheeted workmen 
guilty of neglect of duty on the assumption that 
the above was their duty, the finding suffers from 
a basic error of fact. 


As to Shri Sushil Das, the Company has found 
him guilty of misconduct mentioned in section 
17(k) of the Standing Orders of the Company. 
That section mentions ‘habitual breach of any 
rules or instructions’. The Company did not 
charge Shri Sushil Das with habitual omission of 
signature on checking slips. He was charged for 
his negligence in signing a particular checking 
slip. This cannot be, by any stretch of imagina- 
tion, be termed 40180110181, So charging Shri 
Sushil Das and finding him guilty under section 
170) of the Standing Orders suffer from a basic 
error of law. 


In view of the above basic errors, T reject the 
finding of the Company on the basis of the 
enquirics held by it. The Company has also 
failed to prove its case by evidence before me. 


Tn the above circumstances, I hold that the cdis- 
missal of Sarbashri Sushil Das and Mukuuda Lal 
Ghose is unjustified. As auch, I order that they 
be reinstated and be paid wages for the period of 
their forced unemployment. The above. order 
shall take effect within a month of the publication 
of this award in the ‘‘Calcutta Gazette’’. 


Taken at my dictation and corrected hy me.

A. N. Banerjee (0.P.W. 2) that the three reasons

(3) He was in the habit of absenting himself

he did so on not less thun 32 occasions im 
course of about 2} years, inspite of 
several oral and written warnings. This 
caused dislocation in the work of the 
department to which he was attached. 


Of the above three reasons, only the first allega- 
tion, viz., the absence of Shri Munilall from 2Uth 
April 1955 to 23rd April 1955 has been mentioned 
in the charge-sheet, dated 21st April 1955. No 
charge.sheet was issued to him on the other two 
allegations. An enquiry was held about the charge- 
sheet; but no proceedings of that enquiry have 
been produced before me. So I am unable to 
decide whether that enquiry was properly con- 
ducted. As such I am unable to act upon the 
decision of that enquiry. 


As tw allegation No. 2, Shri A. N. Banerjee has 
stated in his evidence that he held the enquir 
about that allegation in presence of Shri Munnilall. 
I do nat disbelieve his evidence; but he adinits that 
he did not write any proceedings of that enquiry. 
As no charge-sheet was issued in respect of that 
allegation and as no proceedings of thut enquiry 
were written, I am unable to act upon the decision 
of that enquiry also. 


As to the third allegation, it is admitted by the 
Yompany that no charge-sheet was issued nor was 
any enquiry held about that allegation. 


Tho learned lawyer appearing for the Union has 
argued that the above findings lead irresistibly to 
the conclusion that the action of the Company سا‎ 
discharging Shri Munnilall is unjustified. am 
afraid, I cannot agree with him. ‘There are several 
rulings of the Supreme Court to the effect that 
rejection of the proceedings of enquiry held by & 
munagement does not ipso facto inake the order of 
the management unjustified. When such proceed- 
ings are rejected by a Court, the whole case 1s then 
at lurge before that Court, I am therefore called 
upon to consider the evidence adduced before me 
+n order to come to a finding where the discharge of 


Shri Munnilall is justified. e 


In the written statement of the Union it has been 
stated that Shri Munnilall had several motions on 
way to the office on 20th April 1969. But Shri 
Munnilall has admitted in his evidence that he did 
not stir out of his house on that day. He first said 
that he went to the hospital on 20th April 1955; 
but remembering that the hospital chit 1s dated 
21st April 1955 he corrected himself and anid that 
he went to hospital on 218৮ April 1995. Tt is 
admitted by him that at the relevant time he lived

the four days on which he remained absent on that

occasion he could not send information through his 
father to the Company about his absence. The 
reason of his absence, viz., illness may or may uot 
be true; but the Company has not charged him for 
being absent on a false plea. The charge against 
him as mentioned in the charge-sheet, dated 21st 
April 1988, is that he absented himself without any 
permission or even intimation. As he had enough 
opportunity to intimate his absence to the 01009, 
I hold that the charge mentioned in the charge- 
sheet, dated 2180 April 1955, has been proved. 


As to the second allegation, there is no reason 
to disbelieve the evidence of Shri S.C. Banerjee and 
of Shr A. N. Banerjee on this point. LTurther, the 
allegation made by Shri Munnilall in his letter, 
dated 11118 May 1955, that he was allowed to resume 
duty on 6th May 1955 is unbelievable, as being 
improbable. So I hold that the second allegation has 
been satisfactorily proved. In this connection the 
learned lawyer for the Union has referred to a deci- 
sion of tho Supreme Court in a-case of Lakshimi 
Debi Sugar Mills Ltd., reported at page 443 of 
L.L.J., 1956 Vol. 11. There the Supreme Court 
has held that a management cannot dismigs a work- 
man on a charge which has not been mentioned in 
the charge-sheet. But that was 0৮ case of permis- 
sion under section 22 of the Industrial Disputes 
(Appellate ‘Tribunal) Act. Naturally, there the 
management was required to make out a prima 
facie case on the proceedings of enquiry held by if. 
But in a case of reference under section 10 of the 
Industrial Disputes Act where the munagement 
fails to convince a Court by means of proceedings 
of enquiry held by it, it can 112, udduce 
independent evidence before that Court in justi- 
fication of its action. So even if it be admitted 
that the Company was not justified in taking into 
consideration a charge which was not mentioned 
in the charge-sheet, a Court before which the case 
is at large is entitled to come to a decision of its 
own, on evidence adduced before it. So I am 
entitled to hold and so held that the second ullega- 
tion has been satisfactorily proved. 


As to the third allegation, several warning letters 
issued to Shri Munnilall as also his Jeave chart 
clearly show that he was frequently absent with- 
out intimation, not to speek of permission. It may 
be presumed and there is also evidence to the 
effect that such conduct on the part of Shri Munni- 
lall caused dislocation in the work of the depart- 
ment to which he was attached. The learned law- 
yer on behalf of the Union haa argued that every 
such absence except the one in question was con- 
verted into leave with pay. This may lead to the 
inference that the management was satisfied as to 
the reasons of the absence; but-that does not 
absolve Shri Munnilall of the charge of frequent 
absence without permission or even intimation. 
So I hold that the third allegation has also been 
proved satisfactorily. 


Apart from the believability of the evidence 
adduced on behalf of the Company, there is one 
ertinent question ax to probability. If Shri Munni- 
۳ was innocent of the allegations made against 
him, as contended by the Union, the question arises, 
as to why the Company should take such a drastic 
nection against him. The learned lawyer for the 
Union has suggested to Shri A. N. Banerjee who

a 
مہ سے پیھو‎ 


took the decision of discharge of Shri ۸ 
that he took that decision on 2 question of prestige 
of the Company. The question of prestige might 
come when the Company was trying to maintain 
ita decision to discharge Shri Munnilall. But the 
question arises as to why the Company should at 
all have taken the decision to discharge Shri Munni-

the Company had any extraneous reasons to be dis- 
pleased with him. On the contrary, it cannot be 
expected that a Company should keep in its employ-

that he is systematically unamenable to discipline, 


In view of the above considerations, I hold that 
the discharge of Shri Munnilall is justified. As this

together and this award will govern both. 


2. The employer, the Oriental Research and 
Chemical Laboratory Ltd., which will hereafter 
be referred to as the Company, is a concern of 
about 20 years’ standing producing medicines 
and drugs. The case of the Union is that the 
Company had paid the usual Puja bonus to its 
employees at the time of Durga Puja every year 
for more than 10 vears until 1958 when it stopped 
ruch payment. The claim in the first case is for 
pavment of such bonus for 1958 and that in the 
Recond case for 1959.

bonus in the past ex-gratia out of sympathy and 
consideration for its employees and that the 
emplo®ees could not claim such payment as 179- 
tomary or as an implied term of employment, It 
is also stated that payment of bonus had to he 
stopped on account of the financial difficulties of 
the Company and the losses it sustained in 1958.

mentions only bonus’ without specifving the 
nature of it, the written statements make it 
clear that the bonus claimed is Puja bonus. The 
quantum of bonus claimed is not mentioned in

7. It is now well-settled that Puja bonus is 


. a special kind of bonus prevalent in Bengul and 


that it is paid either as an implied term of 
employment or as a customary and _ traditional 
হাল In the cases of Ispahani Limited and 
rahams Trading Co., Ltd. [1959-IT, L.0..J., 
panes 4 and 393 respectively] the Supreme Court 
aid down the tests for the two types of Puja 
bonus. The three common tests are: (1) that 
the payment has been over an unbroken -eries of 
years, (2) that 1t has been for a sufficiently long 
period, and (3) that the circumstances in’ which 
payment was made must be such as to exclude 
that it was 1১811 out of bounty or depended upon 
profits. All those tests have been satisfied in this 
case. The payment has admittedly been over an 
01110101061) series of years. There was no break 
before 1958. The payment has also been for & 
sufficiently long period—from 1948 at_ lenst 
covering ten years. The payment did not depend 
on profit but was made in three years of 1088 
also. It was not therefore paid out of bounty. 
In the case of Grahams 11 Co. it was laid 
down that where Puja bonus was claimed as 
customary and traditional it would turther have 
to be proved that the payment was throughout at 
8ہ‎ uniform rate so as to justify the inference that 
such rate had become customary and _ traditional 
in the particular concern. Payment at a uniform 
rate was not, however, necesaury where the bonus 
was claimed as an implied term of employment 
and it would he for the Tribunal to decide what 
should be the quantum of bonus in a 7٣ 
year taking into account the varying payments 
made in the past. | 


8. Aa already stated, payment of bonus in 
this case has not been at a uniform rate in the 
past. At first the rate was half month’s basic 
pay, then one month’s basic pay, and finally one 
and half months’ basic pay. So the additional 
test, laid down for customary bonus has not been 
satisfied in this case. Tt has been argued that as 
the Union claimed this bonus in the written 
statements as the ‘usual’ Puja bonus and as in 
its letter of demand, dated 30th September 1958 
(1ম, 1), the claim waa based on usage or custom 
in the absence of proof of a uniform customary 
payment the claims should fail. But the أ۵‎ 
proved ہ1‎ this case certainly make out a case 
that Puja bonus had become an implied term of

employment in this concern and that the 
employees are entitled to claim it on that ground. 
The 010৮ that the claim was not specifically based 
on that ground would make no difference when 
the tests laid down for such claim have been 
satisfied. So far as the quantum of bonus is 
concerned, it is clear from 11300, A that from 1951 
to 1956 it was uniformly paid at the rate of one 
month’s basie wage, in spite of heavy, losses 
during three years and it is also found from the 
Company's balince-sheets that in 1947 the Com-

that it would be fair and reasonable to fix the 


quantum of Puja bonus at one month’s basie pay 
for 1968 as well as for 1959. I award accor- 
dingly that the Company should pay one month’s 
basic wage us Puja bonus to its employees for 
each of the vears 1958 and 1959 and that the 
bonus for 1958 should be paid within one month

that for 1959 within three months from that 
date.

tribunal. The 11010 Appellate Tribunal held

1 by the Union that the first award of the

that the Hon’ble Appellate Tribunal upheld the

grades and scales of pay should be = allowed ٹا‎ 
endure for a reasonable time unleas’ there be 
justifiention for revision of the same. ]ا‎ the case 
of Burn & Co, Lid., reported in 1957, L.L.J.; I,

as intended to have long-term operation and at 
the same time the award is lable to be modified 
by change in the circumstances on which they 
were hased. In fact, the previous award showld 
not he changed except on sound and justifiable 
grounds. Some of these justifiable grounds are: 
(1) change of circumstances, (11) principle of 
gradual advance to the living wage, (11) anomaly, 
mistake or error in the last award involving hard- 
ship to cither party or to both. It was so observed 
that if it would be held that an adjudication loses 
‘ts forea when it is repudiated under section 19(6) 
of the Industrial Disputes Act and the whole 
controversy is at large, then the result would be 
that far from reconciling thomselves to the award 
and settling down to work it, either party would 
treat it us a mere stage in the prosecution of 7 
prolonged struggle, and far from bringing industrial 
pence, the awards would turn out to be but truces

Besides, a preliminary objection had been raised 
by the Company that the previous award is still con- 
tinuihg to be binding on the parties, as no valid 
notice had heen given by the workmen intimating 
their intention to terminate the award. Section 
1006১ of the Industrial Disputes Act provides thnt 
a notice must he given by any party bound by the 
award to the other party intimating its intention to 
terminate the award. In order to terminate a settle- 
ment, a notice in writing has been specifically pres- 
cribed under section 1902) of the Act. There 18 
apparently some difference as to the mode of termi- 
nation of a settlement or an award; but in either 
case 2 notice must be given. )لگ‎ is not the ense of 
the Union that a verbal notice had heen given to 
the employer intimating their intention to terminate 
the award. All that is contended by the learned 
lawyer of the Union is that proper intimation 
conveying an intention to terminate the award had 
been given when on the 21st February 1958, the 
Tnion wrote that the issues contained in that 
memomndum had not been properly considered in 
the previous Tribunal. xt. 6 ts the true copy of 
the said letter, dated the 21৭1 February 1958. Alang 
with this letter a memorandum of demand had 
been submitted. [ have carefully gove through 
the contents of the letter, Ext. 6. By that letter 
the Union requested the management to hold a 
joint discussion and proceed towards an agreement 


on the line of the memorandum of demands, which 
included tle question of wages of the sub-staif, 
It 1s also stuted in tho letter that due to some reasons 
technical or other the issues contained in the present 
memorandum were not properly considered by the 
previous Tribunals. The question that arises for 
consideration if this letter can be treated as & notice 
intimating the intention of the recognised Union 
to terminate the previous award. It is true that 
no prescribed form as to the notice is contemplated 
under section 19(6) of the Industrial Disputes Act. 
But at the sume time an intention to terminate the 
award must be expressed specificully through tho 
notice by the party, willing to terminate the award. 
All that is stated in the letter is thut tho issues 
cdntained in the memorandum of*demands had not 
been properly considergd by the previous Tribunal. 
But it cannot he said even by implication from 
the wording of this letter that the previous awards 
made by the Tribunal or Tribunals were being ter- 
minated. The learned lawyer for the Company 
rehed on the case reported in 1968, A.T.R. p. 4 
(Maharaja Shri Umaid Mills ltd. vs. The Textile 
Labour Union), as decided by Hon'ble Mr. Justice 
Wanchoo and Justice Dave of the Rajasthan High 
Court. On the other hand the Union relied on the 
case reported in 1956, L.A.C. p. 719 (Messrs 
Bhutoria Jute Mills, Howrah vs. Howrah Zillah 
Chatkal Mazdoor Union and others) as decided by 
the Hon’ble Labour Appellate Tribunal. These 
decisions appear to be contradictory. The crux 
of the point is the intention expressed, in termi- 
nating an award, in clear unequivocal terms, It 
is to be seen, if the letter be it in any form can be 
construed as a notice expressly signifying an inten- 
tion to termmate the award. The mere fact that 
the manngement held a joint discussion on the 
basis of the letter of demands put forward by the 
Union on 218: February 1958, does not give any 
additional force to the contents of the letter. Upon 
giving my careful consideration to the contents 


.of the letter, Ext. 6, [ hold that it does not so 


signify any intention to terminate the award and, 
therefore, the Tribunal cannot entertain the dispute 
when the award is still binding on the parties.

practice to take the consumption unit at 3.2307 at

issue No. 2 


This issue relates to the claim of gratuity in 
favour of Shri M. N. Bose, whose service had 
heen terminated with effect from lat Novemper 
1958. The snid employee had served under the

۱ 
employee was in the 618٦ year of age at the time he

superannuation took place before this accident. 
The Mercantile Tribunal in the award, dated 17th 
May 1949, decided the issue as to retiring age which 
was issue No, 12(d) on the following lines :— 


‘‘We decide that a man shall retire on com- 
pleting 55 years. We do not favour exten- 
sion of services, thereby blocking the way 
for younger people to get employment. In 
exceptional cases where both the employer 
and the employee agree, extension of services 
may be granted’’. | 


It is thus clear that extension of service beyond 
65 years of age was a matter of discretion, depend- 
ing و‎ the joint agreement of bath the রিটা টিক 
and the employee. There was no 01011296101) on the 
part of the employer to retain a man in service 
after he had crossed the 55th year. The Union 
has referred to a letter, dated 9th: October 1958, 
written by the management to Shri Bose wherein 
it is mentioned that ‘‘the normal retiring age has 
always been 55 to 60 and though we may have on 
occasions granted extensions of service to employees 
over that age, who were still in good health, we 
are obviously unable to, do so in the 0986 of 
employees who are not fit to work’’. The only 
inference that can be drawn from the letter is that 
the Company in their discretion had been liberal in 
retaining the employees in employment in excep- 
tional case beyond even 60 years of age though 
they normally adopted the age of retirement bet- 
ween 55 and 60 years. Naturally, Shri Bose was 
on such extension bevond the age of 60 venrs when 
he was in employment after Ist July 19457. His 
termination of service took vlace at the 62nd vear 
of his age. The mere fact that the Company in its 
sole discretion retained the man in service up to 
that age, does not in any way mean that it was 
anything more than an act of grace and in fact 
f concession shown to the employee by ৮9 
employer. The man was retired at the time when 
he was under treatment in the hospital, annenra to 
he completely irrelevant for the purpose of deciding 
the issue. Admittedly, the Company has got a non- 
contributory provident fund. Besides, an emplovee 
who had put in more thon 20 years of service 1s 
nllowed a pension. Shri Bose admitted that accord- 
ing to rules he was entitled to get a pension of 
Rs. 81.25, hut, os a matter of fact, he was miven

it nnpears from the award of the Hon’ble Aprellate

deoth or 7141191111৮ of a workman, gratnitv should

of service took place as the workman hand long

other reason. T hove carefullv gone through ۶۳ 
previous award and T feel that no gratuity is nav-

the age of superannuation. In fact, gratuity has 
heen made pavable only in case of death and dis-

imply provides that un industrial dispute might 
fe ruised for claim of gratuity when the company 
improperly refused to sanction such retirement. 
therefore hold that the claim for gratuity in favour 
of Shri Bose is unjustified. 


The learned lawyer for the Company urged that 
a retired workman cannot be said to be a workman 
within the meaning of section 2(s) of the Industrial 
Disputes Act.” Section 2(s) of the Act runs as 
follows :— 


‘‘Workman’’ means any person (including an 
নদ employed in any industry tv do 
any skilled or unskilled manual, supervisory, 
technical or clerical work for hire or reward, 
whether the terms of employment he 
expressed or implied, and for the purposes 
of any proceeding under this Act in relation 
to an industrial dispute, includes any such 
person who has been dismissed, discharged 
or retrenched in connection with, or as a 
consequence of, that dispute, or whose dis- 
missal, discharge or retrenchment hus led to 
that dispute’. 


Naturally, a dispute means a dispute or difference 
between un employer and workman and so a dispute 
in favour of a person whose service had been ter- 
minated by retirement cannot be suid to be an indus- 
trial dispute involving a ‘‘workman’’ as defined 
under the Act. There ia nothing here to challenge 
the propriety of retirement of Shri Bose. In fact, 
the issue as framed is simply concerning the claim 
of gratuity and all that I am to see here whether a 
retired workman دہ‎ claim gratuity on the basis 
of the rights and obligation created between the 
employer and the employee by the previous award. 
The learned lawyer for the Union urged that the 
dispute regarding the claim of gratuity arose 1n 
consequence of the retirement of Shri Bose and as 
wuch is an industria] dispute over which the ‘Tribunal 
has got jurisdiction to ad judicate eas In support 
of his contention he relied on the case of the 
Dahingeapar Tea Estate reported in 1958 [I L.L.J. 
at page 498. In that case the question nrose (1) 
whether on the transfer of management the ‘pur- 
chaser can put an end to the services of old 
employees and (ii) whether the members of the 
ataff can be deprived of their right of service under 
their original contract of service and their con- 
tinuity of service. The learned Tribunal found 
that as the garden was sold in a running condition, 
the transfer could not affect the service condition 
of the staff, aud the refusal of the purchaser to 
empley the persons or to retrench “he stuff was 
not justified. This decision was ultimately upheld 
hy the Supreme Court. The facts and circum- 
stances here are entirel different. Therefore, 
this decision does not. help the Union. 1 accord- 
ingly hold that Shri Bose is not  ‘‘workman’ as 
defined under the Act and as such the dispute 
over the claim of gratuity is not ھصم‎ industrial 
dispute and, therefore, this Tribunal has no juris- 
diction to adjudicate upon the question. So bath 
in fact and in law I decide this issue in favour of 
the employer. 


This single award govern the adjudications in 
both the orders of reference.

RULES FOR MANACEMENT OF NON-COVERNMENT HIGH SCHOOL 
INCLUDING AIDED SCHOOLS 


The Committee 


1. Definition.—The word 50000056629 in the following rules means 
Executive or Managing Committee or Goyerning Body of a school. 


2. A register of eligible voters for the constitution of the Managing 
Committec shall be prepared by the Head Master or Head Mistress of every 
Secondary School, in consultation with the existing Committee where there 
15 any, and shall be revised annually with such consultation as aforesaid, 
The register will be provisionally closed on the 15th March eyery’ year. 
It will be open to public inspection for at least one month from that date 
and will be finally closed on the last day of April every year with such 
revision as may be made by the Committee. 


{n the year in which an election for the constitution: or re-constitution of 
the Managing Committee takes get such a register of eligible voters 
shall be provisionally closed, and the electoral rolls published  simuls 
taneously, on the notice-bourd of the school at least one’ month before the 
date of the election. The register of cligible votefs shall be‘ finally closed 
at least fiftten days before the date of election with such revision as may 
be made by the Managing Committee.

Instructions for filling up the houselist 


Column 1,—Line Number. 


Only one digit of the line number has been printed in this column. The 
line numbers should be continuous for your block. Where the line numbers 
exceed 9 write the earlier digit(s) yourself. 


Column 2.—Sulding Number (Municipal or Local Authority or Census 
Number, if any). 


This refers to the entire structure on the ground. ‘There are, however, 
high, large or long buildings along a street or lane which have heen parti- 
tioned or portions of which have been sold, which have distinct, separate 
mun exit on the road and which belong to separate owners or occupiers or 
alternatively there are a series of different houses joined each to each by 
common wulls on either side to make the whole look like one building but 
parts of which have been built at different times and belong to separate 
owners. Such distinguishable structures, although not separate from each 
other, should be regarded as separate buildings and given separate numbers. 
Kach building should have a separate number, Uf in big cities a large man- 
sion or building containing several census houses has ua well-known name 
by which it is generally known then the name of the building should also 
be recorded for convenient reference. 11 there are more than one structure 
within an enclosed or open compound belonging to the same person, e.g., 
the main house, the servants’ quarters, the garage, etc., only one building 
number should be given. If the locality consists of u number of streets in 
a village, the buildings in the various streets should be numbered conti- 
nuously and the streets should be taken in uniform order, from North-West 
to South-East. Experience suggests that the best way of nambering is to 
continue with one consecutive serial on one side of the street und complete 
the numbering on that side before crossing over to the end of the other side 
of the street and continuing with the serial, stopping finally opposite to 
where the first numbering began. In a city enumeration block, the number- 
ing will have to respect the axis of the street and not) ديس‎ preeonceived 
geographical direction like North-West. A building under construction 
should also be given a number in tde serial. Lf a new hut or building is 
construcled between the time when the housenumbering and houselisting 
have been completed and the census count ‘it should be given a new number 
heyond the last number of the serial for the village. Arabic numerals 
should be used for building numbers, 


This will facilitate verification by supervisors. In areas, e.g., urban, 
where the buildings are already numbered by the municipal or other autho- 
ities, the enumerator may adopt the existing numbers in the Houselist. ta 
such cases, column 2 will carry the established municipal or local authority 
number which will facilitate identification. Where there are municipal or 
local authority numbers but there are reasons to believe that the number is 
incomplete or unsatisfactory, the municipal or local authority number may 
still be entered in column 2, but at the same time it will be necessary to 
serially number the buildings afresh for the purposes of census houselist. 
In that cnse, the new census serial for buildings will be entered ino colwun 
Gand the vew census nymbers for the buildings will have to be painted on 
the buildings themselves, In those cases where there are no municipal or 
local authority numbers in existence, all buildings will have to be serially 
numbered for the census and column 2 will contain entries of this census 
serial. This number will have to be repeated in column 3 with sub-numbers 
for census houses, if any. 


Column 3.—-Burilding Number (Column 2) with sub-numbers for each 
census house, 


6 
@ 


A census house is a structure or part of « structure inhabited or vacant, 
or a dwelling, a shop, a shop-cum-dwelling or a place of business workshop, 
achool, ete., with a separate entrance.

Tf a building has a number of flats or blocka which have separate 
entrances of their own and are independent of each other giving on the road 
or a common staircase or a common courtyard leading to a main gate, they 
will be considered as separate census houses. If within an enclosed or open 
compound there are separate buildings then euch such building will also he 
a separate census house. If all the structures within an enclosed compound 
are together treated as one building then each structure with a separate 
entrance should be treated as a separate census house. 


The order in which census houses within a building should be numbered 
should be continuous, preferably clockwise, or in any convenient manner if 
it is at all difficult to do it clockwise. [f a building itself is a census house, 
then it will have only one number, namely, that of the buildings. If within 
a building thore are a number of census bouses, then each census house will 
have two sets of numbers, e.g., the number of the building and the sub- 
number of the census house. The census house number should be written 
after the building number in arabic numerals in’ brackets such,as 2(2), 
3(2), ete. A census house may contain more than one household in which 
case, each household will have to be denoted by a separate alphabetical 
sub-number (see instructions for column 11 below). 


Column 4.—lurpose for which census house used, e.g., drelling, shop, 
shop-cum-dwelling, business, factory, workshop, school or other institu- 
tion, 16021) hostel, hotel, etc. 


The actual use to which a census house is put should be written here. 


In the case of a factory or workshop ‘Factory’ should be written for a 
large factory if registered under the Indian Factories Act and ‘Workshop’ 
for a small unregistered workshop. A workshop is a place where some kind 
of production, repair or servicing goes on or where goods or articles are 
made and sold. Similarly, a shop 1s a place where articles are sold for cash 
or for credit. Business houses are those where transactions in money or 
other articles are taking place, e.g., bank, etc. But rooms or apartments 
where professional consultations are held such as by doctors, hakums, 
pleaders, etc., should he described as ‘professional consultation rooms’ and 
not workshops. In the case, however, of a dispensary where, in addition 
to consultation by a doctor, medicines are prepared and sold, the house 
should be described as a dispensary, Write ulso if used for place of worship 
or congregation or if unoccupied, ‘vacant’. If the census house is a shop, 
business house, bank, eto., but is not a factory or workshop as defined 
above, the name of the proprictor, manager or director should be entered 


in column 18. 


Columns 6 to ৪.1 this census house is used as an establishment, work- 
shop cr factory’’. 


These columns apply only in cases where the census house is a factory 
or a workshop, i.e., where some kind of production, processing, repair or 
servicing is undertaken or where goods or articles are made and sold. Tf 
the census house is not used for purposes of a factory or workshop write 


‘X’ in each of the columns 5 to 8. 


Column 5.—Name of establishment or proprietor, 


Write the name of the establishment in the case of factories or large 
manufacturing concerns and write the name of the proprietor in the case of 
small workshops and establishments like confectioneries where no distinct 
name has been given to them like Halwaa shop, etc. df the census house is 
not used for the purpose of a factory or workshop put 44501 in each of the 


columns 6 to 8. 


Column 6.—Name of product(s), repair or servicing undertaken. 


Tn this column enter the actual work that is being done in the establish- 
ment, factory or workshop, like paper making, shoe making, cycle repairing, 


motor servicing, etc.

Column 7.—Average number of persons employed daily last week (including 
proprietor or household members, if any). 


The total number of workers including apprentices, either paid or un- 
paid, employed in the factory or workshop, including the owner or 
proprietor and any of his family members (if working), should be entered. 
The average number of persons working per day during the week preceding 
the date of your visit should be entered. 


In case more than one product is produced it is not necessary to enquire 
the number of persons employed in the production of each product. It may 
not he possible to get this information in cases where the operations may be 
com posite, 


Column 8.—Aind of fuel or power, if machinery is used, 


If the factory or workshop uses steam or diesel engine or fuel, e.¢., 
kerosene, soft coke, electricity, water-mill, etc., for running the machinery 
حا‎ for production, servicing or repairs, write what fuel or power is actually 
used. 


Columns 9 and 10.—Descripticn of census house. 


Column 9.—Material of wall. 


Under this coluinn the material out of which most of the walls of the 
house are made, £.6.) grass, leaves, reeds, bamboo, unburnt bricks, mud, 
burnt bricks, stone, eement concrete or timber should be written. Where a 
house consists of separate structures each of different materials, the material 
out of which the walls of the muin bedrooms are made are to be recorded. 


Column 10.—Material of roof. 


The material out of which moat of the outer roof exposed to the weather 
und not the ceiling is made, t.6., tiles, thatch, corrugated iron, vine or asbestos 
cement sheets or concrete, etc., should be written. In the case of a multi- 
ھن‎ building the intermediate floor or floors will be the roof of the lower 

oor. 


Column 11.—Sub-number of each census household with census house 
number (Column 3). 


A household is a group of persons who commonly live together anid 
would take their meals from a common kitchen unless the exigencies of work 
prevented any of them from doing so. 


There may be one or more households in a census house. Each house- 
hold should be separately numbered. This can be done by using the 
alphabets as (A), (B), 0 ete. For example, if building No. 2 is also a 
census house and has three households, the household numbers will be 2(A) 
2(B) and 2(C). If building No. 4 has two census houses, the houses will be 
numbered as (ا)4‎ and 4(2). If within each house there are respectively 3 
and 2 households, then they will be numbered us 4(1A), 4(1B), 4(1C) and 
4(2A) and 4(2B). 


Column 12.—Name of head of household. 


The name of the head offeach household given in column 11 should he 
written here. The head of a household, for census purposes, is the پا‎ 
on whom falls the chief responsibility for the maintenance of the house- 
hold. The name of the person who is actually acknowledged os head of the 
household should be recorded. In the case of places like messes, boarding

If the census house is used as a sitting place, cattle shed, etc., write the 
use tu which it is put (aud add the name of the owner). 


Column 13.—Number of rooms in census household, 


If a census house is occupied by one household the enumeration of rooma 
should be simple. 


If a census house consists of u number of households the number of room+ 
occupied by each household should be entered on each line against the name 
of the head of the household. In cases where more than one household 
occupy 2, single room or share more than one room in such a way that it is 
not possible to say the number of rooms occupied by each household, the 
number of rooms should be given together within brackets as common to 


both the households. 


A room should usually have four walls with a doorway with a roof 
overhead and should be wide and long enough for a person to sleep in, 1.e., 
it should be at least 6 ft. long. Unenclosed verandah, kitchen, ৪601৪) 
gurage, cattle shed and latrine which are not ordinarily used for living and 
sleeping should not be treated as rooms. An enclosed room, however, which 
is used for living, dining, storing and cooking should be regarded as a room. 


Column 14.—Does the household live in own or rented house? 


If the household lives in own house write ‘‘O’’. If the household lives 
in a rented house write ۰ 


In the case of public buildings like schools, hospitals, etc., or places of 
worship, put 5017 in this column. 


Columns 15 to 17.—Number of রি residing in census household on 
y of visit. 


Write the number of males residing in the household in column 16, the 
number of females residing in the household in column 16 und the total 
number of persons in column ۰ 


Column 18.—Hemarks. 


In this column should be entered any useful or significant information 
about the building or the census house or the census household that has not 
been entered in any other column. For example, if the census house is a 
shop the name of the proprietor or owner should be recorded in this column. 
If a census house is vacant at the time of houselisting but there is reason 
to believe that the house will be occupied in the course of the next few days 
and almost certainly before the census enumeration period, then the word 
“vacant” should be entered in column 4 and a remark should be entered in 
column ۱۸ to the effect “likely to be occupied shortly’’. Thus, the 
remarks column should be utilised for recording all significant information 
reluting to the building or census house or census household. 


If the members of the household living in the census house belong to & 
Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe then write SC. or ST., as the case may 
be, in this column.
