SCHEDULE “B’’ 


A.— Instructions for filling up the Household Schedule (Part 1) 


At the top of the Schedule you will find the Location Code, You will 
have to write the Location Code of the household here. Your supervisor will 
give you the Code numbers representing your district, tehsil/thana/town, 
village/wand/block. You should take care to write these three numbers 
connected together by oblique strokes in between on every household schedule. 


When you are visiting each household for enumeration you should write 
the code number of the household also on the Household Schedule. For 
purposes of the census a census house has been defined as a structure or a 
part of structure, a dwelling, a shop, workshop, factory or place of business, 
or shop-cum-dwelling giving on the road or a common staircase or a common 
courtyard leading to a main gate or enjoying a separate entrance. A 
household means the entire group of persons who commonly live together in 
the same census house and tuke their meals from a common mess unless the 
exigeucies of work prevent them from doing so. [nn some census houses 
{here may be more than one group of persons, each group with a common 
mess. In such cases, each group should be era) us a separate house- 
hold fon purposes of the census and a separate household schedule should 
1১৪ prepared. You should wstte the household number from the extracts of 
the house list given to you by your supervisor. If, in any 0588১ you find a 
census house or a household satisfying the definitions given above has not 
heen numbcred you should bring it to the notice of your supervisor and have 
a separate number given to the house on household and enumerate the 
household,

At the right hand corner of the Location Code you will find a question

house, etc., you should write the nature of the institution within the

Below the Location Code you will find a column for recording the full 
name of the head of the household. ‘The head of the household for census 
purposes 18 @ person on whom falls the chief responsibility for the muin- 
tenance of the household. Thus the head of the household need not neces- 
sarily be the eldest male member but may even bea female or a younge) 
member of either sex. You need not, however, make any elaborate enquiry 
about this and should record as head of household the name of the person 
who 19 actually acknowledged as such. 


Institutions like boarding houses, messes and chummeries should also be 
regarded as census households but of ‘un-related persons living together’. 
Iu such a household the manager or superintendent or the person who has 
administrative responsibilities or who by common consent is regarded us the 
head, should be recorded us head of the household. If in ২00 institution 
separate families are also living, each such family should be treated as a 
census household and a separate household schedule should be filled. In 
such cases the full name of the recognised head of the household should be 
written. 


If the Head of the household is a person who spends the weekdays in 
town and spends the week-ends at home, he should be recorded as Head of 
Household and entered for enumeration at his hume. If he should be away 
for w fairly long time which covers the entire enumeration period than the 
Ber ধা is incharge in his absence should be recorded as the Head of the 
household. 


You will find a parallelogram at the right hand side against the Full 
Name of the head of the household marked ‘‘S.C./S.T.’’. If the Head of 
the household is a member of a Scheduled Caste or a Scheduled Tribe 
obtaining in your State or in your district you should write the name of 
the particular Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe in which the head of the 
household belongs within the parallelogram. 


You should then fill up the part of the household schedule relating to 
Cultivation and Household Industry. Sub-part ‘A’ relates to Cultivation ; 
sub-part ‘B’ to Household Industry und sub-part ‘C’ to Workers at Cultiva- 
سنا‎ or Household Industry. 


Sub-part ‘A’ relating to Cultivation will have to be filled in only where 
the household cultivates land. (14900 includes all land normally used for 
cullivation purposes including tenrporary fullows.) Three categories of 
land are given in items 1(i), L(ii), and 2. Items 1(i) and 1012) relate to 
land actually cultivated by the household. Item 2 relates to land which 
is not cultivated by the household but has been given by it to private 
persons for cultivation for payment in money, kind or share. In each of 
the three cases the total of separate plots or parcels of land in different places, 
owned or held, or taken or given should be made and entered. A 
number of lines has been provided for this 5 in 101) and 1011) to 
account for separate plots or parcels of land held or owned or taken under 
different recognised local rights. If the household (a) cultivates Jand owned 
or held trom Government or taken from private persons or institutions or 
(b) has given land to private persons for cultivation purposes you should 
axcertuin the local name of the right on such lund and record in the 
column relating to ‘local name of right on land’. Category 10) land owned 
or held from Government, will include the total of all pieces of land owned 
or held in owner-like possession, e.g., land held directly from Government 
under a grant, lease or assignment, 030 with rights of permanent, heritable 
and transferable possession, (ii) with rights of permanent and heritable 
possession, but without the right of transfer and (111) temporary or condi- 
tional leases of any kind with the Government. Category 101) land taken 
from private persons or institutions for payment in money, kind or share, 
will include land (i) with rights of permanent, heritable and transferable 
possession, (ii) with rights of permanent and heritable ppssession but with- 
out right of transfer; (iii) held in a variety of tenancies or tenures which 
may be broadly classified as follows :— 


(a) tenants holding land with موہ مسا‎ and heritable rights whose 
land cannot be resumed by the owner on grounds of personal 
cultivation (such tenants may in some cases have the right of 
transfer also) ;

(‘ategories 1(i) and (11) will include only those plots or parcels of land

This sub-part will not apply to households which do not possess any 
land. Thus, it will not apply to households which consist of only agri-

Land under any of the items in sub-part ‘A’ includes rent-free Jani,

Sub-part ‘B’ relates to Household Industry. This part will be filled up 
only where there is a Household Industry conducted by the 1160 of the 
household himself and/or mainly by members of the household ut home or 
within the village in rural areas and only at home in urban areas. The 
industry should not be on the scale of a registered factory. The participa- 
tion of the Head of the hoysehold and/or members of the household is an 
ewential feature of the Household Industry. In a rural area the Household 
Industry can be located either at home or within the village. But in an 
urban area the Household Industry or at Jeast the major part of its work 
must be located only at home. A Household Industry should relate to 
production, processing, servicing or repairing and includes makers and 
xellers of ০০৫৪,

The test for a Household Industry is mainly threefold :— 


(a) Household Industry should embrace manufacture, processing or 
servicing and may include sale but should not be confined simply 
to buying and selling. At least part of the goods offered for sale 
from the household shauld be manufactured or processed hy 
members of the household. 


(b) Household Industry should be on the household scale where the 
workers mainly will bo the Head of the household himself and 
members of the household, the role of hired workers from outaide 
being of secondary, importance. Thus, in any Household 
Industry, ‘members of the household should be in a position to 
lend a hand in the industry whenever they find the time in the 
course of their daily chores. Household Industry cannot, there- 
fore, be on the scale of a registered factory but can use machinery 
and employ power like steam engine or oil engine or electricity 
to drive the machinery. : 


(0) Location also is و‎ Weslo for proximity decides participation by 
members of the household. In a village this participation hy 
possihle if the 11059915017 Industry is located at home or within 
the village, because village organisation is such as makes it 
possible for members of the household to move about freely in 
the village to look after their work. In urban areas such a free 
movement is rtot possible and, therefore, for Household 7 
in urban areas we should consider only those industries which 
are located at home. Where, however, part of the work is done 
outside the house, e.g., preparing and dyeing the yarn for 
Weaving or winding into warp and wool or cleaning metal 
surfaces before electroplating in baths, it should still be con- 
sidered a Household Industry, even in urban areas, as the main 
operation of weaving or of electroplating is conducted within 
the house and only one or two operations are conducted outside. 


The following activities should also be regarded as illustrative of House- 
hold Industry. Biri-makers who either alone or with help of members of 
the family roll biris at home, for wages at piece rates, while the contractor 
supplies the materials. Certain processes like buttoning and handsewing 
of tailored cloths, dyeing and printing of cloth, are carried out at home by 
members of the household both at residence and at ‘place of work’ or where 
womenfolk of the houschold fill in at home with lac gold ornaments prepared 
at the shop by male members of the household, 


Ascertain from the Head of the household whether there are any 
Household Industries and write the nature of the industry(ies) in the 
column provided, if there are any. Then ascertain for how many months 
in a year roughly they are conducted and put down the number of months 
in the appropriate column. If the industry is conducted throughout the 
year write ‘12’. If there is no Household Industry of any sort put an ‘X’ 
in each of the places in the right hand corner where the answers will be 
written and put a bold cross on this sub-part.

SCHEDULE ‘C” 
A. Instructions to EKnumerators: 


The 1961 Census count will relate to the sunrise of Ist March, 1961. 
The count will be spread over a period of 19 days, beginning on the 10th 
February and ending on the 28th February, 1961. During this period you 
should visit every household in your block for enumeration. On the night of 
28th February you will have to go round your enumeration block and 
enumerate all persons who are houselew, (In large cities the enumeration 
of houseless persons will have to be undertaken in a different manner for 
which more elaborate arrangements will be made.) During the period Ist 
March to 5th March you all have to pay a revisional round to every house- 
hold and verify that vour earlier work of enumeration has been completed 
in every respect. If during this revisional round you find that a birth has 
taken place in any household between the time of your first visit and the 
sunrise of Ist March, 1961, you will have to fill up a new slip for this birth; 
1f there has been a death in any household during the same period you will 
have to cancel the slip of the dead person; if there is a visitor in any house- 
hold who has come to stay during the same period and has not been 
enumerated elsewhere, you will have to fill up.a new slip for this visitor. 
But you will not have to take notice of any birth or death or visit occurring 
atter sunrise of Ist March, 1961. 


You will have been supplied by your Supervisor household schedule 
forms in books of 50 or 25 each for recording information relating to the 
household as a whole and enumeration pads consisting of 400 or 25 slips 
each to record information of individuals living in the household. Instruc- 
tions for filling up the household schedule and the individual slips are given 
in this booklet. You should carefully observe them when filling each 
household. You can fill up the household schedule first or the enumeration 
slips first but for every household you should fill up both before you leave 
the household and also fill up the Census Population Record at the back of 
the household schedule. 


B. Instructions for enumerating individual members of households: 
I. GENERAL— 


1. Enumerate all persons who are normally resident in the household, 
i.e., those who live in the household and also those who have recently become 
members of the household through marriage or birth or other vital social or 
domestic ties and are present at the time of your visit. 


2, Enumerate also all persons who are normal residents in the house- 
hold even if they are absent at the time of your visit, provided they left 
the household on or after the 10th February, 1961, or if they had left 
earlier than 10th February, 1961, are likely to return before the sunrise of 
Ist March, 1961. 


3. Enumerate a visitor, a boarder, or a guest found in the household 
at the time of your visit, 1/ he had not heen Cnumerated befare and if he will 
be away from his household between the 10017) and 28th February, 1961, and 
warn him not to permit any other enumerator to enumerate him even if he 
goes back by Ist March, 1961. 


4, Do not enumerate pavement dwellers or others who do not form part 
of the household, when you are enumerating the households, These along 
with persons who do not normally reside in houses, i.e., members of wander- 
ing tribes, tramps, sadhus, ete., would be separately enumerated on the night 
of the 28th February and on the Ist and 2nd March, 1961. 


5. Kach individual has to be enumerated in one slip Before commenc- 
ing enumeration of an individual make sure to fill the Location Code in each 
case, The Location Code in the slips will be the same os in the household 
schedule to which the individuals relate. 


এ 
6. The questions have been briefly printed in the slips, but only briefly, 
and you should study the detailed question forms and instructions for 
answering them without which you will be liable to miss some of the range 
and implications of the questions. You should ask the questions in the order 


Pant [| THE CALCUTTA GAZETTE, EXTRAORDINARY, SEPTEMBER 26, 1960 2597 


17) which they are given in the slips and proceed to record the answers in 
their given order. You should i i use of the abbreviations recommended 
in these instructions for recording the anawers to the various questions. All 
abbreviations required to he entered within the geometric designs should 
be written well within the designs. 


t, Make repeated enquiries about new born babies and very young 
children for they are liable to be missed because they neither talk nor walk 
wand no meals are usually cooked for them. 


8. Before leaving one household for the next make doubly sure that all 
the persons that ure to be enumerated in the houschold have been enumerat- 
ed. As soon as you have completed the enumeration of the household fill 
up the Population Record at the back of the Household schedule for that 
household before you proceed to the next household. Strike the total for 
the number of males and females in the household and check it with the 
number of enumeration slips used before you sign the Population Record. 


9. Youn should revisit every household in your block during the period 
of final check (Ist to 3rd March) when you showla enumerate every birth 
that hag taken place in the household since your visit but before sunrise of 
lst March. You should cuncel the slip for any death that might have taken 
place since your last visit but before sunrise of 186 March by drawing a bold 
line diagonally across the slip and write DEATH along the diagonal line. 
You should enumerate any visitor who may have arrived to stay since your 
last visit and who says he has not been enumerated anywhere else. But you 
should not take notice of any birth or death or visit occurring after sunrise 
of Ist March, 1961. After your revisit if you have added any new slip or 
cancelled any slip already prepared you should make corresponding changes 
in the Census Population Record at the back of the Household Schedule. 


10. As soon as you have completed ua pad, you should fill up the 
enumerator’s abstract on the cover of the pad. After yqu have completed 
the enumeration of your block and filled up all the abstracts in the pads, 
you should total up your figures and prepare your abstract for your eptire 
block and hand it over to your supervisor along with your pads. 


11. Under the Census Act, every person is legally bound to furnish you 
with the information you need for recording your answers. You must not 
ask information on any matters not necessary for the purposes of the census, 
for exumple, the amount of any person’s income. Nor must you disclose to 
any unauthorised person any information given to you or the results of the 
enumeration. All census entries are confidential and cannot be admitted 
as evidence in any civil proceeding whatever or in any criminal proceeding 
other than a prosecution for a census offence. 


If. INSTRUCTIONS FOR FILLING UP THE SLIPS— 


In each household you should first enumerate the Head of the household 
followed by other members of the household in the most convenient order 
and see that none of the persons in the household are left out. Please make 
repeated enquiries about infants and very young children, for they are liable 
to be left out. of count. Count near relatives first, such as wfie, son, 
daughter-in-law, daughter, son-in-law, grand-children, then distant relations 
and then domestic servants or other employees living in the household, 
boarders, visitors, etc.

Laplanation— 


(1) An Employer is a person who has to employ other persuns in 
order tv perform the work entered in q. 1104), That is to say, such ৪ 
person is not only responsible for his own personal work but also for giving 
work to others in the business mentioned in (1. 1109). But a person who 
employs domestic servants for household duties or has subordinates unde: 
him in an office where he is employed by others, is not an employer, even 
if he has the power to employ another person in his office on behalf of his 
own employer or employers. 


(82) An Employee is a person who usually works under some other 
person for salary or wages in cash or kind. There may be persons 
who are employed as managers, superintendents, ugents, etc., aud in 
that cupacity employ or control other workers on behalf of their own 
employers. Such persons are only employees, as explained above, and 
should not be regarded as employers. ۱ 


(167) ۸ Single Worker for the purpose of Q. .116)6( is & person who 
works by himself but not as Head of household in a Household Industry. 
He is not employed by ony one else and 10 his turn does not employ 
anybody else not even members of his household except casually. ‘This 
definition of a Single Worker will include a person who works in joint 
partnership with one or several persons hiring No employees, and also a

In the matter of an industrial dispute between

Shri HEM RANJAN DEB, Presiding (0

«West Bengal,

For the Union: Shri N. 1). Manna, Counsel with

For the Company: Shri Sailesh Sen, Advocate. 


By order No. 5642-1.R./1R/111-626/58, dated 
Calcutta, the 30th December 1958, Government of 
Labour Department, referred. an 
industrial dispute between ieee Dhootapapeswar 
Sales Corporation (P) Ltd., and their workmen 
represented by Burrabazar Jamadar Sangh to the 
Second Labour Court for adjudication regarding. 
the issue mentioned in the order of reference, 


Issue 


Whether the dismissal of Shri Baijnath 'Tewari 
is justified P To what relief he is entitled? . 


The Company has raised a sae objection 
that this is not an industrial dispute on the ground 


10016 its employees are not concerned in the 


(11810188801 of Shri Baijnath Tewari which is the issue 
mentioned in tho order of reference, 


The Union, on the other hand, contends that this 
is an industrial dispute on the ground that at the’ 
time when Shri Baijnath Tewart waa -dismixaed, 
majority of the employees of the Company - were 
members of Burrabazar Jamadar Sangh, the Union 
which has espoused the cause of Shri Baijhath 
Tewari, ho : ৮ 

As this award ‘relates to the’ above preliminary 
objection vraised: hy the Company, the point for 
determination is whether -this if an industrial 
dispute. 

r ' FINDINGS ae 


The various decisions of the Supreme Court have 
made clear the baste rgason why an individual 


2614(1) 


2614(2) 


dispute could be taken up by a Union and thereby 
transformed into an industrial dispute. The 
Industrial Disputes Act is a legislation intended to 
ensure industrial harmony. When an individual 
case ix taken up by a class of workmen, it, becomes 
an industrial struggle and loses its limited scope. 
That is why the Supreme Court has consistently 
held that when the cause of an individual dispute 
is taken up by a Union of workmen or substantial 
portion of them, the dispute becomes an industrial 
dispute. In the present case the Union has adduced 
evidence to the effect that five out of the eight 
persons who were employees of the Company on the 
date of dismissal of Shri Baijnath Tewari were 
members of Burrahazar Jumadar Sangh. Though 
P.W.. 4 Baijnath Boram and P.W. 5 Ram Mohan 
Tewari have denied in their examination-in-chief 
hat they were members of Burrabazar Jamadar 
Sangh, their evidence in cross-examination as also 
the evidence of O.P.W. 1 Shri Ram Chandra 
Pandey, Office Secretary of Burrabazar Jamadar 
Sungh, and of O.P.W. 2 Shri Baijnath Tewari 
clearly show that the above Baijnath Boram and 
Ram Mohan Tewari, two employees of the Company 
were members of Burrabazar Jamadar Sangh at the 
relevant time. . So it is clear that a majority of the 
employees of the Company were members of Burra- 
bazar Jamadar Sangh at the time of dismissal of 
Shri Baijnath Tewari. Hence it must be held that 
Burrabazar Jamadar Sangh was u Union of the 
employees of the Company at the relevant time. 


The next question arises whether the above fact 
alone could transform the present dispute into an 
industrial dispute. O.P.W. 1 Shri Ram Chandra 
Pandey and O.P.W. 2 Shri Baijnath Tewari havé 
deposed to the effect that on the day. following the 
dismissal of Shri Baijnath Tewari those employees 
who were members of Burrabazar Jamadar Sangh, 
went to the office of the Union and requested the 
General Secretary and the Office Secretary of the 
Union to take up the case of Shri Baijnath Tewari. 
It is clear from evidence that Shri Baijnath Tewari 
went to the office of the Union on that day; but 
the evidence as to whether the other employees 
went to the office of the Union on that day and 
requested the General Secretary and the Office 
Seeretury’ to take up the case of Shri Baijuath 
Tewari is not convincing. Even if it be held that 
they did so, the fact remains that all the persons 
who were employees of the Company at the relevant 
time and the persons who became employees of tho 
Company subsequently have stated before me on 
solemn affirmation that they are not concerned in 
the dispute arising out of diamisaal of Shri Baijnath 
Tewari. So the question is whether I should brush 
asile their evidence before me, 


The learned Jawver for the Union has argued 
that once the employees have taken up the cause 
of Shri Baijnath Tewari, they cannot now turn 
round and say that they are not concerned in the 
dispute, as thia nmounta’ to a revocation of their 
conseut, In support of his contention he has drawn 
inv attention to the decision of Ton’ble Mr. Justice 
Sinha in the case of Reckitt and Colman, reported 
in ۸.۲.11. 1956, Caleutta, page 358. But that 
decision relates to an entirely different matter and 
can have no bearing on the question uow heing 
decided by me. On the contrary, the view on this 
question appenrs in his decision in the case between 
Express Newspaper (P) Limited and Virst Labour

Court, West Bengal and others, reported at page 
600 of L.5.3., 1959, Voluthe .ا‎ “Therein he has 
held that the fact that the cause.of a workman hag 
been taken up by the Union does not clinch the 
issue whether a particular dispute is an industrial 
dispute. In that decision he ie observed, ‘‘when 
a workman is represented by a Union of the work. 
men of the employer or a large portion thereof, and 
if the employer alleges that the Union does not 
represent the views of the majority of the workmen 
or large portion thereof, then in the first instance, 
it would be for him to prove the same.”’ Thi 
shows that the Hon’ble Mr. Justice Sinha allow: 
the employer to adduce evidence to the effect that 
his employees are not concerned in a dispute, even 
though it has been taken up by a competent union. 
He makes the position clear by holding that the 
whole point is as to whether the employer is fighting 
with a large number of his workmen, and that until 
thut 165৮ is passed, an individual dispute cannot be 
transformed into an industrial dispute. This is 
exactly the situation in the present case. Though 
admittedly the Union has espoused the cause of 
Shri Baijnath Tewari, none of the present 
employees of the Company is concerned in hia 
dismissal. So it is clear that the Company is 
fighting with Shri Baijnath Tewari alone and none 
else of its employees. The above decision of 
Hon’ble Mr. Justice Sinha is not in conflict with 
the successive decisions of the Supreme Court on 
the distinction between an individual dispute and 
an industrial dispute. So that decision of 6٤6 
Mr. Justice Sinha is a precedent for me. As held 
in that decision, in the present case the Company 
has adduced the evidence of all its workmen to the 
effect that they are not concerned in the dispute 
] have no reason to disbelieve them. 


[In view of the above considerations, ٢ hold that 
the present dispute is not an industrial dispute.

atrict accuracy and actuality should be — insisted 
Upon in respect of any vartictlar point an 6+

notional in the sense that there is no evidence that

PRESS NOTE 


WHITE TWO-ANNA AND WHITE 
HALF-ANNA COINS 


Demonetisation from Ootober 


Al) two-anna and half-anna coins of cupronickel 
composition (white in colour) will cease to be 
ا‎ tender with effect from October 1, 1960. 
On that day, the demonetisation notification of the 
Government of India issued on March 2, 1960 will 
come into effect. 

These coins will, however, continue to be 
accepted for the next six months, till March 91, 
1961 at all offices of the Reserve Bank of India, at 
all agency banks of the Reserve Bank conducting 
(lovernment business and all treasuries and sub- 
treasuries in payment of dues as well as for 
exchange. During this period, these coins will 
also be accepted at all railway and post and 
telegraph offices, but only in payment of dues, such 
us payment for railway tickets, booking of goods 
by railways, for postage stamps and other postal 
atationery, radio licence fee, etc. Thereafter, 
these coins will continue to be accepted at the 
seven offices of the Issue Department of the 
Reserve Bank of India at Bombay, Caloutta, 
Madras, Kanpur, New Delhi, Bangalore and 
Nagpur.

THE COMMISSIONERS FOR THE PORT OF 
CALCUTTA 


Summary of the Minutes of the Proceedings of the 
2ر‎ 10th Meeting, held on the 20th June 


AT the 10th Meeting of the Commissioners held on the 
20th June 1960 the following business was transacted:— 


1. Development scheme for 11011881011 In the Third Five- 
Year Plan.—The Commissioners approved the Chairman’s 
proposals for the inclusion of certain Development 
schemes in the Third Five-Year Plan. 


2. Application for a loan of Rs. 1 orore from Govern- 
ment for financing the Second Five-Year Plan Projects.— 
The Commissioners decided to apply to Government for the 
grant of a loan of Rs, 1 crore for financing the Second 
Five-Year Plan Prdjects. 

3. Valuation of property vested in the Commissioners 
for the purposes of payment of municipal tax to the Cor- 
poration of Caloutta.—The Commiasioners approved certain

DECISION 


issue No. 1 


The only one issue whieh awaits adjudication 
under this order of reference is ‘‘Working hours’. 
It is not disputed that the present dispute 68 
regarding fhe working hours of the staff 
(excluding the officers) of the Head Office of the 
Company, namely, Airways (India) Limited, 
situated at 31 Chittaranjan Avenue, Calcutta and 
that. the present working hours for this staff of 
the Head Office of this Company are from 
9-30 a.m. to 5 pam. with half-an-hour’s break, t.e., 
from 1] p.m. fo 1-30 p.m., for luneh. This is the 
evidence of D.W. ۱ Shri Rangaswami, the 
Manager of the Company and. it is also the case 
of the Union in paragraph 1 of its written state- 
ment although no evidence has heen adduced 
hefore this Tribunal on behalf of the Union. 


The grievance of the Union is that the general 
office hours in all mercantile firms and Govern- 
ment offices are from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. and that 
the existing working hours for the Tend Office 
staff of the present Company caused hardship. to 
the workmen. The Union accordingly prays that 
the Company may be directed to fix the working 
hours for the emplovees of the Head Office from 
10) acm, to ة5‎ pom. with a break of 45 minutes, 


To this claim of the Union, the Company has 
raised three-fold objection, namely— 


(1) that the present reference is bad in law 
Innxanuch as there was no industrial dis- 
pute between the management and its 
Head Office employees regarding 0٥ 
working hours prior to the reference, 

(9) that the emplovees of the Head Office 
never raised any dispute regarding — the 
existing working hours in the Head

Office of the Company and that 8ج‎ 
present there is no industrial dispute in 
existence because of the ‘fact that the 


Head Office employees do not make 
any 17716201000 regurding their existing 
working hours, and 

(3) that on merits also the claim of the Union 
that the working hours should be fixed 
from 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. with a break of 
45 minutes is yureasonable and unjus- 
tified im view of the fact that the 
existing working hours of the Company 
for its Hend Office staff, namely, from 
9-30 a.m. to 5 p.m. with half an hour’s 
break from 1 p.m. to 1-30 p.m. for lunch 
are fair and reasonable on in line with

a number of similar concerns. So, in 
nut-shell, the contention of the Company 
is that the claim ‘of the Union should be 
rejected both on point of law and on

As I have stated before the first two objections 
taken by the Company are legal objections 
regarding maintainability of the present reference. 


So far as the first objection is concerned, 
namely, that the present reference is bad in law, 
the Company’s objection is that prior to the order 
of reference the employees of the Head Office

from the annexures A to 0) to the written state- 
ment of the Company which are not disputed by 
the Union, it is clearly established that in July 
1958 the President of the Aero Employees’ Union, 
West Bengal, submitted a charter of demand 10 
the Labour Commissioner, West Bengal (26th 
July 1958), wherein the Union raised a dispute 
regarding the working hours. At that time the 
working hours for the Head Office staff of the 
present Company were from 9 a.m. to 5 ٠۰ 
(vide annexure A). ۸ true copy of the Jetter 
embodying the demahds including the office 
hours was forwarded to the Company for com- 
ments by a letter, dated 12th August 1958. The 
Company submitted its comments upon — those 
demands and on 18th February 1959 the Assistant 
Secretary to the Government of West Bengal. 
Labour Department, intimated to the Secretary of 
Aero Kimployees’ Union as also to the Company 
that the demands made by the Aero Kmploye7s’ 
Union regarding gradex and scales of pay and 
working hours were not justified and that Govern- 
ment did not consider any further intervention 
to be made in the matter. With regard to the 
working hours, as it is found from the letter, the 
{iovernment stated that the Company’ waa 
following working hours generally observed by a 
number of such concerns. So, the dispute raed 
hy the Union regarding working hours of the 
Head Office staff in July 1948 found its burial in 
February 1959. After that on Ist August 0 
the existing working hours for the Head Office 


৪101) namely, from 9-30 a.m. to 6 pom, with half- 
an-hour’s brenk for tiffin were fixed [vide para-

is admitted that tho present working hours ere 
from 9-30 a.m. to 5 p.m. with  half-an-hour’s 
recess for tiffin. 


Thereafter the Union appeay to have suddenly 
revived tho dispute regarding’ the working hours 
in its lotter, dated 8th April 1959, to the 
Assistant Secretary, Government of West Bengal, 
Iubour Department, amongst other matters. That 
was referred to the Company for comments, But 
from that letter annexure C (the original of

From annexure ]) it is found that there were

The Company’s specific case is that prior to the 
سس‎ reference there was no industrial dispute 
vetween the management and its Head Office

pec examined to support the claim of the 

nion. 


From al] these documents and oral evideure

between the Head Office employees and the pre-

_ Next ٤ come to the second objection. Kven if 
1 he taken for granted that the reference is valid 
and legal the Wnion has no case so far ax the 
nresent referenee is concerned. It  tronspires

Be that as it may, from the above evidence it

But for the sake of completeness ] must. also 
discuss point No. 8, namely, the claim of the 
Tnion on merits. Admittedly the existing work- 
ing hours for the Head Office staff are from 
9.40 a.m. to 5 p.m. with half-an-hour’s break

also prevailing in 2 number of similar concerns 
and are fair. This wus alsa the view of the

(government in its) letter, dated 18th February

In view of my above findings I hold that both

DECISION 


At the outset the luwyer on behalf of the 
employer has argued that whereas the name of the 
hotel is admittedly “South Caleutta Hindu Hotel’, 
in the order of reference the name appears as 
“South Caleutta Hotel’. On this he contends that 
the order of reference is bad and cannot be entered 
into. But this is obviously a technical mistake 
and has not any way misled either of the parties. 
So | overrule this objection and enter into the 
merits of the case. 

The employer has produced a page of the pay 
register wherein the three workmen in question 
have written to the effect that they received their 
up-to-date wages and were resigning of their own 
accord, Shri P. )'. Misra, the only workman who 
has deposed before me says that they were forced 
by threat to write to the above effect. He says 
that they went to Tollygunge Thana and made a

the above. But that diary or any evidence in 
support of the existence of such a dinry has not 
been produced before me. He also says that they 
reported the matter to the Union which wrote a 
le(fer to the Proprietor of the hotel; but no copy 
of such a letter has been produced before me. ۷ 
appears from his evidence that he is in the habit

ullege that he was dismissed from those hotels. 
So the contention of the emplover that he resigned 
the service in the hotel in question is probable. 
The other two workmen in question have not 
appeared before me. So they have not stated

suvs that they were dismissed, as they asked for 
leave. This contradiction between the statement 
of the Union and the evidence of Shri P. ) Misra 
inakes the contention of the ‘Thion unbelievable. 
Sy T hold that Sarbashri P. 0. Misra, Dilip Bhanja 
and Malin Chandra Dey resigned their services of 
their own accord. Hence the question whether 
the termination of their employment is justified 
rnised in the issue in the order of reference, does 
not arise,

DECISION 


The only issue for adjudication under this refer- 
ence is ‘‘Pay for the strike period’. It is an 
admitted fact that the workmen of Messrs. Dabur 
(Dr. S. K. Burman) Private Ltd. with its work- 
shops at Caria and Ballygunge staged a strike on 
and from 30th January 1059 and it continued till 
15th March 1959 when a settlement was arrived at 
between the Company and the Union. So, admit- 
tedly the period of strike is from 308 January 1959 
to 15th March 1959. The present. Union represent- 
ing the workmen of this Company prays — before 
this Tribunal for payment of full wages for the 
period of strike. : 


The case of the Tnion in its written statement 
is that the strike was legal and justified as well 
as provoked by the management and that as such 
the workmen are entitled to full wages for the 
period of strike, i.e., from 30th January 1959 to 
15th March 1959. The Union has stated in its 
own way the facts which led to the strike. Accord- 
ing to the Union the strike was due to the fact 
that the Company did not agree to consider its 
charter of demands submitted to the management 
on Lst December 1958 (Ext. B on admission) and 
that it dismissed six prominent members of the 
Union without just and sufficient cause on 5th 
December 1958 and dismissed them for the second 
{ime with effect from 22nd January 1959. 


The Company meets the case of the Union with 
its contentions that the strike of the workmen was 
improper and unjustified and was not at all pro- 
voked by the management, but that it was the result 
of a deliberate plan to coerce the management to 
accept their unfair demands. The Company further 
eontends that the alleged ground for resorting to 
the strike on behalf of the workmen was dismissal 
of six persons mentioned in paragraph 4 of Union's 
written statement who were guilty of gross ۰ 
conduct and were properly dismissed after issue 
of charge-sheets against them and on proper enquiry 
into the charge-sheets on consideration of explana- 
tion ৮10১1010166] by the workmen concerned. So, 
according to the Company the strike being unjusti- 
fed and unprovoked the workmen are not entitled 
fo any wages for the strike period. 


Refore [ go into the merits of the case T must 
consider the legal position regarding the strike. 
It is one of recognised principles of law that strike 
is n legal weapon in the hands of the workmen for 
collective bargaining and for redress of their 
grievances againat the employer. The right to 
atrike ia in the nature of a fundamental right of 
workmen, Aa it has been very recently observed 
bv the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of 
Swadeshi Industries Tid. vs. their workmen repor- 
ted in 1960 T..0.3.. Vol. ,1ا‎ page 78 at page ۰ 
collective hargaining for sectring improvement on 


[ Part gd 


matters like basic pay, dearness allowynce, bonus, 
provident fund, gratuity, leave and holidays is the 
rimary object of a trade union, and when demands 
like these are put forward and thereafter a strike 
ix resorted to in an attempt to induce the company 
tu agree to the demands or at least to open 
hegotintions, the strike must prima facie ص۷‎ 
considered justified. 


Under the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, sume 
strikes have been prohibited and those are 
illegal strikes. Sections 22 to 25 of the said Act 
refer to such strikes and  lock-outs. Unless a 
strike is prohibited under the provisions of these 
sections of the Industrial Disputes Act, it must 
be treated as a Jegal strike because it is a weapou 
which can be legally employed by the employees 
against their employer for redress of grievances 
by constitutional means. As defined under  sec- 
tion 2(q) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, a 
strike means a cessation of work by‘a body = of 
persons employed in any industry acting in 
combination, or concerted refusal. or a refusal 
under a common understanding, of any number 
of persons who are or have been so employed to 
continue to work or to accept employment. So 
fer as the instant case of sttike is concerned, if 1s 
not disputed that it was a strike within this defi- 
nition und was not a strike prohibited under sec- 
tions 22 to 20 of the Industrial Disputes Act. So, 
the strike which the employees of the present 
Company resorted to from 30th January 1949 to 
15th March 1959 must be considered to huve been 
a legal strike. 7 


It is now woll-settled that if a strike is ihegal 
if cannot be justified and the workmen — resort'ng 
to such a strike are not entitled to anv wages for 
the strike period (vide the case of Rohtas Industries 
Ltd., reported in F.J.R., Vol. XVI, page 3897). 
The Hon'ble Supreme Court has held in the case 
of Indian General Navigation and Railway Coz- 
pany Ltd. (1960 .آ1‎ Vol. ,ا‎ page (8ا‎ that 
the law has made a_ distinction between strike 
which is legal and which is not and that an illegal 
strike cannot be justified. 


I have already found that the present strike was 
a legal strike, i.e., recognised under the law. 
But in order to claim wages for the strike period 
the Union representing the workmen must prove 
that the strike was not only legal but was 
justified. The principle recngnised in the decisions 
of the tribunals is that if a strike is not Wegal, 
and is justified, the workmen resorting to such a 
atrike will be entitled to the wages for the period 
of strike. 

So, in the present case it has got to be scen 
whether the strike in queation was justified... The 
justifiability of a atrike depends upon proof of 
several factors, which are among others, (1) 
conduct of employer and also of the employees 
which includes provocation on the part of ۶ 
employer by its high-handed action and un- 
sustainable rensons for the strike on the part. of 
the workmen. (2) the nature of the strike, whether 
penceful or violent is also a relevant fact, and (3) 
whether the strike was resorted to after exhaust- 
ing all the means of redress allowed under the 
law. / 

Now. J shall discuss merits of the case to 
ascertain whether the strike which was launched

apon by the workmen of the present Company on 
-$Uth January 1959 and = was continued till ldth 
March 1959 was justified. As IL have already

was provgked by the management and that it was 
caused also by the refusal of the management to 
(00৮6 to the demands of the workmen as_ per

January 1959 und the strike was launched upon 
on d0th January 1959, 


In view of the ubove facts and circumstances 
disclosed in evidence | come to find that the second 
order of dismissal could not be a reasonable and 
sustuinable ground for the workinen to 8০ on 
strike. The conduct on the part of the employer 
before the strike cannot be looked upon as having 
given provocation for the strike. There was no 
motive for victimiyation or any unfair labour 
practice on the part of the employer to give effect 
to the order of dismissal dated bth December 8 
from 22nd January 1959 in the circumstances 01 
the case. So, the dismissal of these six workmen 
on oth December 1958 or on 22nd January 1959 
cannot be looked upon as a legitimate and reason- 
able ground for the workmen to go on strike from 
80th January 1959 to 16th March 1959. I, there- 
fore, find that the reason for the present strike 
was unreasonable and unsustainable. The 
employer’s conduct cannot be looked upon us 
wiving provocation for the strike. The Union’s 
allegution that Company provoked the strike has 
not been substantiated. Furthermore, 1٤ trans- 
pires from the evidence that the strike was not 
wholly peaceful. There were occasional outbursts 
of violence resulting in assault on an officer of the 
Company and crimial cases against some of the 
strikers which were ultimately withdrawn or not 
proceeded with as a result of the agreement xt. 
۸۱۱ which brought the strike to a close. Tf, 
therefore, hold that the strike resorted to by the 
workmen of the Company from 30th January 1959 
to 15th March 1959 though not illegal was not all 
justified and as such the workmen concerned are 
not entitled to any wages for the period of the 
atrike. Thus T answer this issue against the 
workmen. 


Before | leave, T must add that the Company 
had udvanced a sum of Rs. 20 to each of the 
strikers as an ex-gratia payment as per clause ۵ 
of the agreement, dated 15th March 1959 (Ext. 
A/1 on admission) which ended the strike and on 
the basis of which the workmen returned to their 
work. No further relief is admissible to the work- 
men hy way of wages for the strike period. If 
ig also ndmitted that out of the six dismissed 
workmen the Company took back — Alok Shaw, 
Harinandan Singh (P.W. 2) and Jagdish Jha 
(vide Kxts. H to H/2) and the other 3, namely, 
Rammuni, Lakeman Munia and Kanduri resigned 
their job (vide PLW. 1 7۶۴ Narayan Singh). 
By the agreement Ext. ۸۱۱۰ dated 15th March 
1959, peace and industrial harmony have been 
restored between the Company and the workmen 
after termination of the strike and it is hoped that 
both sides should respect the agreement and act 
well their parts. Under the said agreement only 
the pay for the strike period was referred to this 
Tribunal for adjudication and on evidence — on 
record Tam unable to give any relief to the work- 
men on this count, though T feel that non-payment 
of wages for the strike period would mean a lot 
of hardship to the workmen, The trike being 
not justified in the circumstances _ disclosed in 
evidence, the workmen are not entitled to any 


wages for the strike period as claimed by the 
Union representing the 56011510191).

The present reference relates to a _ dispute 
between Messrs. Nandy & Co. (hereinafter to be 
described as the Company) and their workmen 
represented by the Howrah Small Factories 
Workers’ Union (hereinafter to be described as 
the Union) over the two issues mentioned above. 
The reference, was received by this Tribunal for 
adjudication on 16th Mareh 1960. Due notices 
were served upon the pirties. The Union did not 
file any written statement. On 2196 April 1960) 
Shri N. K. Das, appearing for the Company, stated 
that the matters in dispute referred to ۵٥ 
Tribunal under the aforesaid reference hud been 
amicably settled between the parties outside tha 
Tribunal and that a joint petition would be filed 
hefore this Tribuna) in due course. Several dates 
were fixed for filing the joint petition embodying 
the terms of the alleged settlement and _ for 
necessary orders as the parties did not take any 
steps. Thereafter, the reference was put up on 
2nd August 1960 for hearing in case the joint 
petition for compromise was not filed or no steps 
were taken hy the parties on that date. On 22nd 
August 1960 Shri N, K. Das, Assistant ۱۸۳٣ 
Adviser of the Company and Shri Anadi Dus, 
President of the Union, appeared and intimated 
the Tribunal that the compromise petition had 
heen signed by them and that the same would be 
filed before this Tribunal by 3810٦ August 1960. 


On 318٥ August 1960 Shri বি. .ا‎ Bhanja 
Chowdhury, the Labour Adviser for Howrah 


Nanufacturers’ Association, appeared = and filed 
the petition of compromise along with the copy 
of the terms of the settlement arrived at and 
signed between the parties on 7th April 1960. The 
petition of compromise and the terme of settle- 
should have been filed much earlier before this 
Tribunal and the parties should not have kept the 
Tribunal waiting for so many montha. However, 
when the matters in dispute have been amicably 
settled between the parties and peace and harmony 
have been restored hetween them by virtue of this 
amicable settlement, I do not feel it proper to 
decline to accept the terms of the settlement which 
appear to me to he fair and reasonable. 


T have carefully gone through the terms of the 
settlement. Clause 4 of the settlement read with 
the list of increment of wages of workmen men-

covers issue No. 1 (wages and dearnesa allowance)

settlement. In the joint petition filed on behalf

under the present reference have been amicably

the circumstances, there is no dispute whatsoever

31. The question that arises now is if 
decision of the Enquiry Committee oul he oe 
ported by this Tribunal. [t has been decided by 
the Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of Indian 
Iron & Steel Co., reported in 1958(1) |1 .1., 260 
that the Management of a concern has ower to 
direct its own administration and Tc but 
the power’is not unlimited und when a dispute 
arises, industrial tribunals have been riven the 
power to see whether the termination of servi¢ 
of « workman is justified and to give appropriate 
relief. In cases of dismissal, on misconduct, the 
Tribunal does not act asa court of appeal and 
substitute its own judgment for that of ‘the 
Management. It will interfere (i) when there in 
want of good faith, (ii) when there is victimisa- 
tion or unfair labour practice, (iii) when the 
management has been guilty of a basic error or 
violation of principle of natural justice, and (iv) 
when on the materials the finding is completely 
baseless or perverse. It is for the management to 
determine what | constitutes major misconduct 
within its Standing Orders sufficient (0 merit 
dismissal of a workman, but in determining ৪8018 
misconduct, it must have facts upon which to 
base its conclusions and it must act in good faith 
without caprice or discrimination aud without 
motives of vindictiveness, intimidation or resort- 
ing to uufair labour practice and there must be 
no infraction of the accepted rules of natural 
justice, When the Management does have facts 
from which it can conclude misconduct, its judg- 
ment cannot he questioned, provided the above- 
mentioned principles are not violated. But in the 
absence of these facts or in case of violation of the 
principles set out above, its position is untenable 
The same principles have been accepted hy the 
Hon'ble Supreme Court in the case of G. M uKenzie

“For the unfair labour practices of respondent

employees had the right to strike but they had no 
licence to connmit acts of violence or to seize their 
employer's plant**. The seizure and holding of 
the buildings was itself a wrong apart from any 
acts of sabotage. But in its opal aspect the 
ousting of the owner from luwful possession is not

It is, therefore, clear that any unfair labour 
ractice which the Company might have committed 
by way of non-implementation of the award, will 
not justify the launching of the stay-in-strike by 
the workmen. The learned Advocate for the Union 
laid great stress on the fact of the Company not

October 1957, and it was stated with emphasis 
that this non-implementation of the award was a 
violation of the Industrial Disputes Act and was,

tion on the part of the employer which justified at 
least partially the workmen to launch a stay-in- 
strike. The evidence of Shri Satya Ranjan Sen

in the strike was the non-implementation of the 
award of the Fifth Industrial Tribunal, dated 26th 
September 1957. The witness states in his croas-

and they did not want that a Stay Order should he 
obtained by the Company from the Hon’ble 
Supreme Court and they were under the impression 
that a strike would somehow force the Company 
to implement the award. The Union Secretary 
and the other Union leaders who deposed in this 
case, stated that they all tried their utmost to see 
that there was no untoward incidents during the 
period of the strikes. Even though there was no 
violence, a stay-in-strike is an invasion of the 
rights of the employer and is a grave misconduct 
on the part of the employees. The Hon’ble Judge 
in the case of Sadul Textile Milla observes that 
even without violence a stay-in or sit-down strike 
is an invasion of the rights of the employer in the 
property of the Company and the reason why there 
was no violence in that case seemed to the Hon’ble 
Judge to be due to either the weakness or for- 
bearance of the employer. The Hon'ble Judges 
state that they have little doubt that if the employer 
had insisted on the removal of the striking 
‘employees, there would have been trouble. The 
same principles have been enunciated by the 
Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case of the Punjab 
National Bank and their workmen, reported in 
1959 (IT) L.L.J., 666. The Hon’ble Fades at 
page 686 approved of the decision of the Supreme 
Court of America in the! case of Fansteel Metallur- 
gical ‘Corporation. In this case; as has heen 
mentioned above in the case of Sadul Textile Mills, 
the Hon’ble Court observes that this was not really 
the exercise of the right to strike to which the 
Act referred. It was wholly seizure of the buildings 
in order to prevent their use by the employer in a 
lawful manner and thus by acts of force and 
violence compelled the employer to submit. This 
is exactly what happened in the present case.

| 84. It was next suggested that in view of the 
ecisions of the Hon’ble Supreme Court in the case 
f Model Mills, reported in 1958 (I) L.L.J., 639, 
the cessation of work by the employees on 20th 
November 1957 and on 11 and 12th December 
957, were not strikes under the Industrial 
isputes Act, as they were not in furtherance of 
an industrial dispute. It was pointed out that 
দাদার of an award did not give rise 
ہ‎ an industrial dispute, as the dispute between the 
arties had merged in the award. This argument 
is not worthy of support. This case of Model Mills 
was governed by tie C.P. and Berar Industrial 
‘Disputes Settlement Act, 1947, and not the 
ndustrial Disputes Act. The C.P. Act has its own 
definition for a strike in section 2(27) of the Act. 
The C.P. Act also defines industrial dispute in sec- 
tion 2(12) of the Act and makes a question per- 
taining to a right or claim under an award in an 
industrial dispute. The strikes in question were, 
therefore, strikes under the C.P. Act. Under the 
I,D. Act, a strike means a cessation of work by a 
body of persons employed in an industry acting in 
epmbination. It need not be in connection with an 
Austral dispute. There can be, therefore, no 
৯৬ that the cessations of work by the workmen 
on 20th November 1957 and on {ith and 12th 


December 1957, were strikes under section 2(q) of 
the Industrial Disputes Act. The plea that there 
was no strikes on the dates in question is, there- 
fore, unacceptable.
